Hospital Course:

A 79-year-old male patient presented with chronic, lancinating pain in his tongue, pharynx, and ear on the left side. The pain was triggered by talking, coughing, and swallowing, leading to a decrease in his quality of life. He was diagnosed with Glossopharyngeal neuralgia (GN) and treated with Carbamazepine (CBZ) but later developed diminishing efficacy of the medication with recurrent severe pain.

Diagnosis and Treatment:

Various other medications such as Gabapentin, Pregabalin, and Diazepam were tried, but there was no relief, and the patient developed severe generalized weakness and syncopal episodes. Thus, he was referred to the neurosurgery department for potential surgical intervention. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed an offending vessel compressing the root exit zone (REZ) of the glossopharyngeal nerve. Microvascular decompression (MVD) was performed to remove the compressing vascular loop. Intraoperative monitoring (IONM) including BAEPs and facial MEPs was performed during surgery to prevent postoperative sequelae. A piece of shredded Teflon was inserted to separate the PICA loop and the affected nerves.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient had a successful microvascular decompression (MVD) surgery, and his pain symptoms were relieved. The patient was discharged with mild dysphagia and hoarseness that resolved within two months postoperatively. The patient had an excellent outcome on follow-up 18 months postoperatively, with no recurrence of symptoms.

The patient was discharged from the care of the hospital with instructions to continue taking her medications as prescribed. She was advised to maintain a healthy lifestyle and diet, and to follow up with her primary care physician and dermatologist, as needed.

Follow-up:

The patient was scheduled for outpatient follow-up visits with her primary care physician and dermatologist to monitor the progression of her vitiligo and any potential changes to her AKU diagnosis.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 21-year-old female (G2A1)
Date of Admission:  [date]
Date of Discharge: [date]
Length of Stay: [number] days

Chief complaint: Abnormal pelvic mass and vaginal discharge 

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was admitted to the Tumor Clinic of Ghaem Hospital with the complaint of an abnormal pelvic mass and vaginal discharge. Pelvic ultrasonography revealed the presence of a mixed echogenic mass in the left adnex with multiple internal septation and adhesion to surrounding organs. Pelvic examination also detected a palpable, firm, irregular mass in the posterior vaginal fornix. An exploratory laparotomy was subsequently performed during which a predominant mass situated in the pelvis in the broad ligament was observed. The tumor was soft and friable with hemorrhagic, necrotic, and cystic lesions, and the uterine serosa was coated with the tumor. The tumor infiltrated most of the posterior peritoneal wall. The resected tissue was sent for frozen-section analysis which identified a malignant tumor, probably lymphoma of the pelvis. 

The patient underwent additional tests including a bone marrow aspiration which showed normocellular bone marrow without evidence of metastatic involvement and a bone scan which was negative for metastasis. Permanent sections and immunohistochemical profile with positive immunoreactivity for HMWCK, vimentin, and CD-99 as well as negative immunostaining for LCA, desmin, NSE, and chromogranin allowed the pathologist to distinguish the PNET from other small round cell tumors. 

The patients' tumor was deemed non-resectable, and an aggressive multi-agent chemotherapeutic  regimen including the BEP regimen (Bleomycin, Cisplatinum, and Etoposide) was initiated. Unfortunately, the patient passed away due to pulmonary metastasis 3-4 months after diagnosis. 

The patient was provided with appropriate supportive care throughout their stay in the hospital, including pain control, management of vaginal discharge, and counseling services. The patient's family was kept informed of the clinical situation throughout the patient's hospitalization. 

In summary, the patient presented with an abnormal pelvic mass and vaginal discharge, and was subsequently diagnosed with a non-resectable malignant PNET with pulmonary metastasis. The patient underwent aggressive multi-agent chemotherapeutic regimen but, unfortunately, succumbed to the disease several months after diagnosis. The patient and their family were provided with appropriate supportive care throughout their hospital stay.

Patient: 73-year-old male

Chief Complaint: Fever and Candidemia

Discharge Summary:

Patient is a 58-year-old male with a medical history of hypertension, high cholesterol, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction. The patient underwent coronary artery bypass grafting with lateral internal mammary artery to left anterior descending artery, SVG to first diagonal, ramus intermedius, and right coronary artery one year ago. Post-surgery, the patient had symptoms of shortness of breath, fatigue, and decreased functional capacity. Upon admission to our facility, the patient had unstable angina.

Diagnostic testing revealed native three-vessel atherosclerotic coronary artery disease. The patient had 99% stenosis of mid LAD, 30% stenosis of proximal circumflex, and 100% stenosis of proximal RI. Right heart catheterization showed significant step-up of oxygen saturation from inferior vena cava and underwent right and left heart catheterization which showed native three-vessel atherosclerotic coronary artery disease including 99% mid LAD, 30% proximal circumflex, and 100% proximal RI. There was no hemodynamically significant result from the fractional flow reserve measurement. The LIMA to LAD, and SVGs to D1 and RI were patent. SVG destined to RCA was anastomosed to an anomalous right coronary vein which drained into right atrium. There was a patent SVG to small right coronary vein with flow distal into the right atrium. The RCA coursed immediately subjacent to the right coronary vein, though the graft did not anastomose to the RCA. Approximately 50% focal luminal narrowing of the RCA was immediately subjacent to the aforementioned anomalous vein as above. Luminal reconstitution was appreciated distal to this stenotic segment.

A multidisciplinary “Heart Team” meeting was had during which coiling was decided upon and performed. Coil embolization of the SVG to right coronary vein was performed. Using a Prowater coronary wire, the guide catheter was placed in the proximal and mid segments of the graft and a Direxion 0.021 × 130 cm microcatheter was placed in mid segment of graft. Five diamond-shaped interlock-18 coils (Boston Scientific) were implanted to occlude the shunt.

Post-procedure evaluation showed complete obliteration of iatrogenic aorto-right atrial shunt. The patient's condition improved significantly and he was discharged.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

DOB: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: 15-year postoperative sphenoorbital meningioma

Principal Diagnosis: Recurrent left sphenoorbital meningioma

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our hospital due to progressive proptosis of the left eye. MRI and CT revealed a hyperostotic tumor of the left sphenoid wing with orbital and middle fossa extension compatible with recurrent sphenoorbital meningioma. Preoperative embolization using N-butyl cyanoacrylate was performed 1 day before surgical resection. Subtotal resection was performed, leaving residual tumor in the cavernous sinus and SOF. Postoperative CT showed extensively drilled skull base bone, and no neurological deficits were observed. A lumbar spinal drain was placed for 5 days postoperatively to prevent CSF leaks. Histopathological examination identified the tumor as meningothelial meningioma, World Health Organization grade I. Follow-up MRI showed residual tumor only in the cavernous sinus and SOF.

Course in Hospital:

During the patient's hospital stay, he underwent surgical resection through combined simultaneous transcranial and endoscopic endonasal approaches for aggressive surgical resection with minimized risk of postoperative CSF leakage. The transcranial surgeon approached the tumor through a frontotemporal craniotomy made 15 years earlier, and after drilling out the thickened hyperostotic sphenoid wing and lateral wall of the orbit, further drilling around the SOF and floor of the middle fossa was performed. The endoscopic endonasal surgeon prepared a pedicled nasoseptal flap and employed the transmaxillary transpterygoid approach to remove the tumor expanding laterally in the sphenoid sinus. The tumor-involved dura was resected and repaired with a free graft of fascia lata, and the large bone defect of the sphenoid sinus was covered with a free graft of fascia lata and fixed with fibrin glue. The NSF was secured with placed Surgicel® and buttressed by gauze packing in the sphenoid sinus.

Discharge Disposition:

The patient was discharged to home.

Condition at Discharge:

At the time of discharge, the patient was in stable condition and had no neurological deficits.

Instructions:

The patient was instructed to follow up with his primary care physician for further evaluation and care. The patient was also instructed to follow up with his ophthalmologist for further evaluation of his left eye.

Follow-up:

The patient was to return for a follow-up appointment with his primary care physician and his ophthalmologist in three months.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 70-year-old African-American man, presented to the hospital with complaints of increased shortness of breath and lower extremity edema. Upon admission, he was diagnosed with congestive heart failure exacerbation. During the hospital stay, he developed new-onset pancytopenia, which was attributed to hyperthyroidism. The patient was started on methimazole, which improved his cell counts. However, he did not present for further follow-up visits and stopped taking methimazole after a few weeks.

One year later, the patient presented to the hospital with fatigue, weight loss, failure to thrive, and acute kidney injury. The physical exam revealed diffuse nontender enlargement of the thyroid gland and mild tremors. The patient also had warm and moist skin with mild jaundice. Labs showed abnormal levels of serum creatinine, TSH, FT4, WBC, hemoglobin, MCV, RDW, platelets, bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, folic acid, and vitamin B12. Peripheral smear was notable for marked anisocytosis and some spherocytes, but no schistocytes.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which was believed to be a complication of Graves' disease.

Treatment:

The patient was treated with glucocorticoids (prednisone 70 mg/day) and folic acid. Additionally, the diagnosis of Graves' disease was confirmed by elevated levels of thyroid stimulating immunoglobulins and diffuse thyromegaly and increased uptake on radioactive iodine thyroid uptake and scan. The patient underwent radioactive iodine ablation with 21.6 mCi of I-131 and was started on methimazole 10 mg/day.

Follow-up:

The patient's hemoglobin improved with medical treatment and he did not require blood transfusion. At the 6-month follow-up, his lab work showed improvement in his hemoglobin levels, TSH, and FT4 on methimazole. Methimazole was stopped and the patient was started on thyroxine.

Disposition:

The patient was discharged with instructions to continue taking thyroxine and follow-up with his primary care physician regularly.

Patient Name: [redacted]

Gender: Male

Age: 51

Discharge Date: [redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: Diffuse-type giant cell tumor of bone

Discharge Diagnosis: Diffuse-type giant cell tumor of bone, status post transfemoral amputation and post-operative chemotherapy.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 51-year-old male, presented with a history of pain and swelling below his left knee, along with repeated episodes of fever. On examination, a firm mass of 30*18*12 cm was observed at the upper part of tibia, along with a large discharging ulcer of 12 cm diameter anteriorly with necrotic areas. Pulsations of dorsalis pediis, posterior tibial and popliteal arteries were present. Plain radiography showed a large lesion in the left tibia with soft tissue opacity, suggesting a tumor, possibly an enchondroma, osteosarcoma or chondrosarcoma with extensions into the soft tissue of proximal leg. Tc99m radio isotope bone scan showed increased tracer uptake in the shaft of the left tibia and proximal soft tissue with no skeletal metastasis.

Due to financial constraints, MRI was not done. Based on presentation and radiographic appearance, differential diagnoses included osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma of tibia.

The patient was started on intravenous antibiotics and analgesics, and counselled on different treatment options. The patient opted for transfermoral amputation as treatment modality, followed by post-operative chemotherapy.

The cut section from the amputated leg revealed a gray-white tumor measuring 28*16*10 cm involving the upper half of tibia and fibula with haemorrhagic, necrotic and focal myxoid characteristics, and soft tissue extension up to the knee. Microscopy revealed tumor tissues arranged in small and large irregular lobules of hyaline cartilage. The chondrocytes showed atypia and spindling. Section from tissue surrounding the necrotic area showed spindle cells arranged in interlacing bundles, fascicles and a focal storiform pattern with many tumor giant cells present, which led to the diagnosis of diffuse-type giant cell tumor of bone.

Following amputation, the patient received intravenous antibiotics and analgesics, and was administered Cisplatin and Doxorubicin as a first line chemotherapy. A soft elastic dressing was applied with regular changes monitored for signs of infection. Exercises were initiated to prevent contractures and strengthen the upper extremity, and isometric muscle training of the residual limb was started. Discharge Summary:

Patient: 47-year-old male

Admission Date: N/A

Discharge Date: N/A

Diagnosis: Benign left intraorbital mass of angiomatous nature

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with progressive diplopia lasting 4 months, and ophthalmological examination revealed a marked hypofunction of the left inferior oblique muscle. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed an intraorbital, extraconal, oval, capsulated mass measuring 2.0 × 1.5 cm, located inferomedially in the anterior part of the left orbit. The provisional radiological diagnosis was benign tumour with a high vascular component.

Surgical operation was performed to remove the tumour. The postoperative course was uneventful, and neither diplopia nor alterations of extrinsic ocular motility were observed. After 3 years of follow-up, the patient is free from disease.

Macroscopy revealed the tumour as a well-circumscribed nodule of 1.5 × 2.0 cm in diameter with a brown coloration. At histology, the neoplasm showed a well-circumscribed, capsulated, expansive growth, formed by a cell proliferation arranged in vascular trabecular features, or in solid cords. The cells were plump and large, showing an epithelioid phenotype with vesicular round nuclei, nucleoli, and a low mitotic activity. The cells showed a clear or finely granular cytoplasm, sometimes containing a granular brown pigment. No necrosis was observed.

A panel of histochemical and immunohistochemical staining was performed, and the histological diagnosis was a myomelanocytic tumour or melanocytoma belonging to the Perivascular Epithelioid Cell neoplasms (PEComas) group without true evidence of malignancy.

Conclusion:

The patient was diagnosed with a benign left intraorbital mass of angiomatous nature. The tumour was successfully removed through surgical operation, and the postoperative course was uneventful. The patient is now free from disease. Due to its infrequent location, the case was sent in consultation and confirmed to be a myomelanocytic tumour or melanocytoma belonging to the Perivascular Epithelioid Cell neoplasms (PEComas) group without true evidence of malignancy.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification: 78-year-old female with L1 osteoporotic vertebral collapse

Hospital Course:
The patient was referred to our hospital after two months of conservative treatments by the former doctor. The patient's chief complaints were severe back pain, motor weakness, and pain of bilateral lower limbs, and bladder-bowel dysfunction. Upon evaluation, the patient was diagnosed with both myelopathy and cauda equina syndrome, including sensory loss below T10 dermatome, bilateral positive Babinski reflex, hyporeflexia and motor weakness of the bilateral lower extremities, and neurogenic bladder.

Diagnostic Results:
The plain X-rays confirmed L1 vertebral collapse with an intra-vertebral cleft. The patient was then referred for MRIs that showed dorsal epidural soft tissue mass that caused posterior compression of the spinal cord at T9-T12 levels. There was continuity observed between the intra-vertebral cleft and epidural soft tissue mass on the MRIs, and both contained some amount of gas inside.

Treatment:
The patient underwent one-stage posterior surgery to cure lumbar canal stenosis, thoracic epidural hematoma, and L1 vertebral collapse. Posterior decompression at L3-4 and L4-L5 was performed, followed by partial laminectomy at T9 and T12, and laminectomy at T10-T11. This was followed by removal of the epidural soft tissue mass, which was surrounded by a capsule and fibrous tissue and contained coagulated blood and reddish-brown fluid. Posterior segmental instrumentation was performed at T11-L2, and transpediclar vertebroplasty was performed using the calcium phosphate cement. After decortication of the posterolateral fusion bed, a mixture of local bone and bone graft substitute was grafted. A brace was used for two months after surgery.

Outcome:
At postoperative 12 months, posterolateral bony fusion was achieved, back pain and neurological symptoms were completely resolved, and the patient was able to walk without a cane. The operation time was 240 minutes, and intraoperative blood loss was 571g.

Follow-up:
The patient will be scheduled for follow-up appointments to monitor any future developments.

Hospital Course Summary:
This is a summary of the hospital course for a 69-year-old male patient who was admitted for poor hemodynamics and recurrent dizziness and ventricular tachycardia after implantation of a HeartWare HVAD as destination therapy for ischemic cardiomyopathy.

Initial Assessment:
Upon admission, the patient's LVAD speed was set to 3000 RPM due to mild biventricular filling pressure elevation and a cardiac index below 2.0 L/min/m² seen on pulmonary artery catheter monitoring. However, he developed intermittent symptoms of dizziness and ventricular tachycardia, which prevented rehabilitation.

Diagnostic Workup:
The patient underwent physical examination, echocardiography, and CT angiogram with 3D reconstruction. Based on the findings, there was a possibility of inflow cannula obstruction or outflow graft kinking that might be responsible for abnormal baseline hemodynamics at rest and suction with positional change.

Treatment and Management:
The patient was brought to the cardiac catheterization laboratory for an invasive assessment. Intracardiac echocardiography was performed, and at 3000 RPM, there was no aortic valve opening. The inflow cannula was septal-facing but normal flow was observed. There was suction with interruption of flow in the inflow cannula seen in a sitting position, which also occurred at 2800 RPM. No suction occurred at 2600 RPM.

Diagnostic Finding:
A multipurpose guide catheter and high-fidelity micromanometer wire were used to measure the pressure gradient across the obstruction in the outflow graft. The pressure drop across the kink was measured at 20 mmHg at 3000 RPM, which decreased to 16 mmHg in a sitting position. There was no flow deficit with sitting at 2600 RPM. Therefore, changes in the outflow graft obstruction were unlikely to increase the risk of suction events, and no intervention was chosen.

Discharge Plan:
The patient experienced an improvement in orthostatic symptoms with speed changes and was managed with medical therapy. However, intermittent symptomatic ventricular arrhythmias continued, requiring ventricular tachycardia ablation. An appropriate follow-up plan is recommended.

After tracheal intubation, the surgery lasted for approximately 7 hours, during which vital signs were adequately maintained. After completion of surgery, the neuromuscular blockade was reversed, and the patient was extubated in the operation room. The patient was then transferred to the intensive care unit with continued monitoring.

Severe kyphosis due to spinal tuberculosis.

The patient was transferred to the general ward without any significant problems. Hospital Course:
A 48-year-old female patient was admitted to the emergency department due to a stab wound of the neck region. The rescue team leader informed us that the patient had attempted to commit suicide. The neck injury exploration was then conducted, and a tangential damage to the tunica adventitia of the esophagus was addressed with simple monolayer interrupted stitches. After a seven-day hospital stay, the patient was discharged to a psychiatric hospital with a follow-up visit scheduled for ten days after the surgery to remove the stitches. No complications were noted during the stay or follow-up visit. In the meantime, the patient is advised to follow-up and continue therapy with the psychiatric hospital for further treatment and management of suicidal thoughts and behaviors.

FINAL DIAGNOSIS:
Small cell carcinoma of the lung with tumor lysis syndrome.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted with complaints of generalized fatigue, anorexia, worsening abdominal distension and right upper quadrant pain, which had been ongoing for 5 weeks. On admission, the patient was noted to have an ill-appearing appearance and bilateral enlarged supraclavicular lymph nodes. Physical examination showed marked hepatomegaly extending more than 10 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory findings revealed acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, and high-normal inorganic phosphorus level, suggestive of tumor lysis syndrome (TLS). Imaging studies showed hepatic masses with multilevel vertebral body metastases, extensive bilateral supraclavicular, mediastinal, hilar and retroperitoneal adenopathy, suggestive of either lymphoma or metastatic solid tumor. A peripheral blood flow cytometry was negative for lymphoma or any hematological malignancy, while a supraclavicular lymph node biopsy revealed small cell carcinoma. With aggressive intravenous hydration, insulin administration, potassium binders and rasburicase, as well as the use of chemotherapy, the patient's renal and electrolyte abnormalities showed correction in the subsequent days.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
The patient's condition has improved after receiving five out of six planned cycles of chemotherapy. Follow-up continued to be scheduled in the outpatient clinics.

Hospital Course:

A 42-year-old male was admitted to the hospital with progressive dyspnea. He had a history of smoking, and upon physical examination, recurrent oral and genital ulcers were detected. The initial laboratory examination revealed mild leukocytosis and elevated levels of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP).

Diagnostic Testing:

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and transesophageal echocardiography were performed, which revealed mitral valve prolapse (MVP) and severe mitral regurgitation. The patient underwent positron emission tomography (PET) to evaluate the possibility of inflammatory involvement of Behçet's disease, given his recurrent ulcers and elevated ESR and CRP. PET revealed increased uptake along the mitral annulus.

Treatment and Intervention:

The patient was treated with prednisolone for 2 weeks before undergoing mitral valve replacement with a St. Jude #29 valve. Pathologic examination of the valve revealed infiltration of inflammatory cells composed of lymphocytes.

Follow-up and Outcome:

The laboratory examination was performed every three months, and after 3 months, the levels of ESR and CRP decreased. Following the successful operation, the patient continued to take prednisolone and azathioprine and was maintained on anticoagulation. However, 15 months after the operation, the patient was readmitted to the hospital with fever and severe dyspnea. TTE revealed detachment of the prosthetic mitral valve from the annulus and displacement into the left atrium. The levels of ESR and CRP were greatly elevated, suggesting the possibility of reactivation of mitral annular inflammation. The patient experienced severe pulmonary edema and secondary pneumonia and passed away seven days later.

Summary:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with progressive dyspnea, and upon physical examination, multiple recurrent oral and genital ulcers were detected. TTE and transesophageal echocardiography revealed MVP and severe mitral regurgitation with aneurysmal changes of the aortic valve. PET revealed strong uptake along the mitral annulus, and the patient underwent mitral valve replacement with a St. Jude #29 valve following prednisolone treatment. The patient continued to take prednisolone and azathioprine with anticoagulation after the successful operation. However, 15 months later, the patient was readmitted with severe dyspnea and fever, and displacements of the prosthetic mitral valve and greatly elevated levels of ESR and CRP were observed. The patient developed severe pulmonary edema and secondary pneumonia and passed away seven days later.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: N/A
Age: 66-year-old female
Admission Date: N/A
Discharge Date: N/A

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 66-year-old African-American woman with a history of bilateral lung transplantation with distant history of breast cancer who presented to our clinic with progressive shortness of breath, wheezing, and cough of 2 months’ duration. Following admission, the patient was found to have pancytopenia, hypertension, stage IV chronic kidney disease, and diabetes.

During her stay, the patient's CT scan revealed a new endobronchial lesion in the left mainstem near the anatomic anastomosis. A diagnostic bronchoscopy demonstrated a fibrinous mass protruding into the left mainstem proximal to the anastomosis. Histopathology demonstrated fragments of partially necrotic granulation tissue with extensive inflammation. GMS staining demonstrated intracellular bacilli and the AFB stain highlighted numerous intracellular AFB. The tissue culture and bronchial wash grew MAC, which was identified as the causative organism.

The patient was initiated on therapy with azithromycin, ethambutol, and rifampin, but rifampin was exchanged for moxifloxacin nearly immediately due to concerns about a possible significant interaction with her calcineurin inhibitor. She continued on triple therapy with azithromycin, ethambutol, and moxifloxacin for the first 2 months, although she experienced significant nausea and anorexia and developed visual disturbances with bilateral optic neuritis approximately 2 months after initiation of therapy. Ethambutol was immediately discontinued. She continued on dual therapy with azithromycin and moxifloxacin for the remainder of her antibiotic course, although she continued to have intermittent nausea, diarrhea, and poor appetite. After several negative sputum cultures, her therapy was discontinued approximately 12 months following initiation.

When the patient was discharged from the hospital, her visual disturbances had nearly resolved, but unfortunately, her long-standing chronic kidney disease secondary to calcineurin inhibitor use and diabetes did progress over time. Approximately 7 months following completion of her MAC therapy, she developed the need for hemodialysis. She died from complications of end-stage renal disease and hemodialysis 6 months later.

The patient was diagnosed with Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection of the respiratory system that was discovered after presenting with progressive shortness of breath, wheezing, and cough.

The patient is to follow up with her primary care physician and nephrologist for ongoing management of her chronic kidney disease and diabetes. Hospital Course:
A 36-year-old female with a history of placenta previa and placenta accreta underwent an elective caesarean section at our hospital at 38 weeks gestation. The patient had previously undergone two caesarean sections, one of which was due to placenta previa.

Procedure:
During the surgery, there was difficulty in removing the placenta from the uterine wall, leading to a diagnosis of placental invasion anomaly. Retroperitoneal dissection was performed to visualize the retroperitoneal vessels and bilateral hypogastric artery ligation was performed 5 cm distal of the arteria iliaca communis bifurcation. The placenta was subsequently removed from the uterine cavity with minimal cutting of placental tissues using a metzenbaum. Bleeding in the cervical region was observed, necessitating placement of a Bakri balloon to control bleeding.

Postoperative Care:
The patient's hematocrit level decreased from 30.2 before the operation to 26.8 after the operation. Pain management was provided with 50mg Pethidin administered every 6 hours and two applications of Diclofenac sodium. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 3. Follow-up transvaginal ultrasonography showed no residual placental mass in the uterus. The patient remained asymptomatic during the puerperium period, with a beta human chorionic gonadotropin level of 5mUI/mL in the 40th postpartum day.

Impression:
The patient had a successful elective caesarean section with bilateral hypogastric artery ligation performed due to placenta increta. Bleeding control was established via placement of a Bakri balloon and the patient was discharged home in stable condition.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 41-year-old female with a BMI of 31, diagnosed with stage II carcinoma of the right breast. She underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by bilateral total skin sparing mastectomies with immediate reconstruction using tissue expanders and acellular dermal matrix (ADM). On post-operative day 18, the patient developed bilateral breast seromas, requiring needle aspiration. Mild erythema was noted, and a ten-day course of oral antibiotics was started. Aspiration was performed again on the right side two days later. Both seroma cultures grew Mucor colonies (few colonies). Antifungal therapy was initiated, and tight glycemic control was maintained by the endocrinologist.

On post-operative day 23, dehiscence was noted at the apex of her vertical incision abutting the areola, with an area of skin necrosis from mastectomy skin flap ischemia. Debridement of the skin and closure of the wound was performed, preserving the tissue expander and ADM. Subcutaneous tissue and fluid cultures were positive for Mucor. Antifungal therapy was switched, and the patient received repeat seroma aspiration over the next 3 weeks.

The patient required additional right breast seroma aspirations, two more times over the next 3 weeks. Her recurrent seromas resolved, but three months later, her right breast cellulitis recurred, which again responded to IV antibiotics. Thereafter, her healing became uneventful, and she completed a one-year course of antifungal. Bilateral tissue expander exchange was performed, followed by monitoring by infectious disease consultants. Post-operatively two years later, the patient has had no recurrent infections. She is currently 3 years after her second-stage breast reconstruction and doing well.

Summary:
The patient with a history of breast cancer underwent bilateral total skin sparing mastectomies with immediate reconstruction using tissue expanders and ADM. Post-operative bilateral breast seromas were identified requiring needle aspiration with Mucor growth. Antifungal therapy, close follow-up of glycemic control, and infectious disease consultation were initiated with repeat seroma aspirations and antibiotics required. Eventually, the patient underwent bilateral tissue expander exchange and had no further infections identified.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 30-year-old female

Chief Complaint: Intermittent pain in relation to lower left back tooth region for the past 20 days

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with a complaint of intermittent pain in relation to lower left back tooth region for the past 20 days. The patient had a history of mandibular left third molar tooth extraction a few weeks back, following which the patient developed pain in the extracted region. The patient underwent surgical excision of the lesion, and tissue was sent for histopathological examination. Microscopically, granulation tissue exhibiting fibroblasts, numerous vascular spaces, multinucleated giant cells and an intense inflammatory cell infiltrate, predominantly neutrophils were seen.

Diagnosis and Treatment:

A provisional diagnosis of post extraction granuloma was made. The tissue was examined histopathologically, and the presence of numerous thin walled yellow-brown ring and band–like structures of varying sizes suggestive of foreign bodies were noted. These structures appeared refractile under polarizing light. The patient underwent surgical excision of the lesion, and the foreign bodies were removed.

Conclusion:

The patient suffered from a foreign body reaction as a result of the presence of foreign bodies within the extracted tooth socket. The foreign bodies were removed surgically, and the patient was discharged from the hospital after recovery.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 17-year-old female with a long-standing history of fibrostenotic Crohn's disease necessitating ileocecostomy who presented with worsening abdominal pain and increased stool frequency. The patient was prescribed methotrexate for enteropathic arthritis and reported increased fatigue. Physical examination showed mild abdominal tenderness. CT enterography revealed active inflammation of the ileum and multiple small branching low-density areas in the liver and near the porta hepatis, suggestive of small fluid collections versus thrombosed peripheral veins.

Diagnosis:

The patient was admitted to the hospital for broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic therapy due to concern for CD exacerbation and hepatic abscesses. Laboratory workup revealed elevated C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate. A coagulation panel showed elevated D-dimer and elevated fibrinogen. Further testing ruled out portal, mesenteric, and splenic vein thrombosis. A liver ultrasound with Doppler was performed and demonstrated small, ill-defined, echogenic areas near the porta hepatis and in the inferior aspect of the right lobe of the liver, corresponding to the low attenuation area on the CT enterography, with sonographic appearance most consistent with focal fatty infiltration. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen with fat saturation confirmed that the hepatic lesions represented focal areas of fatty deposition.

Treatment:

The patient's blood cultures did not grow any organisms. Methotrexate was optimized at 25 mg per week, and intravenous antibiotics were discontinued. The patient was discharged home on a taper of budesonide.

Outcome:

The patient tolerated the treatment well and had a satisfactory response. On discharge, the patient was instructed to maintain a healthy diet and regular exercise. Follow-up with gastroenterology and rheumatology was arranged.

Patient: 35-year-old female with a history of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), recurrent miscarriages, and a marker chromosome. 

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with hirsutism and menstrual irregularity. Physical examination revealed a history of early miscarriages and an intramural myoma myomectomy operation. The patient had also experienced disc hernia and peptic ulcer. She had been married for seven years and had undergone intrauterine insemination twice.

The patient's ultrasonography showed polycystic ovary appearance, but the uterus and endometrium were normal. Chromosome analysis on peripheral blood revealed a marker chromosome: 47XX+m. On the second day of menstruation, hormonal analysis was performed, which revealed AMH- 6.4 ng / mL; Estradiol- 52.23 pg / mL; FSH- 6.16 mIU / mL; Lh- 21.22 mIU / mL; Prolactin- 10.35 ng / mL and TSH- 0.99 μIU / mL. Based on the patient's history, PCOS was considered to be the most likely diagnosis. 

Treatment:
After genetic consultation, the patient's polycystic ovary appearance, recurrent miscarriages, and marker chromosome were taken into consideration, and IVF and preimplantation genetic diagnosis were planned. 

Follow-up:
The patient will continue to be monitored on an outpatient basis. Further treatment may be required depending on the results of the planned IVF and preimplantation genetic diagnosis. 

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in a stable condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Not provided
Date of Admission: Not provided
Date of Discharge: Not provided

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with complaints of sudden onset isolated foot drop on the left side. Initial physical examination at an outpatient clinic in another hospital revealed left foot drop as the sole sign. A nerve conduction study showed normal parameters, however, the needle EMG study revealed decreased maximal voluntary effort recruitment in the left anterior tibialis and extensor hallucis longus. Lumbar MRI showed no abnormal findings and a diagnosis of foot drop caused by peripheral neural lesions was given, along with physiotherapy treatment.

The patient returned to our outpatient clinic after two months with progressive symptoms. A neurological examination revealed increased Achilles reflex, absence of left superficial abdominal reflex, and Babinski sign on the left side which indicated a central cause of foot drop. Cerebral MRI was ordered, which revealed a right parasagittal meningioma (4 × 5 × 6 cm). Brain surgery was performed to remove the tumor and the histopathological finding determined a diagnosis of meningothelial meningioma. During an 18-month postoperative follow-up, the patient showed improvement in their muscle power.

Clinical diagnoses:
1. Foot drop caused by peripheral neural lesions
2. Meningothelial meningioma

Hospital outcomes:
1. Diagnosis of foot drop by peripheral neural lesions
2. Diagnosis of meningothelial meningioma
3. Brain surgery to remove the tumor noted
4. Improvement in muscle power reflected.

Patient was discharged to continue with follow-up appointments with their primary care provider.

Hospital Course Summary: 

Patient is a 34-year-old Japanese man who presented to the hospital with an incidentally detected renal tumor. No significant past medical history was noted, and the patient had no family history of renal cell carcinoma or any signs of hereditary renal cell carcinoma syndrome during examination. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) confirmed the presence of a 2.5 cm left kidney tumor along with a presumptive diagnosis of retroperitoneal liposarcoma.

Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a tumor located in the interaortocaval space with high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. Left partial nephrectomy and resection of the retroperitoneal tumor were performed, and the pathological diagnoses were clear cell renal carcinoma and retroperitoneal liposarcoma. No adjuvant treatment was performed, and the surgical margins of both tumors were negative.

Over the ten years of follow-up, the patient did not experience a recurrence or metastasis. The patient's age did not suggest any hereditary RCC syndrome. Additionally, the case was unique as most previously reported cases of concurrent liposarcoma and RCC were found in males diagnosed with papillary cell RCC. Our patient's RCC histology was clear cell, and his liposarcoma was located in the interaortocaval space.

Follow-up is still necessary as late recurrences with liposarcoma are common, although generally, the prognosis after complete excision is good. Retroperitoneal liposarcomas have been classified into several clinico-pathological subtypes, and five-year and ten-year disease-specific survival is the highest for well-differentiated liposarcoma (100% and 87%). Pleomorphic liposarcoma has the lowest survival rate of 56% and 39%.

Overall the patient had no significant complications during their hospital stay and was discharged in a stable condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: March 2014

Discharge Date: Day 8 of hospitalization

Diagnosis: Suspected leptospirosis with rhabdomyolysis

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 27-year-old male, presented to the emergency department with symptoms of back pain, chills, fever, headache, eye pain, and arthralgia. Physical examination revealed jaundice and icteric sclera, dry oral mucosa, and tender calves. Laboratory tests indicated thrombocytopenia, elevated total bilirubin, and creatinine phosphokinase (CPK). Urinalysis showed hematuria and bilirubinemia. The initial diagnosis was suspected leptospirosis with rhabdomyolysis.

The patient was hospitalized and treated with IV ceftriaxone and fluid replacement. Approximately 24 hours after arrival at the hospital, his thrombocytopenia worsened, and serum creatinine and LFTs were elevated. On day 2 of hospitalization, the patient had vomiting, further elevation of serum creatinine and LFTs, and an increase in CPK. Treatment with ceftriaxone and fluid replacement continued, and antiemetics were given. On day 3, the patient remained afebrile, and the platelet count stabilized. CPK decreased, and the patient's symptoms improved. Vomiting stopped, but jaundice and icteric sclera persisted through day 4. A renal sonogram on day 5 showed fluid along the right upper quadrant. The patient was discharged home on day 8.

Tests for Hepatitis A, B, and C and blood cultures were negative. A leptospirosis IgM antibody test was negative. However, Leptospira interrogans DNA was detected by PCR in a serum specimen collected on day 3. The serum collected upon discharge had a reciprocal MAT titer of 1,600 against serogroup Bataviae (serovar Bataviae).

Summary:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with suspected leptospirosis with rhabdomyolysis, which was supported by laboratory findings. The patient's condition was treated with ceftriaxone and fluid replacement, and he showed improvement over the course of his hospitalization. Further tests showed evidence of Leptospira interrogans DNA in a serum specimen, and the serum collected upon discharge had a high titer of antibodies against serogroup Bataviae. The patient was discharged on day 8 of hospitalization with instructions for a follow-up appointment with his primary care provider.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 70-year-old man, was admitted to the clinic with a gait problem and obvious disturbance three months after he had a foot slip while running. On physical examination, he was found to have a swollen ankle with a loss of the Achilles contour. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was subsequently conducted, and it indicated an Achilles tendon rupture. The patient underwent surgery to fix this problem.

Hospital Course Details:
The surgical procedure was performed under general anesthesia with a regional block. The surgical approach was conducted through a mid-axial incision, and the surgeon discovered that the distal stump of the tendon was fragile and ragged. A 7-cm half-width of Achilles tendon was taken to serve as a reconstructive graft, which was then inserted into the calcaneal prominence and secured using a double-strand Bunnell fashion. A double-core Bunnell/modified Kessler suturing technique was used to suture the graft to the proximal Achilles stump using polypropylene 1-0. The patient's ankle was then immobilized in a below-knee circular cast for six weeks. 

Follow-up and Final Outcome:
During the six weeks in the cast, the patient performed isometric muscle contraction exercises and was trained to perform active ankle stretching. He then participated in a graduated full weight-bearing program. The patient was able to walk normally six months after surgery and stand on tip-toe. However, he experienced light pain on the anterior dorsum of the ankle when walking down stairs. Nonetheless, he was able to climb steps normally without any discomfort.

Summary:
A 70-year-old man underwent surgery due to an Achilles tendon rupture resulting from a foot slip while running. A 7-cm half-width of Achilles tendon was taken to serve as a reconstructive graft, which was used to connect the distal stump to the calcaneal prominence. After a period of immobilization, the patient gradually participated in a graduated full weight-bearing program. At a follow-up six months after surgery, the patient was able to walk normally and stand on tip-toe, but experienced slight pain when walking down stairs. Nonetheless, he was able to climb steps normally without any discomfort.

An immunological examination revealed that the levels of serum IgG and IgG4 were within normal ranges (Table).

Imaging:

CT showed perihilar and distal bile duct stenosis and wall thickening without swelling or abnormal enhancement of the pancreas. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography showed perihilar and distal bile duct stenosis, but the main pancreatic duct was normal. Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography showed a slight uptake by the distal bile duct. Intraductal ultrasonography showed circular-symmetric wall thickening at the perihilar and distal bile ducts. ERCP showed perihilar and distal bile duct stenosis.

Treatment:

Based on the findings, a preoperative diagnosis of perihilar and distal bile duct cancer was made, and the patient underwent left hepatectomy and pancreaticoduodenectomy.

Diagnosis:

A histopathological examination revealed lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis in the perihilar and distal bile duct. Lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, inflammatory change, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis were shown in the pancreas. A final diagnosis of IgG4-SC with AIP was made based on the histological and immunohistochemical findings.

Hospital Course:

This 64-year-old female presented to dialysis after missing three sessions, and was noted to be lethargic and experiencing twitching in her extremities. After experiencing a convulsive seizure, she was intubated and received a loading dose of levetiracetam. Continuous EEG was on the ictal-interictal continuum, showing extended runs of generalized periodic discharges. Despite electrographic improvement, the patient was arousable only to significant noxious stimuli and did not follow commands.

Physical Examination:

Patient's gaze was conjugate, and pupils sluggishly reactive to light. The patient's bilateral corneal, oculocephalic, and cough reflexes were intact. The patient also exhibited a triple flexion in her right lower extremity, subtle withdrawal in the left lower and bilateral upper extremities, and had reflexes that were 2+ in the upper extremities and absent in the lower extremities. The patient's Babinski sign was positive bilaterally. She also had a bilateral Hoffman’s sign.

Imaging Studies:

Initial head CT scan demonstrated hypodensities concerning for brainstem and cerebellar white matter edema in a diffuse and symmetric pattern. A brain MRI demonstrated T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inverted recovery (FLAIR) confluent hyperintensities in the pons, bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles (with associated restricted diffusion), cerebellar hemispheres, periventricular and subcortical matter, extending down to the medulla and proximal spinal cord. Patchy hyperintense signals were also seen in the bilateral corona radiata, and left insula with restricted diffusion. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) was negative for any abnormalities.

Diagnosis:

The differential diagnosis included PRES secondary to hypertension, infarcts secondary to basilar occlusion, metabolic encephalopathy, and infectious encephalitis. Based on the MRI findings and a concern for PRES, the patient was initiated on aggressive blood pressure control with a systolic blood pressure goal of less than 180 mmHg with hydralazine, carvedilol, and lisinopril.

History of Present Illness:
The patient, a 53-year-old African American female, presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of upper and lower extremity weakness and paresthesias.

Past Medical History:
The patient had a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, pulmonary hypertension, nonischemic cardiomyopathy, and systolic heart failure.

Medications:
The patient was taking simvastatin, furosemide, digoxin, carvedilol, lisinopril, spironolactone, insulin, ferrous sulfate, and potassium chloride.

Hospital Course:
Upon admission, the patient displayed flaccid paralysis in both upper and lower extremities, with normal cranial nerves and sensation. Lab results indicated an acute renal failure, hyperkalemia, and low sodium and carbon dioxide levels. Electrocardiogram revealed a first-degree atrioventricular block with peaked T waves. The administration of calcium gluconate, regular insulin plus dextrose, and sodium bicarbonate initiated therapy. Repeat labs showed improvements in serum potassium levels, and neuromuscular symptoms and ECG returned to baseline within 24 hours of presentation. Serum potassium returned to normal levels at approximately 36 hours.

Outcome:
Upon discharge, lisinopril, spironolactone, and potassium chloride were discontinued, and hydralazine and isosorbide mononitrate were initiated. Appropriate follow-up was scheduled to monitor the patient's renal function and electrolyte balance.

Discharge Summary:

Reason for Admission: Surgical correction of a left superficial femoral artery aneurysm.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 43-year-old male with a past medical history of Crohn's disease, was admitted for surgical correction of a left SFA aneurysm. The patient had been previously diagnosed with CD in 2008, which had led to occasional oral ulceration, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea. In 2011, the patient was diagnosed with CD-related spondyloarthritis, and in 2014, the patient experienced myopericarditis. The patient was taking sulfasalazine 1000 mg twice daily at the time of admission.

One month prior to admission, the patient presented to another hospital with a 5-day history of low-grade fever, asthenia, oral ulcers, and painful edema of the left lower limb. An abdominal CT angiogram showed deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the left popliteal vein and bilateral SFA aneurysms. The patient was started on rivaroxaban and referred to our facility for further evaluation.

Upon physical examination, the patient had multiple oral ulcers, left lower limb edema, and a pulsatile mass with an overlying bruit on the left thigh. The patient's laboratory tests revealed an inflammatory anemia and high acute phase reactants. Various tests were negative for HIV, hepatotropic viruses, HLA-B51, HLA-B27, cryoglobulins, rheumatoid factor, complement, the pathergy test, and antinuclear, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic, and antiphospholipid antibodies.

Surgical correction of the left SFA aneurysm was immediately pursued due to its size, which posed an increased risk of rupture. Bypass surgery with aneurysm resection and a polytetrafluoroethylene interposition graft was performed without complications. Histology of the aneurysm revealed leukocytoclastic vasculitis of the vasa vasorum with accompanying transmural infiltration of PMNs and fibrinoid necrosis of the intimal layer.

After surgery, the patient was diagnosed with Behçet syndrome with active mucosal and vascular involvement and treated with 6-monthly intravenous pulses of cyclophosphamide 1 g, followed by azathioprine and bypass surgery of the contralateral SFA aneurysm. Three months into therapy, the patient's liver function tests prompted the discontinuation of azathioprine.

At 1-year follow-up, the patient was in remission while on infliximab 5 mg/kg every 8 weeks, low-dose prednisolone (2.5 mg/day), and rivaroxaban 20 mg/day.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 70-year-old male with symptomatic sinus node dysfunction and normal coronaries.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with recurrent episodes of unprovoked syncope. After admitting the patient and obtaining informed consent for permanent pacemaker implantation, LBBP was attempted. The attempt to deploy a 4.1-French lumenless 3830 SelectSecure™ lead failed at the first site, which was 1.5 cm below the His bundle along the imaginary line joining the distal His bundle signal to the RV apex. After positioning a C315 sheath 2 cm inferior to the previously attempted site toward the RV apex, five rapid turns allowed successful placement of the pacing lead deep inside the septum, capturing the left posterior fascicle. The unipolar pacing impedance was 680 Ω, and the capture threshold was 0.5 V at a 0.6-ms pulse width. The atrial lead was positioned at the right atrial appendage. The patient recovered well after implantation and was discharged the next day without any complications.

Diagnosis:
Symptomatic sinus node dysfunction

Treatment:
Permanent pacemaker implantation with left posterior fascicular pacing

Outcomes:
The pacing parameters at three months after discharge remained stable with the pacing threshold at 0.5 V at a 0.6-ms pulse width and a sensed R-wave of 9.5 mV. The patient did not experience any episodes of syncope following the pacemaker implantation. 

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient is to attend regular follow-up appointments to ensure that the pacemaker is functioning correctly.

Admission Diagnosis: Well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the left fifth metatarsal

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient was admitted to the Dermatology Department of the University of Brescia with a 2-year history of a slowly growing tumor of the plantar region of the left forefoot. The patient had been previously hospitalized and underwent magnetic resonance and cultural exam of bone biopsy of the lesion of the foot. The diagnosis was acute osteomyelitis caused by Staphylococcus lugdunensis for which he was treated with oxacillin 2 g IV every 4 h for 4 weeks with benefit. However, two months after discharge, the patient had reported a new worsening of the pain symptoms. A new bone biopsy had shown only fibrous rehash, and a preventive systemic therapy with 4.5 g IV every 8 h piperacillin/tazobactam for 4 weeks was performed.

On inspection at the initial visit to our clinic, the presence of a nodular lesion of the fifth metatarsum of the plantar and lateral surface of the left foot, with a draining sinus tract that was malodorous was noted. Incision biopsy of the lesion was performed, which revealed pseudo-epitheliomatous hyperplasia. After a new biopsy was planned, the second diagnosis was squamous atypical proliferation, and a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma cannot be excluded. The patient was sent for an orthopedic consult which suggested a fifth metatarsal amputation of the left foot. The patient was discharged in stable condition with ambulation assisted by orthotics.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Physician: ENT Service

Hospital Course:

A 39-year-old male patient was referred to the ENT service with a 4-month history of left-sided, painless swelling in the face. Clinical examination revealed a semimobile, nontender, round mass in the left parotid gland. Sonographic findings revealed a hypoechoic mass measuring about 20 × 18 mm in the left parotid gland suggesting a tumoral lesion. Multiple lymph nodes with benign appearance were also identified in the left side of the neck.

Spiral CT scan of head and neck with contrast showed a hyperdense soft tissue lesion measuring 17 × 15 mm in the posteromedial part of the left parotid gland suggestive of a lymph node. The patient underwent sonography-guided fine needle aspiration (FNA) from the mass. Prepared slides showed cellular smears, composed of numerous lymphocytes with variable size. Some clusters of acini and ductal epithelial cells were also present. There were no oncocytes or fat cells in prepared smears. Therefore the diagnosis was made as benign process, suggestive of intrasalivary gland lymph node with reactive changes.

Excision of the mass was planned in a complete parotidectomy and the specimen was sent for pathology. Grossly there was a well-defined shiny light brown mass M: 3.5 × 3 × 2 cm with attached normal parotid gland tissue. No necrosis or hemorrhage was seen.

Microscopically, the lesion was completely encapsulated and showed ductal epithelial components with squamous and sebaceous differentiation. The lymphoid background was composed of multiple lymphoid follicles with germinal centers. There was no evidence of residual lymph node architecture in the specimen. There was no giant cell reaction in the specimen.

The last follow-up of the patient was after 6 months and showed no sign of recurrence. The accompanying enlarged neck lymph nodes had also vanished.

Diagnosis:

Benign process suggestive of intrasalivary gland lymph node with reactive changes.

Treatment:

Excision of the mass was performed through a complete parotidectomy.

Follow-up:

The last follow-up of the patient was after 6 months and showed no sign of recurrence.

Discharge Summary:

This is a summary for a 46-year old male with relapsed small cell lung cancer (SCLC) who ultimately succumbed to the disease in October 2018. The patient underwent treatment with multiple chemotherapy regimens, radiation therapy, surgical interventions and participation in clinical trials. He was treated with nivolumab after other treatments failed and experienced a notable partial response, but ultimately progressive disease occurred. 

Hospital Course:
The patient initially presented in 2007 with right supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and SCLC was diagnosed. Imaging showed limited stage disease and treatment was initiated with chemotherapy and concurrent radiation therapy. After systematic progression in 2009, multiple chemotherapy regimens were administered with responses, however, ultimately the patient developed several metastases and was enrolled in a clinical trial with Aurora A kinase inhibitor in April 2012. In September 2013, there was evidence of progression of disease with aortocaval lymphadenopathy, and over the next 18 months, several chemotherapeutic agents were utilized with disease progression as the best response. 

In August 2015, the patient started treatment with nivolumab (3 mg/kg every 2 weeks) based on initial results from a phase I/II study and had a partial response. Despite treatment with nivolumab, recurrent pleural and pericardial effusions developed and required interventions. The patient showed near complete response by 16 weeks of therapy in December 2015. In May 2016, there was an indication of local recurrence in the right adrenal gland that was treated by right adrenal gland resection. Unfortunately, in April 2018, there was progression of disease with a transient response to platinum doublet, and ultimately disease progression occurred and the patient succumbed to the disease in October 2018.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course Summary: The patient was admitted multiple times with high grade fevers, increasing anemia, and thrombocytopenia. A bone marrow biopsy revealed treatment related myelodysplastic syndrome with refractory anemia and excess blasts. Patient declined chemotherapy and opted for supportive treatment. She died a week later due to pneumonia and respiratory failure.

Hospital Course: 

Admission 1: The patient was admitted for further evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding. An endometrial biopsy revealed high grade endometrial carcinoma with serous features. The patient underwent surgical staging 4 months later with total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, pelvic lymphadenectomy, and omentectomy. Out of the total 21 resected lymph nodes, one was involved with cancer and the carcinoma was staged at T3aN1M0, Stage 3.

Admission 2: The patient was admitted for chemotherapy with three cycles of carboplatin and paclitaxel at 21-day intervals, followed by pelvic radiotherapy (planned total dose 5040 cGy), and finally three additional cycles of carboplatin and paclitaxel. The patient experienced radiation related Grade 3 colitis, and radiation therapy was stopped after receipt of 1980 cGy.

Admission 3: The patient was admitted for worsening anemia and thrombocytopenia during this period which prompted a bone marrow biopsy. This revealed a hypercellular marrow with overall 5% myeloblasts with megaloblastic changes in the red cells and myeloid series and normal appearing megakaryocytes. The findings were consistent with treatment related myelodysplastic syndrome with refractory anemia and excess blasts.

The blasts exhibited both myeloid and monocytic features and a diagnosis of acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AML; FAB classification: M4) was made. Peripheral smear also showed persistent leukocytosis with blasts >27% along with anemia and thrombocytopenia which eventually required transfusions.

Discharge Diagnosis: Acute myelomonocytic leukemia (M4), related to treatment received for high grade endometrial carcinoma with serous features. The patient later declined chemotherapy and opted for supportive treatment.

HOSPITAL COURSE:

Admission: A 36-year-old man was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of fatigue, fever, and cough. Diagnostic testing revealed anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukocytosis. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed acute myelogenous leukemia with monocytic differentiation. Induction chemotherapy with prophylactic antibiotics, antifungals, and antivirals was initiated.

Course: On day 4 of induction chemotherapy, the patient developed right lower quadrant abdominal pain. Despite treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics, the pain worsened. Repeat computerized tomography (CT) revealed cecal necrosis with extension into the abdominal wall. Emergency surgery was performed, during which the patient underwent hemicolectomy and end ileostomy. Tissue culture confirmed Rhizopus microsporus and mixed anaerobic flora.

Post-Operative Course: The patient was transferred to the surgical ICU where he continued to receive broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy. However, a large abdominal abscess was detected, which could not be successfully treated despite multiple drainage catheters and both intravenous and intraperitoneal amphotericin.

On hospital day 42, the patient underwent incision and drainage of complex retroperitoneal abscess and evacuation of 15 cm of semisolid necrotic tissue with superimposed fungal infection. Microscopy confirmed the presence of broad non-septate hyphae consistent with Rhizopus microsporus.

Following definitive surgical source control, the patient began a long recovery process and achieved a complete remission of his AML. On day 77, he was discharged home. He is currently receiving consolidative therapy with Azacitidine and remains on a prolonged course of antifungals.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:
1. Acute Myelogenous Leukemia with Monocytic Differentiation 
2. Typhlitis
3. Cecal Necrosis with Extension into the Abdominal Wall
4. Abdominal Abscess with Contamination
5. Rhizopus microsporus Fungal Infection

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Continue to take all medications as prescribed, including antifungals.
2. Follow up with your primary care physician as recommended.
3. Contact your provider immediately if you experience any fever, chills, abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting.
4. Avoid exposure to sick individuals and practice good hand hygiene to reduce the risk of infection.
5. Maintain a healthy lifestyle, including a nutritious diet and regular exercise.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 29-year-old male, presented to our tertiary care facility following a road traffic accident that resulted in a closed head injury. Computed tomography revealed skull base fractures of the greater wing of sphenoid, but no parenchymal injuries were evident. The patient was discharged after improvement of symptoms.

Presenting Complaint:
The patient returned to our facility 3 months later with progressive swelling of the left eye over the past 15 days, coupled with a progressive loss of vision in the same eye for the past 10 days.

Assessment:
Clinical examination revealed severe periorbital edema and chemosis of conjunctiva with associated loss of vision (only perception of light) and restricted extraocular movements of the left eye. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a large, ill-defined lesion in the left supraclinoid and paraclinoid region with variable contrast enhancement, raising suspicion of an aneurysm.

Management:
Digital subtraction angiography confirmed the presence of a 2.8 cm × 0.9 cm supraclinoid aneurysm that had ruptured inferiorly into the cavernous sinus forming a carotid-cavernous fistula (CCF) with an associated dilation of superior ophthalmic veins (SOVs). The patient was then planned for coiling of the supraclinoid pseudoaneurysm, and the CCF was completely obliterated by coiling of the aneurysm alone.

Follow-up:
The patient reported an improvement in vision (6/36) in his left eye during follow-up and underwent DSA one year postoperatively, which suggested complete obliteration of the aneurysm and fistula with no recurrence.

Date of Admission: Not Provided

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 31-year-old female with a congenital right ureteral triplication who presented with recurrent right-sided pyelonephritis and persistent right-sided flank pain refractory to medical management. Delayed phase computed tomography (CT) scan with intravenous contrast revealed the presence of three right-sided ureters that were associated with their own collecting systems and emptied separately into the bladder. The uppermost moiety showed sequelae of chronic obstruction. The patient underwent a robotic right uppermost pole moiety nephroureterectomy after a complete discussion of its risks and benefits. The patient consented to the off-labeled use of ICG, which was used to locate the diseased ureter and identify the ureter of interest for the surgery. The diseased ureter fluoresced green under NIRF, and the other two healthy ureters did not fluoresce. The diseased, fluorescent ureter was circumferentially dissected distally. Two Weck Hem-o-lok clips were secured on the ureter at its junction with the bladder prior to transecting the ureter. The diseased ureter was then dissected proximally to its associated renal pelvis. By toggling the NIRF on and off, the surgeon was able to clearly distinguish between the green fluorescing renal pelvis and ureter from the non-fluorescing fibrotic tissue. After identifying the arterial and venous branches of the main renal artery and vein supplying the uppermost pole, the surgeon clipped the proximal and distal ends and transected the vessels. The patient was discharged without complications. 

Discharge Diagnoses:
1. Congenital right ureteral triplication

1. Robotic right uppermost pole moiety nephroureterectomy

The patient was managed conservatively with antibiotics and antidiabetics.

The patient was advised to continue with her medications for Type II diabetes mellitus and hypertension. The patient, a 71-year-old male, presented to our hospital with complaints of anorexia and weight loss over the past three months. He had a family history of diabetes mellitus and was diagnosed with the same condition at the age of 63. A physical examination revealed megaloblastic anemia, low levels of cobalamin, and positive autoantibody to intrinsic factor, which were consistent with pernicious anemia. Atrophic gastritis was identified in gastroscopy. The patient received intramuscular cyanocobalamin and his weight recovered to 69 kg over the next three months.

Further evaluation revealed positive antiglutamic acid decarboxylase autoantibody and islet cell antibody, indicating slowly progressive type 1 diabetes mellitus (SPIDDM). The patient exhibited numbness of the foot and reduced vibratory sensation in the ankle. Diabetic retinopathy was absent, but his urinary excretion of albumin was 63.0 mg/g-Cr. Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome (APS) type 3 with SPIDDM, pernicious anemia, and Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

The patient's insulin secretory capacity was not impaired, but his blood glucose level worsened after he regained his appetite. Multiple daily injections of insulin (total: 28 units per day) were administered, and his HbA1c (NGSP) decreased to 9.9% over three months. The patient did not exhibit adrenal insufficiency, and his urinary excretion of cortisol was within normal limits.

The patient should continue to receive injections of insulin multiple times per day for diabetes mellitus. Discharge Summary:

Patient: 50-year-old postmenopausal female

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with symptomatic anemia and abdominal pain. She had been diagnosed with nodular sclerosis classic Hodgkin lymphoma in July 2017 and had initially opted for holistic/natural medicine treatment. She was found to have hypercalcemia, acute kidney injury, anasarca and abnormal liver function tests in January 2018, and had a common bile duct stenting performed. Pap smear examination revealed atypical squamous cells with cellular infiltrate in cervical biopsy tissue confirming NSCHL involvement.

Treatment:
Chemotherapy with ICE regimen was started. The patient was also prepared for allogeneic bone marrow transplant which was successfully performed in January 2019. Her stem cell transplant course was complicated by GVHD treated with steroid and subsequently, she developed steroid-induced diabetes mellitus.

Follow-up:
The patient had multimodal recurrence in multiple organs, including the base of the skull, cervical spine, lung, liver, and rib, as well as right side pleural effusion and was confirmed to have NSCHL involvement. She was deceased as a consequence of multiorgan failure and septicemia.

Admitting Diagnosis: Nodular lesion of the palatal gingiva

Hospital Course:

The patient presented at the Department of Oral Surgery and Orthodontics of the Medical University of Graz with a nodular lesion of the palatal gingiva. The lesion was located between the first and second incisor on the right upper jaw and had been present for a long time, growing larger within recent months. The patient denied experiencing any pain.

Pre-operative X-rays showed no tumor involvement of the neighboring maxillary bone. Clinical differential diagnoses were epuliform lesions, most likely a fibroma or peripheral ossifying fibroma. Under local anesthesia, the lesion was totally excised down to the periosteum and examined histopathologically.

Operative specimen:

The operative specimen, covered by an otherwise inconspicuous mucous membrane, measured 7:5:3 mm. The cut surface showed gelatinous tissue. Microscopically, the specimen was covered superficially by reactive hyperplastic squamous epithelium. In the underlying stroma, a multinodular lesion was found. The nodules varied in size and consisted of myxoid/chondroid stroma, in which many cells, mostly spindle-shaped, were embedded. The lesional cells showed variable expression of S-100 protein and smooth muscle actin (SMA). The Kiel 67 protein (Ki67)-associated cellular proliferation rate was <5%.

Follow-up:

A follow-up after 41 months showed no recurrence of the lesion.

Final Diagnosis:

Based on the patient's case report and histopathological examination, the diagnosis was nodular lesion of the palatal gingiva, with multinodular lesions found in the underlying stroma. Immunohistochemically, the lesional cells showed variable expression of S-100 protein and smooth muscle actin (SMA).

Treatment:

The lesion was totally excised down to the periosteum under local anesthesia (Ultracain dental® 4%, Sanofi-Aventis, Frankfurt am Main, Germany).

No further follow-up care is needed at this time.

Complete regression of swelling on the lateral aspect of the chin was achieved ten days postoperatively, and the mentolabial fold could be appreciated. The patient was reevaluated at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months postoperatively. No further treatment was required after 1 year.

Further evaluation with computed tomography angiography (CTA) head and neck and Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain was unremarkable, but an MRI cervical spine exhibited multilevel degenerative disc disease without spinal canal narrowing. The surgery involved dissection of the omohyoid muscle and the sternal head of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, followed by an incision and reflection of the fascia overlying the longus colli muscle in an attempt to protect the sympathetic chain. Then, the oblique fibrous band across the vertebral artery was dissected carefully and severed using a 15 blade.

The patient recovered from the surgery without any issues. He denied postoperative recurrence of preoperative symptoms at follow-up and was discharged with instructions to follow-up with the neurologist for further evaluation and management of his symptoms.

Hospital Course Summary:

Chief Complaint: Persistent and painful oral ulcers

History of Present Illness: 

The patient is a 44-year-old female who presented with an 8-year history of persistent and painful oral ulcers. The patient received several medical therapies, but none provided any relief of aphthosis. She also self-medicated with oral prednisone for several years, which controlled the disease activity. However, she developed incapacitating attacks of oral aphthosis a few months before consult. This was not associated with fever, weakness, joint pains, photosensitivity, and genital or ocular symptoms.

Physical Examination:

Physical examination revealed multiple oral ulcers on the right tonsil, tonsillar pillar, and posterior pharyngeal wall. Palpable, tender lymphadenopathy was noted at her right level II neck, measuring approximately 1 × 1 cm with surrounding edema. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable, including normal genitalia and ocular findings. 

Investigations:

Multiple laboratory tests were conducted which included complete blood count, HIV screening, ELISA desmoglein 3 level, bacterial culture, mycology, and tzanck smear. Herpes simplex virus IgG was positive, implying a previous infection. However, her clinical findings did not fit for an active herpes infection during the time of her admission. Nutritional deficiency screening was deferred due to the patient's limitation in resources. 

Diagnosis:

Diffuse mixed infiltrates and granulation tissue reaction were seen with no signs of atypia or viral cytopathic changes. Hypertrophic tonsils with ulceration were revealed, and no fungal elements were found. The diagnosis of CA was favored, based on history, clinical evaluation, and the exclusion of underlying diseases.

Treatment and Outcomes:

During the postoperative period, the patient developed more aphthous ulcers around the buccal mucosa, gingiva, and tongue. Colchicine was started and gradually titrated up to 1.5 mg/day. This was combined with topical glucocorticoids and intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injection (10 mg/mL). Significant reduction of severity, duration, and frequency of aphthosis was observed while the patient was on treatment. However, colchicine was discontinued after 3 months due to gastric intolerance. Recurrence of oral ulcers was then noted on follow-up 1 month after discontinuation of therapy. A trial of montelukast (10 mg/day) combined with topical therapies were given, during the 5-month period while the patient was on montelukast, a significant reduction in pain, duration, and attacks of oral aphthosis was noted. Specifically, the patient reported a 50% decrease (from 8/10 to 4/10) in her pain score, after the first week of treatment. In addition, the patient was noted to have an average of 3 or less small ulcers per month during the entire period of observation. Faster healing time of her ulcers was also reported, from approximately 4 weeks without medication to 1–2 weeks while on montelukast. 

This case is a good example of the importance of recognizing aphthosis and its effective treatment using the proper medications. Outpatient follow-up is recommended to monitor for complications and to adjust the patient’s medication regime as necessary.

Patient: 83-year-old male heavy smoker

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our department after CT detected two masses adjacent to each other in the left S10. There were no significant lymphadenopathy and metastases. Hence, left lower lobectomy was performed. Pathologically, both tumours were classified as predominantly papillary adenocarcinomas. One tumour included lepidic construction, while the other included relatively large amounts of acinar components without a lepidic component. There were some morphological differences observed between the two groups, which led to a diagnosis of double primary lung cancer. EGFR L858R mutation was detected in one tumour (left 10A) but not in the other tumour (left 10B), supporting a diagnosis of MPLC.

Discharge Summary:
The patient, an 83-year-old male heavy smoker, was admitted to our department after CT detected two masses adjacent to each other in the left S10. He underwent left lower lobectomy and was diagnosed with double primary lung cancer. One tumor included lepidic construction, while the other included relatively large amounts of acinar components without a lepidic component. EGFR L858R mutation was detected in one tumor (left 10A) but not in the other tumor (left 10B), supporting a diagnosis of MPLC. The patient was discharged after successful surgical management of his condition.
