Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Unknown polyneuropathy
Discharge Diagnosis: Lewis-Sumner syndrome (MADSAM)

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with isolated paresthesias, weakness, and cramps of the right upper limb that had progressively worsened over the course of three months. Neurological examination revealed isolated distal muscle weakness of the right upper limb and the presence of pes cavus bilaterally with reduced vibration sense in the lower limbs. Nerve conduction studies were consistent with moderate primary demyelinating sensory-motor polyneuropathy of the upper limbs and severe sensory-motor polyneuropathy of the lower limbs. MRI of the brain, cervical spine, and both plexus brachialis showed normal findings.

The patient underwent intensive long-lasting immunomodulatory therapy with methylprednisolone, prednisone, IVIG, plasma exchange, and ocrelizumab without any clinical improvement. Weakness and muscle wasting spread to proximal upper limb muscles bilaterally. Minimal weakness progression was also registered in the distal muscles of both lower limbs.

The patient has been diagnosed with Lewis-Sumner syndrome (MADSAM) based on clinical, laboratory, and radiological findings. Genetic testing revealed a novel, missense variant of LITAF in the heterozygous state, making it plausible that the patient's symptoms were associated with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.

The patient was discharged with ongoing weakness and muscle wasting and has been referred to a genetic counselor for further evaluation of the LITAF mutation and familial implications.

Discharge Medications: None prescribed

Follow-up: Genetic counseling

A pedicle omental flap was harvested and used for wrapping around the prosthetic graft and for filling the left retroperitoneal cavity resulting after hematoma evacuation. Patient Information:
45-year-old female patient reported to Department of Prosthodontics with difficulty in mastication due to loose teeth in the lower front region for 3 months. 

Hospital Course:
Patient underwent prophylaxis, extraction of tooth 31 and 42, and immediate placement of dental implants with immediate loading by temporary prosthesis. Appropriate antibiotics and analgesic were prescribed, and standard postoperative instructions were given. After 3 months, provisionals were removed and impression was made with closed tray technique using light body and putty polyvinyl siloxane rubber base material (Aquasil, Dentsply, Surrey, UK). A 3-unit porcelain fused to metal (PFM) bridge was fabricated and cemented to the abutments. Follow-up was done after 3, 6, and 12 months interval.

Clinical Findings:
Clinical examination revealed missing 41, bleeding on probing, gingival recession, and Grade II mobility in relation to tooth 31 and 42. Radiographic examination of teeth revealed poor prognosis. 

Treatment Plan:
Patient was explained about all the available treatment options with possible drawbacks of each. She agreed to undergo immediate implant with immediate loading procedure, citing her concern for esthetics and willingness for earliest possible replacement of teeth in question. 

Implants:
Dental implants (Touareg-OS, ADIN Dental Implant System, Afula, Israel) were selected for insertion based on the appropriate length and width of available bone as determined by dentascan. Following injection of 2% lignocaine local anesthetic solution, both the teeth were atraumatically removed. Extraction sockets were thoroughly debrided, and osteotomy sites were prepared with sequential order of drills recommended by the manufacturer. Implants were inserted in the prepared osteotomy sites with insertion torque of 45 Newton-centimeters, and adequate primary stability was obtained. Postoperative intraoral periapical radiograph was taken, confirming the accuracy of placement of implants. Abutments were attached to the implant body and prepared for parallelism and adequate space. 

Provisionals:
Laboratory fabricated self-cure acrylic (Pyrax Polymers, Roorkee, India) crowns were used for provisionalization. They were relieved from occlusion.

Discharge:
Patient was discharged in stable condition with normal vital signs. She was advised to continue with her standard oral hygiene routine and schedule follow-up visits with her dentist as directed.

Discharge Summary

Patient: _____ (name not provided)

Admission date: _____ (date not provided)

Discharge date: _____ (date not provided)

Hospital course:

The patient was admitted to our institution with a 5-day history of binocular diplopia. Neurologic and ophthalmologic examination revealed a right pupil-involving partial third nerve palsy. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and time-of-flight MR angiography (MRA) demonstrated an arteriovenous malformation (AVM) in the right frontal operculum extending to the anterior insula with venous drainage into the right basal vein of Rosenthal.

A diagnostic cerebral angiogram was performed, which revealed a 1.9 cm × 2.2 cm AVM fed by the right middle and accessory meningeal and sphenopalatine arteries and opercular branches of the middle cerebral artery (MCA). The patient underwent staged embolizations of the feeding pedicles using Onyx-18 embolic material to facilitate planned surgical resection.

In the first stage, superselective catheterization of the right middle meningeal, accessory meningeal, and sphenopalatine arteries was performed. In the second stage, the feeding branches of the opercular segment of the MCA were accessed. On the following day, the patient underwent a right pterional craniotomy for resection of the AVM. An intraoperative control angiogram confirmed complete obliteration of the AVM.
 
At the 4-week follow-up, the patient reported complete resolution of the diplopia. Neurologic examination demonstrated no deficits and isocoric pupils with intact extraocular movements bilaterally. There was no recurrence of the diplopia 6 months after surgery.

Diagnosis:

Arteriovenous malformation (AVM) in the right frontal operculum extending to the anterior insula with venous drainage into the right basal vein of Rosenthal.

Treatment:

Staged embolizations of the feeding pedicles using Onyx-18 embolic material to facilitate planned surgical resection. Surgical resection of the AVM via right pterional craniotomy.

Follow-up:

Patient was followed up at 4 weeks and 6 months after the surgery. At both follow-ups, the patient reported no recurrence of diplopia, and neurologic examination showed no deficits.

Hospital Course:
The 15-year-old male patient presented with acute back pain and progressive sensorimotor disorder of the bilateral lower extremities. He had known hemophilia A with inhibitors. One week previously, he had developed a hemorrhagic episode of the left knee joint and was treated with PCCs at 20 U/kg per day for 2 days; however, the hemorrhage persisted, and he therefore received preliminary treatment with a 400-mL plasma transfusion. Despite this treatment, his symptoms deteriorated with increased weakness, numbness, and hypoesthesia of the bilateral lower extremities and urinary incontinence. He presented again to our institution 22 hours after the onset of back pain.

Medical History:
The patient had a 14-year history of severe hemophilia A with recurrent episodes of subcutaneous ecchymosis, hematuria, and swelling of large joints. Hemorrhagic episodes had occurred three times during the past 4 months. His medical treatment included repeated infusion of factor VIII before the appearance of inhibitors 4 years previously, and PCCs and plasma transfusion treatment had been administered thereafter.

Diagnosis:
The diagnosis was spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma, incomplete bilateral lower extremity paraplegia, cauda equina syndrome, and hemophilia A with inhibitors.

Multidisciplinary Consultation:
A multidisciplinary consultation, which included professionals from the departments of medicine, anesthesiology, orthopedics, neurosurgery, and radiology, was immediately conducted, and an agreement regarding treatment was reached.

Treatment:
Because of the risk of thrombosis, the patient was treated with bypassing agent therapy using regular PCCs at a volume of 20 U/kg. Intravenous pulse methylprednisolone therapy was administered for 1 day to prevent obstructive complications in the spinal column. The patient's symptoms were intensively monitored and neurological examinations were strictly implemented. A bypassing agent therapy with PCCs at 20 U/kg was subsequently administered continuously twice a day for the next 6 days until the patient was discharged.

Outcome:
Ten hours after PCC infusion, autonomic urination and improvement of weakness and sensory loss were observed. After 5 days of conservative therapy, the patient was discharged with normal sensory function and almost complete muscle strength recovery of the lower extremities. Three weeks later, the patient had completely recovered.

Follow-up:
Magnetic resonance imaging conducted 1 year later showed that the hematoma had been completely absorbed.

Blood biochemistry analysis and chest X-ray observations were normal. Plain X-rays of the lumbar spine, sacrum, and pelvis revealed a large amount of expansile osteolytic destruction of the sacrum involving the upper foramina and right iliac bone, as well as a pathological fracture. The diagnosis of chordoma was confirmed by CT and MRI scans.

The pelvic ring was reconstructed using an arc pelvic reconstruction plate connected to the bilateral ilia. The remaining sectional S1 vertebrae received two massive allografts, which were fixed with screws. The patient required transfusions with 1,950 ml of enriched red blood cell suspension and 900 ml of platelets.

At three months post-surgery, plain X-rays of the pelvic and sacroiliac regions showed no looseness or fractures of internal fixation and no new bone destruction. The patient performed exercises to strengthen the function of the bladder, anal sphincter, and muscles of the lower limbs in bed 600 times per day. The patient was able to pass urine two months postoperatively and stool three months postoperatively. Six months after surgery, the patient was able to walk with a cane and had control of the urinary bladder and anal sphincter. One year later, the patient was able to walk without a cane and had good control of the urinary bladder and anal sphincter, despite losing the two bilateral S2 nerve roots.

Chordoma involving the sacrococcygeal region.

The patient was discharged and received regular follow-up appointments.

The patient should continue completing bladder, anal sphincter, and lower limbs exercise routines to regain full strength. Additionally, the patient should continue with regular follow-up appointments.

Discharge summary:

Patient Information:

Name: N/A

Age: 30 years

Gender: Female

Admission Date: N/A

Discharge Date: N/A

Diagnosis:

1. Congenital heart disease consisting of PA/VSD with major aortopulmonary collateral arteries
2. Elevated neck veins with estimated central venous pressure at 15 cm H2O
3. Severely dilated RV with severe hypertrophy and moderately reduced systolic function
4. RV systolic pressure was severely elevated near systemic pressures, estimating ∼90–100 mmHg based on tricuspid regurgitation Doppler signal
5. Severely calcified RVPA conduit with severe RVOT stenosis
6. Fibrin-associated Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (FA DLBCL) with similar cytological findings in the distal PA thrombus
7. Subsegmental pulmonary emboli

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 30-year-old female with congenital heart disease consisting of PA/VSD with major aortopulmonary collateral arteries who presented with worsening dyspnoea and progressive exercise intolerance. The patient was normotensive and had slightly tachycardic HR: 110 b.p.m. An elevated neck vein was noted with estimated central venous pressure at 15 cm H2O. Laboratory evaluation revealed slight monocytosis at 12.2% and elevated prohormone of brain natriuretic peptide at 4843 pg/mL.

The patient underwent a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE), which demonstrated a severely dilated RV with severe hypertrophy and moderately reduced systolic function. The RV systolic pressure was severely elevated near systemic pressures. The RVPA conduit was severely calcified with severe RVOT stenosis. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) was performed and revealed a stenotic RVPA conduit by a calcified mural mass with subsegmental pulmonary emboli.

Surgical RVPA conduit revision with thromboendarterectomy of bilateral PAs was pursued. Intraoperatively, extensive calcification was noted of RVPA conduit with severe stenosis and erosion into the sternum and left lung. The Gore-Tex tube used to connect the RVPA homograft to the right and left pulmonary artery was full of clots, organized calcium deposits, and atheromas. The patient underwent systemic chemotherapy, resulting in the resolution of the previously noted increased metabolic activity in the cervical lymph nodes.

Follow-up TTE at 3 months revealed favourable RV reverse remodelling with improvement in RV systolic function and normal RVOT haemodynamics without significant stenosis.

Impression:

The patient exhibited congenital heart disease consisting of PA/VSD with major aortopulmonary collateral arteries with several complications. Surgical repair was successful, and the patient underwent systemic chemotherapy for Fibrin-associated Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (FA DLBCL) with similar cytological findings in the distal PA thrombus and subsegmental pulmonary emboli. The follow-up TTE at 3 months was stable and revealed an improvement in RV systolic function, underscoring the success of treatment.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Patient Name: Confidential
Medical Record Number: 0000
DOB: Unknown
Sex: Female

Hospital Presentation:
The patient presented to our hospital with a history of perennial rhinorrhoea, nasal obstruction, sneezing, and ocular symptoms for years. She had no other known comorbidities. SPTs showed Dermatophagoides farina (DF), and Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus (DP) sensitivity. Complete blood count was normal. She was diagnosed with severe persistent allergic rhinitis. Allergen avoidance was advised, and intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) and oral H1-antihistamines (OAH) were prescribed. At third month of her therapy, since she was still symptomatic with high dose INCS and OAH, subcutaneous immunotherapy was planned.

Hospital Course:
At that time, due to a misunderstanding, SPTs were performed as panel A to one arm and panel B to the other arm, simultaneously. The tests were performed by the same personnel, the same technique, the same type of lancet, and the same brand of extracts which were not expired. Results showed positive DF and DP with panel A on the right arm and negative DF and DP with panel B on the left arm. She had no skin lesions, comorbidities, any kind of topical medicine application history at the test sites, or recent anaphylaxis history that may explain this discordance. Therefore, extracts of panel A was applied to the left arm as well but the tests were negative again. In order to enlighten these results, serum mite specific IgEs and phadiatop were studied. One month later, after OAH discontinuation, informed consent was obtained from the patient and the tests were reperformed by the same personnel, the same bottle of extracts and the same technique. Panel A was negative on the left arm and only DF was positive on the right arm. DP and DF of panel B were negative and DP of panel A was positive on the dorsal skin. Mite specific IgEs and phadiatop were found negative.
  
Disposition:
The patient was discharged with no recommendations for further treatment.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was advised to regularly monitor his health for any changes or concerning symptoms. He was recommended to follow-up with his dermatologist for annual skin exams and keep current on his melanoma screening. Patient: 67-year-old Caucasian male with a medical history of ischemic heart disease, COPD, and arterial hypertension.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a persistent cough and a whole-body CT scan detected a solid nodule with speculated margins, measuring approximately 33x33mm in the apical segment of his left lower lobe and an infiltration of the pleura and of pulmonary vessels. A CT-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy confirmed that the tumor was a wild-type EGFR adenocarcinoma. The patient underwent first-line cisplatin-gemcitabine chemotherapy for six courses, followed by radiation therapy when the surgery of the lung lesion was excluded due to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The patient achieved a partial response to the treatment. However, 8 months later, a CT scan established disease progression. A second-line therapy of erlotinib was initiated, at a dose of 150mg/day, which continued for 1 year. A new CT scan exhibited a significant reduction of the tumor in the lower lobe of his left lung, eventually leading to complete remission.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was admitted with a persistent cough and a CT scan confirmed the presence of a lung tumor, which was subsequently diagnosed as a wild-type EGFR adenocarcinoma. The patient underwent chemotherapy followed by radiation therapy, which achieved a partial response to the treatment. However, disease progression was recorded 8 months later and treatment with erlotinib was initiated, resulting in a significant reduction of the tumor and leading to complete remission. The patient did not exhibit any adverse effects to the treatment, except for a grade 1 skin rash on his face, which was treated with a topical therapy and resolved with time. The patient was discharged with instructions to continue with the current treatment plan. Follow-up appointments were scheduled to assess his condition and further treatment options.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: Secondary Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with symptoms of fatigue and recurrent high-grade fever. She previously had cutaneous lymphoproliferative disorders mimicking hydroa vacciniforme and was diagnosed with Chronic Active Epstein-Barr Virus (CAEBV) at a different hospital. She underwent splenectomy to manage uncontrolled splenomegaly. On admission to our hospital, she presented with oedematous swelling of the cheeks, eyelids, and lips, along with coexisting skin lesions, liver damage, and pancytopenia. Laboratory results indicated a decrease in natural killer (NK) cell killing activity and activated CD107a expression levels, increased ferritin level, interleukin-6 (IL-6) level, and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R) level, and elevated EBV-DNA in peripheral blood mononuclear cells.

The patient was diagnosed with secondary HLH, which was confirmed with familial testing that revealed mutated digenic heterozygous STXBP2 and LYST genes. The patient's mother also had an NK cell dysfunction greater than that of the patient, but she did not exhibit any symptoms. The patient was treated with dexamethasone, which helped manage her symptoms initially. However, the symptoms resurfaced, and the patient received the HLH-2004 protocol with etoposide and dexamethasone. Liposomal doxorubicin, etoposide, and methylprednisolone were provided when HLH relapsed for the second time. The patient's ferritin levels peaked and then began to decline. She is currently waiting for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).

During the hospital course, whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed to identify potential pathogenic mutations in Primary Immunodeficiency (PID) associated genes, and Sanger sequencing tests were performed on the patient's parents. Only mutated genes of the proband identified in the PID-associated genes were found in the proband's parents.

Discharge Diagnosis: Secondary Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with an immunologist and hematologist to manage the secondary HLH. The patient is advised to adhere to a balanced diet and exercise routine and report any signs of recurrence of symptoms such as fever and immunity changes, including increased susceptibility to infections. The patient needs to take care of the transfusions required and follow the guidelines directed by a healthcare professional. In case of any emergency, contact the hospital or nearby healthcare center. 

Follow-up Appointments:
Immunologist, hematologist: Follow up in the next 2 weeks.

Patient Name: Labrador Retriever

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient was admitted for acute constipation, stranguria, and a mass in the sublumbar lymph node region. The dog had reported weight loss over several months, resided in Switzerland, and had a previous travel history to Germany. Upon clinical examination, an enlarged prostate and mass in the sublumbar lymph node region were identified. Abdominal palpation revealed cranial organomegaly. 

A complete blood count, serum chemistry, urinalysis, and coagulation profile were performed. Urine culture revealed no bacterial growth. Abdominal radiographs revealed a large space-occupying lesion in the cranial abdomen, decreased abdominal detail, and a soft-tissue opacity in the prostate region. A CT study was performed, which discovered several large cavernous space-occupying lesions in the liver, a large cystic lesion in the prostate region, and a large paraprostatic cystic lesion. 

Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration revealed a moderately modified transudate and multitocal, acidophilic hyaline membranes interpreted as fragments of laminated, hyaline membranes of hydatid cysts. The cytological characteristics suggested the presence of Echinococcus species. E. multilocularis-DNA was identified by PCR in all aspirates. 

After draining the cystic lesions, the dog could urinate and defecate without difficulty. Discharge Summary for Patient with Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL)

Patient Information
Name: [REDACTED]
Sex: Male
Age: 62
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Rib pain, dyspnea, and fever

Hospital Course
This 62-year-old male was admitted with complaints of rib pain, dyspnea, and fever. Initial laboratory investigations revealed a low white blood cell count, low hemoglobin levels, low platelet count, and elevated levels of fibrinogen degradation products and D-dimer. Bone marrow aspiration and flow cytometry revealed abnormal promyelocytes with a high blast percentage and positivity for CD33 and myeloperoxidase. Cytogenetics showed chromosomal abnormalities consistent with APL, and a STAT5B/RARа fusion transcript was detected by reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction.

The patient was initiated on treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) monotherapy, but no granulocyte differentiation was observed. After the first course, his fibrinogen degradation product and D-dimer levels improved, and he achieved a complete remission. In the second course, ATRA was combined with arsenic trioxide (ATO). However, on the 14th day of the second course, the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit due to severe cardiac insufficiency. Despite this complication, he continued to test positive for STAT5B/RARа. In the following consolidation treatment, the patient received three courses of ATRA, Huangdai tablets (oral ATO tablets), and idarubicin to achieve molecular complete remission after the fourth course. Unfortunately, his STAT5B/RARа levels rose again after the fifth course.

The patient was eventually treated with DCAG (decitabine, cytarabine, aclamycin, and G-CSF) and achieved a second molecular complete remission. At present, he is searching for a suitable donor to prepare for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).

Discharge Instructions
The patient is instructed to continue all prescribed medications as directed and to follow up with his hematologist-oncologist regarding any relevant changes or concerns. He is advised to avoid strenuous activity and to adhere to a nutritious and well-balanced diet to promote optimal health and recovery. The patient is also instructed to follow up with his cardiologist regarding any ongoing cardiac issues. Finally, the patient is encouraged to maintain close communication with his oncology healthcare team and to seek medical attention immediately in case of any new symptoms or concerns.

Patient Name: Not specified
Medical Record Number: Not specified
Date of Admission: Not specified
Date of Discharge: Not specified

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 2-year-old domestic shorthair cat, was admitted to our hospital for ophthalmology referral consultation due to signs of infection from the left eye that had been present for two weeks. The patient had received oral and topical antibiotics prior to admission, but there was a worsening of the clinical signs. Two days prior to admission, the patient began to present systemic signs of disease, including inappetence and lethargy. On physical examination, the patient was mildly dehydrated, but no other abnormalities were detected.

On ophthalmic examination, the patient presented with exposure keratitis of the left eye, along with secondary glaucoma and severe endophthalmitis. In the left eye, the menace response, dazzle reflex, and pupillary light reflexes were negative or impossible to evaluate due to severe corneal opacity. Intraocular pressure measurements were elevated in the left eye compared to the right eye. Differential diagnoses included retrobulbar abscess, cellulitis, hematoma, neoplasia, traumatic injury, and intraocular foreign body. A complete blood count and serum chemistry analysis were performed, and radiological examinations were proposed before a computed tomography scan.

After skull radiographs were taken, an intraocular linear metallic foreign body compatible with a sewing needle was detected inside the left ocular globe. CBC yielded leukocytosis, but the rest of the analytic values were within normal limits. Being a blind, painful eye, enucleation was proposed. The patient was treated with intravenous fluid therapy to correct dehydration. The patient was premedicated with butorphanol, dexmedetomidine, and ketamine for postoperative analgesia and sedation. The patient was then anaesthetised with propofol and endotracheal intubation was performed for maintenance of anesthesia with isoflurane. Cefadroxil and metronidazole were administered intravenously, and meloxicam was given subcutaneously for postoperative pain control.

Surgery was performed using the subconjunctival enucleation technique. After a lateral canthotomy, the bulbar conjunctiva and Tenon's capsule were incised. Extraocular muscle insertions were transected. The globe was carefully removed from the orbit, leaving the sewing needle attached to the back of the orbit. A piece of thread was retrieved during the procedure, which demonstrated that the linear foreign body had migrated retrogradely from the mouth to the orbit through the pterygopalatine fossa. Bacterial culture was negative. Histopathology revealed destructive ocular changes with necrosis and the presence of cocci in the ocular tunica fibrosa and vitreous cavity, but no evidence of neoplastic changes. The specific area of penetration of the foreign body into the eye was identified as corresponding to the lamina cribrosa of the sclera.

Postoperatively, the patient was treated with oral meloxicam and amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid, and topical gentamicin drops were applied to the skin suture. An Elizabethan collar was advised. The patient had no complications and improved during treatment.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Linear metallic foreign body in the left ocular globe with secondary glaucoma and severe endophthalmitis.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should continue outpatient care with the primary veterinarian and return for a follow-up ophthalmic examination in two weeks.

Signed,
[Physician Name] MD

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission and hospitalization:
The patient, a 23-year-old female with a past medical history of depression, borderline personality disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, psychosis NOS, and congenital hydrocephalus with VP shunt, was admitted to the hospital after ingesting approximately 40 g of HCQ. She had been using HCQ for the treatment of pruritus. At the time of presentation, she was being treated with risperidone, clonazepam, and zopiclone for her psychiatric disorder and fluconazole for the treatment of a vaginal yeast infection. Upon admission, she had a Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) of 15/15 but was found to have a metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis, sinus rhythm with a widened QT interval, and elevated serum potassium. She also demonstrated severe hemodynamic instability resulting from myocardial irritability with frequent ventricular ectopic activity leading to runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PMVT) and ventricular fibrillation (VF) requiring multiple defibrillations over the first 18 hours after ingestion. She was subsequently treated with various medications such as intravenous diazepam, epinephrine, norepinephrine, sodium bicarbonate, and magnesium sulfate infusions.

Management:
Various treatments and interventions were initiated during her hospitalization, including gastric lavage and activated charcoal for decontamination, crystalloid and vasopressor support, and initiation of intermittant hemodialysis (IHD). Vascular access for dialysis was established immediately after the bolus dose and thus dialysis overlapped briefly with the infusion of Intralipid ILE. The patient received a total of 500 mL of ILE and was started on piperacillin/tazobactam for possible aspiration pneumonia. Echocardiographic imaging revealed normal global ventricular contractility with an ejection fraction of 60%.

Discharge:
The patient's overall treatment and management was complicated, requiring extensive interventions and pharmacologic therapy. Despite this, the patient demonstrated gradual improvement in her hemodynamic stability and was subsequently weaned off the ventilator and extubated on day 3. The patient was then discharged from the ICU on postadmission day six and advised to follow up with a primary care physician and potential psychiatric care as an outpatient.

Summary:
In summary, the patient was initially admitted for an HCQ overdose with severe hemodynamic instability resulting from myocardial irritability. Various pharmacological interventions and treatments were initiated, and the patient was eventually weaned off the ventilator before being discharged on postadmission day six.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 29 years
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for orthodontic treatment due to occlusal plane inclination and midline deviation causing an unesthetic smile. Clinical examination revealed Angle Class II, Division 1 malocclusion, absence of maxillary left lateral incisor, a peg-shaped maxillary right lateral incisor, and the presence of mandibular left deciduous ankylosed second molar. Panoramic and periapical radiographs confirmed the absence of maxillary lateral incisor and mandibular second premolar. A treatment plan was developed to correct the occlusal plane, obtain a molar Class I relationship on the left side and Class II on the right side, establish canine Class I relationship on both sides, correct the midlines, extract the deciduous molar and replace it with implant-prosthetic rehabilitation, and open space in order to implant a prosthetic rehabilitation of the maxillary left lateral incisor.

The treatment began with bonding of standard Edgewise brackets on both arches, followed by alignment and leveling with Nickel-Titanium and stainless steel archwires. Maxillary right first premolar and mandibular left second deciduous molar were extracted, and maxillary anterior teeth were moved to the right with elastomeric chains to correct the midline and open space. An implant was inserted into the space of the missing premolar to aid mandibular midline correction. A miniplate in the shape of an Y was inserted in left zygomatic buttress and used to intrude all maxillary left teeth and distalize all teeth on the left side. The mandibular arch was extruded with intermaxillary elastics connected directly to the miniplate and on the mandibular teeth and archwire. The maxillary left lateral incisor was inserted, and the appliance was removed after 34 months of treatment.

At the end of treatment, the smile esthetics was improved, the midlines were coincident with the facial midline, and counterclockwise rotation of the mandible reduced convexity. Class I molar relationship on the left side, Class II molar relationship on the right side, and Class I canine relationship on both sides were obtained, with good intercuspation. The panoramic radiograph showed good parallelism among roots, and post-treatment lateral cephalogram, cephalometric tracing, and superimposition examinations confirmed accentuated mandibular counterclockwise rotation. Maxillary left molars were intruded while mandibular molars were uprighted and extruded. Maxillary and mandibular incisors were proclined after treatment. The patient will be monitored every six months for root resorption and treatment stability. 

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:
- Occlusal plane inclination 
- Midline deviation 
- Angle Class II, Division 1 malocclusion 
- Ankylosis of deciduous molar 
- Absence of maxillary left lateral incisor 
- Peg-shaped maxillary right lateral incisor 
- Absence of mandibular second premolar 

PROCEDURES/SERVICES:
- Orthodontic treatment 
- Extraction of maxillary right first premolar 
- Extraction of mandibular left second deciduous molar 
- Implant-prosthetic rehabilitation of maxillary left lateral incisor 
- Insertion of miniplate in left zygomatic buttress 

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
- Follow-up with dentist every six months for monitoring root resorption and treatment stability.

Patient Information: 
Name: [Redacted]
Age: 65 years
Sex: Male
Race: Caucasian
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted for evaluation of gait instability occurring in the context of Sjögren's syndrome (SS). The patient had a 3-year history of sicca symptoms, abnormal parotid scintigraphy and a lip biopsy revealing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus score of 2.3. In the 5 years before evaluation at our center, the patient experienced diffuse neuropathic pain associated with gait imbalance and falls. Two years before evaluation, such progressive gait deterioration led to dependence on a walker.

During the course of hospitalization, neurological examination at our center revealed abnormal cerebellar findings, including evidence of "cerebellar" eye disease, associated with truncal and limb ataxia. The patient also had evidence of a sensory neuronopathy as well as a non-length-dependent, small-fiber neuropathy. Neuroimaging studies of the brain revealed nonspecific white matter disease. Initial electrodiagnostic studies were thought to be consistent with a sensory neuropathy. The electrodiagnostic and skin-biopsy studies were diagnostic of these respective PNS syndromes and were also surrogate indicators of DRG neurodegeneration. In association with cerebellar examination findings, MRI neuroimaging studies now showed cerebellar atrophy.

Further imaging studies were conducted due to symptoms of dry cough and a 20-year history of tobacco use, which revealed no hypermetabolic foci, but interestingly demonstrated cerebellar hypometabolism. Given that both sensory neuronopathies and non-length-dependent, small-fiber neuropathies in SS may respond to IVIg, we are trying to obtain insurance approval for IVIg therapy.

Summary of Treatment:
During hospitalization, the patient was evaluated for gait instability occurring in the context of Sjögren's syndrome. The patient had abnormal cerebellar findings and evidence of a sensory neuronopathy as well as a non-length-dependent, small-fiber neuropathy. Neuroimaging studies showed cerebellar atrophy. Given the imaging findings and symptoms, further imaging studies were performed, which revealed cerebellar hypometabolism. The patient is being evaluated for IVIg therapy.

Follow-up Care:
The patient is advised to follow up with his primary care physician for further evaluation of his chronic sicca symptoms, gait instability, and neuropathy. The patient will also need close monitoring for improvement or exacerbation of symptoms.

Hospital Course:
A 52-year-old female patient was admitted with a chief complaint of left thigh pain and difficulty walking for the past 3 months. The patient had also noted a painless hard lump in her left clavicular region for the last 6 months. On further investigation, the patient revealed the gradual development of temporal alopecia, fine facial hair, and hair growth on her arms and upper back, as well as deepening and hoarseness of her voice.

Clinical Findings:
Upon examination, the patient presented with hirsutism, temporal baldness, coarse hands, atrophy of the breast, clitoromegaly, and pitting nontender edema of the left lower limb. There was also a mass found in the left lumbar area and nontender hepatomegaly. Blood pressure was measured on multiple occasions was not raised.

Diagnostic Assessment:
Hematological tests resulted in normal limits, and liver enzymes were not raised, except for mildly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase. Results for fasting blood sugar, serum Na+, serum K+, and serum urea and creatinine were within normal ranges. However, serum 17 dehydroepiandrostenedione (17 DHEA) was higher than normal values, and a 24-hour urinary cortisol resulted in marginal elevation. Skiagram of postero-anterior view of the chest showed a fracture of the left clavicle. A whole-body bone scan revealed abnormally increased uptake over the left clavicle and distal end of the left femur. The CT scan of the whole abdomen revealed multiple ill-defined hypodense enhancing space occupying lesions of varying sizes involving both lobes of the liver. There was a 7.9 × 6.8 cm irregular heterogenous enhancing lesion of the left adrenal gland displacing the upper pole of the left kidney. Adrenal gland of the right side showed no abnormality. ECG was normal.

Treatment:
The patient was treated by giving external radiation to the areas with skeletal metastases. The left clavicular lesion was treated by a direct AP field to a dose of 2000 cGy in 5 fractions. The left femoral lesion was treated using the same dose. External radiation was given by Co 60. Due to the presence of multiple hepatic metastases involving both lobes of the liver, operative intervention would not be feasible. After completion of radiotherapy, the patient received 3 cycles of chemotherapy with Inj. cisplatin @ 80 mg/m2 Day 1 and Inj. doxorubicin @ 40 mg/m2 Day 1 every 21 days. A repeat CT scan of the abdomen at the end of 3 cycles of chemotherapy showed no response of the tumor to this regime.

Outcome:
The patient received extensive management with radiotherapy and chemotherapy. However, there was no evidence of significant improvement in the tumor. The patient was subsequently discharged with a recommendation of chemotherapy. Follow-up will be arranged to monitor the patient's condition.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension, was admitted for evaluation of rapid increase in serum blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine. The patient's renal function had declined 126 days earlier and his serum creatinine had increased to 2.7 mg/dL. The patient had refused evaluation at that time. However, he was admitted to another hospital for complaints of frequency and nocturia and then transferred to our hospital for further evaluation.

Physical examination on admission revealed that the patient had 2+ pretibial pitting edema, appeared pale and unwell, and had gained 3 kg of weight within the past 3 months. Laboratory findings showed a decrease in hemoglobin levels as well as a significant increase in serum total protein and albumin, total calcium, and phosphorus in the patient's system. The patient's BUN and creatinine levels had increased to 93 and 9.7 mg/dL, respectively. Furthermore, serological tests for antibodies, immunoglobulins, complement, and protein electrophoresis were negative except for p-ANCA. A renal biopsy showed 19 glomeruli, of which 8 showed global sclerosis and 9 were fibrous crescents. Direct immunofluorescence tests showed IgG, IgA, and C3 granular deposits along the capillary walls, and the electron microscopic analysis showed the glomerular capillary walls had epimembranous and intramembranous electron-dense deposits. Chest X-rays and CT scans showed traction bronchiectasis, honeycombing in both lungs, and a ground- glass opacity in the right middle lobe and posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe.

Treatment:

The patient was treated with 500 mg of intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy for 3 days, followed by 60 mg/day of prednisolone and 100 mg/day of cyclophosphamide. However, despite the immunosuppressive therapy, the patient's serum creatinine level continued to increase, and his body weight also increased by 4 kg. He underwent acute hemodialysis, and regular hemodialysis was planned for 3 times per week after his discharge on hospital day 9. The immunosuppressive therapy with prednisolone and cyclosporine was continued during outpatient follow-up before his subsequent discharge.

Follow-Up:

The patient's kidneys were non-responsive to the immunosuppressive drugs at the time of discharge. Therefore, the immunosuppressive drugs were gradually tapered off. Details of outpatient follow-up and future treatment plan are pending further evaluation.

History & Findings:
The patient had a history of coronary artery bypass and chronic pulmonary diseases, including obsolete pulmonary tuberculosis, chronic bronchitis, and emphysema. The heart boundary was enlarged to the left and down, and murmurs could be heard. Laboratory findings at admission showed high elevations in glutamic-pyruvic transaminase, lactate dehydrogenase, leukocyte count, neutrophil, procalcitonin, D-dimer, glucose, and C-reactive protein.

The patient was given high flow intranasal oxygen inhalation with oxygen concentration 100%. However, he still had obvious shortness of breath, 87% pulse oxygen saturation (SpO2), and poor consciousness. Thus he was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU), where invasive ventilation was used for him during the whole hospitalization, maintaining SpO2 at about 95%. Other treatments included prone position ventilation, vasoconstrictor, antibacterial, and antiviral therapy. Subcutaneous emphysema was found in his left neck 5 days after admission and gradually increased in the subsequent days. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our department with sudden-onset stuporous consciousness. A brain CT scan revealed a subarachnoid hemorrhage with a right temporal lobe intracranial hemorrhage and a right subdural hematoma. Following the CT, angiography demonstrated an aneurysmal sac at the right posterior communicating artery. Emergency decompressive craniectomy (DC) and aneurysmal neck clipping were performed. Following recovery there was some sinking of the scalp flap, and the decision was made to proceed with an autologous cranioplasty 61 days after the initial hemorrhage. There were no complications during the cranioplasty procedure, and there was no evidence of cardiovascular instability or cerebral swelling. Epidural and subdural drains were placed and connected to a suction system during skin closure. Following skin closure the drains were connected to a drainage bag to avoid subgaleal and epidural blood accumulation.

However, the patient had a seizure in the recovery room. Emergency brain CT revealed widespread cerebral edema. Increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and cerebral edema were managed with osmotic diuretics, corticosteroids, and antiepileptic drugs. The edema slowly subsided, but new low-density areas were noted on follow-up brain CT 1 week after the cranioplasty. The decision was made to clamp the drain catheters to control the intracranial pressure.

The patient was monitored closely for any signs of complications, and no further episodes of seizure or cerebral edema were observed. The patient's overall condition improved, and she was discharged in stable condition with instructions for continued follow-up care.

Final Diagnosis:

- Subarachnoid hemorrhage
- Right temporal lobe intracranial hemorrhage
- Right subdural hematoma
- Aneurysmal sac at the right posterior communicating artery
- Widespread cerebral edema

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [patient name]
Age: 12 years old
Gender: Male
Breed: Chihuahua
Weight: 4.2 kg

Reason for hospital admission:
The patient was admitted due to chronic coughing with a history of tracheal collapse. Physical examinations revealed a grade III murmur and cough. Respiration rate was 20 breaths/min. The dog was diagnosed with hyperlipidemia and mitral insufficiency whose severity was classified as II b by the International Small Animal Cardiac Health Council.

Hospital Course:
The initial treatment prescribed was alacepril (1.5 mg/kg, SID) and a low-fat meal for a period of two months. However, cardiomegaly continued to progress, whereas the frequency of coughing was not reduced. Moreover, hyperlipidemia was not improved. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed biliary debris that was gradually increasing in size. Consequently, PS (1 mg/kg, SID) was prescribed. Following PS administration, the clinical signs were evaluated, and hematologic, serum biochemical, and radiologic examinations and echocardiographic and circulation parameter measurements were performed. Cough disappeared one week after PS administration.

Clinical Findings:
Blood biochemical tests revealed that the total cholesterol, triglyceride, and N-terminal probrain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) concentrations were significantly decreased from Day 11 to Day 211. No marked changes in the peak velocity of early diastolic transmitral flow (E), peak velocity of late transmitral flow (A), E/A ratio, and deceleration time of early diastolic transmitral flow (DTE) were observed during PS administration. Stroke volume (SV) and cardiac output (CO) decreased on Days 30 and 45 after PS administration but thereafter increased and maintained well. No substantial changes in the maximum systolic mitral regurgitation velocity (MRmax) were identified after PS administration. The maximum systolic tricuspid regurgitation velocity (TRmax) and systolic pulmonary arterial pressure (sPA), calculated using the modified Bernoulli equation (4 x TRmax2 + 10), both decreased after PS administration. The peak velocity of early diastolic mitral annular motion (Em)/peak velocity of diastolic mitral annular motion (Am) ratio increased during PS administration compared with preadministration. E/Em decreased on Days 34 and 65 after PS administration but increased after Day 96, and a higher value was then observed.

Follow-up:
Additional hematologic and biochemical findings indicating renal or hepatic failures and adverse effects were not observed up to 375 days after PS administration.

Outcome:
The radiographic vertebral heart size (VHS) decreased after PS administration. With respect to the echocardiographic and circulation variables, decreases in heart rate (HR) and left atrium/aorta ratio (LA/Ao) were observed during PS administration, whereas LV fractional shortening (FS) and LV ejection fraction (EF) increased from Day 30 to Day 150 after PS administration.

Impression:
Overall, the patient responded well to the treatment and showed improvement in his clinical signs. The medication prescribed reduced the severity of the patient's hyperlipidemia and mitral insufficiency. Cough disappeared one week after the administration of the medication.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 11-year-old male with no known medical history, was admitted to the pediatric hospital with an acute onset of lower limb strength loss one day before admission. Initial cranial CT and CSF analysis were normal. Guillain-Barré syndrome was suspected, and immunoglobulin was administered for four days without improvement. Subsequently, the patient developed strength loss in his left upper limb, and a new CSF analysis showed increased protein concentration, leukocyte count, and serum eosinophilia. Albendazole was given as an empirical treatment for eosinophilic meningitis, along with ceftriaxone and acyclovir. However, the patient's clinical situation did not improve, and he was transferred to another hospital for further evaluation.

Diagnostic Findings:
The patient presented with medullary canal demyelination, medullary cone enlargement in the thoracolumbar region, and a granulomatous lesion, and medullary extrinsic compression in the lower lumbar region, as seen in his neuroaxis MRI. Serologic tests for viral infections used were negative. Two parasitological stool samples were collected, with negative results. CSF and serum exams excluded eosinophilic meningitis but were positive for IgG antibodies for Schistosoma mansoni.
 
Treatment:
The patient was diagnosed with Schistosoma mansoni infection and was treated with praziquantel. The patient received pulse therapy with methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg for three days for the possibility of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis and parasitic infection involving the CNS. He subsequently received oral corticosteroid therapy with prednisolone 30 mg/day. Furthermore, he received physical therapy for rehabilitation.

The patient showed improvement in neurological symptoms, albeit with neuropathic pain in the right hand associated with right-hand paresthesia. He had osteotendinous reflexes of 2+/4+ in his upper limbs and 1+/4 + in his lower limbs, with an absent Achilles reflex. 

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with Schistosoma mansoni infection.

At the time of discharge, the patient was dependent on a long-term urinary catheter for diuresis and required daily physical therapy. 

Follow-up Plan:
The patient should follow up with his primary care physician to monitor his progress and receive further treatment as needed.

Hospital Course:

A 17-year-old male patient with no systemic history presented to the Istanbul University, Faculty of Dentistry, Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery with a large swelling in the left mandibular ramus area, which had developed over the last four years. The swelling was painless, and no orofacial infection signs were reported. On extraoral examination, a hard, subcutaneous, multinodular, painless mass of the complete left mandibular ramus was noted. Deviation of the mandible to the right during mouth-opening and the protrusion were detected. During intraoral examination, there were no signs of pathology at the left mandible or the mandibular ramus area. 

Diagnostic radiological imaging, including panoramic radiographs and Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT), showed that the patient had a lobulated calcified odontogenic tumor developing in his left mandibular ramus area, requiring segmental or block resection. Under general anesthesia, an operation was performed to correct the left mandible, reshaping and removing the lobular part of the lateral and medial side of the ascending ramus. 

The patient also presented with class III skeletal malocclusion, for which orthodontic treatment was administered. Following the orthodontic treatment, wisdom teeth were extracted. Seven years after the osteoma surgery, orthognathic surgery was performed without any complications. Maxilla Le Fort I osteotomy and mandibular bilateral sagittal split osteotomy were performed, and the bone at the left mandibular ramus area was fully regenerated and healthy. One year following the operation, a dental implant was applied to rehabilitate the patient's existing tooth deficiencies.

Discharge Summary:

The patient in this case report, a 17-year-old male with no systemic history, underwent treatment for a large swelling in the left mandibular ramus area. The swelling had developed over the past four years and was painless, with no orofacial infection signs. Diagnostic radiological imaging revealed the presence of a calcified odontogenic tumor, for which segmental or block resection was required. 

The patient was operated on for the left mandible, with no complications, and reshaped with the resection of the lobular part of the lateral and medial side of the ascending ramus. Orthodontic treatment was administered to correct the patient's class III skeletal malocclusion, followed by the extraction of wisdom teeth.

Seven years after the osteoma surgery, orthognathic surgery was performed. Maxilla Le Fort I osteotomy and mandibular bilateral sagittal split osteotomy were performed, and the bone at the left mandibular ramus area was fully regenerated and healthy. One year following the operation, a dental implant was applied to rehabilitate the patient's existing tooth deficiencies.

Medical Summary:
A 5-year-old, intact, male Australian cattle dog presented with oral pain and swelling in the left maxillofacial region that was noticed 1 month earlier. The dog had a history of a stick injury in its mouth about a year earlier. The referring veterinarian had obtained pre- and post-contrast CT scans, which revealed a region of cellulitis and myositis in the proximity of the left temporomandibular joint (TMJ), narrowing of the joint space and osteophytes on the medial aspect of the left condylar process, and periosteal reaction at the lateral side of the left condylar process. At that time, a foreign body was also observed lateral to the TMJ. The patient underwent surgical management of the TMJ, and two small foreign bodies were found and removed. Further evaluation reported severe, chronic, multifocal cellulitis, and steatitis with extensive fibrosis. The administration of antibiotics was modified based on the culture and sensitivity report, with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and metronidazole added for four weeks. The dog was discharged with medications and showed resolution of the swelling at the two-week follow-up. The owner reported freedom from clinical symptoms for the next 7.5 years with no sign of recurrence.

Diagnosis:
Cellulitis and myositis of the left temporomandibular joint with foreign body.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with oral pain and swelling in the left caudal maxillary and zygomatic regions that was noticed 1 month before presentation. The referring veterinarian evaluated the patient and obtained pre- and post-contrast CT scans that revealed a region of cellulitis and myositis in the proximity of the left temporomandibular joint (TMJ), narrowing of the joint space, and periosteal reaction at the lateral side of the left condylar process. A foreign body was also identified lateral to the TMJ. The patient then underwent surgical management of the TMJ, two foreign bodies were removed, and tissue samples were acquired and submitted for culture and sensitivity testing and histopathology. Treatment was initiated with amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and enrofloxacin for 14 days, along with tramadol and carprofen for pain management. The medication was then modified based on the culture and sensitivity report, and metronidazole was added for four weeks. The follow-up at two weeks showed the resolution of swelling, and the patient was free of clinical symptoms for the next 7.5 years.

Follow-Up Instructions:
The owner was instructed to keep the incision site clean and dry and to limit the patient's activity levels accordingly. The owner was advised to continue administering medications as prescribed and to monitor the patient for any signs of recurrence or adverse effects of medication.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED] 

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED] 

Discharge Date: [REDACTED] 

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 50-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia, presented to the hospital with a sudden onset of severe chest and back pain. Upon admission, the patient's laboratory data showed an increased white blood cell count, but no abnormality was detected on further testing. Pentazocine was administered intravenously to manage severe pain. The patient was diagnosed with type B aortic dissection from the descending aorta to the left common iliac artery with narrowing of the true lumen of the abdominal aorta.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed incomplete dissection of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and poor enhancing of the intestinal tract. An angiography performed via the right femoral artery showed occlusion of the SMA. The placement of a metallic stent in the true lumen of the SMA was then considered. 

Due to the unique angle of the SMA, it was difficult to insert the guidewire deeply to the true lumen of the SMA from the right femoral artery. The guidewire was instead inserted from the left brachial artery to the SMA using a 6 Fr multipurpose catheter and a 6 Fr sheath. The use of intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) confirmed the placement of the guidewire in the true lumen. The insertion of a 6mm x 6cm self-expandable E-Luminexx Vascular Stent into the SMA successfully improved the peripheral blood flow. 

As a result of the successful stenting of the SMA, the intestinal tract was checked using laparoscopy and the patient was observed. Discharge Summary:

Patient: 56-year-old Caucasian male

Admission date: [DATE]
Discharge date: [DATE]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with a history of intermittent sharp shooting-type right-sided chest pain. Physical examination was unremarkable. Routine laboratory evaluation, including full blood count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and chest X-ray, were normal.

A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain was normal. However, a spinal MRI scan revealed multiple intradural extramedullary lesions with an intramedullary component at the T1 and T2 vertebral levels. These lesions showed no radiological cord compression, and a conservative approach was adopted with future annual MRI follow-up planned. 

Two years later, the patient presented with severe neuropathic chest pain that was unresponsive to analgesic management. Repeat spinal MRI showed increased size of the spinal lesions with associated spinal cord edema. Subsequently, the patient underwent laminectomy and tumor excision, and the vast majority of lesions were resected. A microscopic examination of the excised tumor revealed features consistent with Antoni A and B growth patterns of schwannoma.

Ten days post-operatively, MRI imaging revealed near-complete resection of the multiple spinal schwannomas. The patient was discharged six days later and had a complete resolution of pain. Six months post-operatively, spinal MRI imaging showed no tumor residuum or recurrence.

Clinical Diagnosis:

Multiple intradural extramedullary schwannomas with an intramedullary component at the T1 and T2 levels causing neuropathic chest pain.

Treatment:

Laminectomy and tumor excision with subsequent resection of the vast majority of lesions was carried out, while a small remnant was left to avoid iatrogenic spinal cord injury.

Follow-up:

Future annual spinal MRI follow-up is recommended to monitor for any possible recurrence.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The patient, a woman in her early 30s, presented to the hospital with a through-and-through gunshot wound to the lower sternum and left posterior chest. Her condition on arrival was critical, with signs of hypotension and tachycardia. Physical examination and chest X-ray suggested a left hemothorax. An emergent left tube thoracostomy drained 200 mL of fresh blood, and a focused assessment with sonography for trauma revealed a trace amount of fluid in the left upper abdomen.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
Due to the high suspicion of cardiac injury and an intra-abdominal involvement, the patient was taken to the operating room for an emergent median sternotomy. During surgery, a 3 cm right ventricle laceration was identified, and a cardiorrhaphy was performed. Intra-thoracic cardiac massages were necessitated. Further examination showed that the bullet trajectory coursed into the abdomen, which required a subsequent exploratory laparotomy. Hemoperitoneum, liver laceration, and spleen laceration were identified, requiring a splenectomy, liver packing, and negative-pressure abdominal packing.

Treatment and Recovery:
The patient received 47 units of packed red blood cells, rationed with fresh frozen plasma and platelets. She became coagulopathic, hypothermic, and acidotic due to the profound hemorrhage and the complexity of multi-trauma. The heart, lungs, and chest wall were tremendously edematous. The sternotomy incision was approximated, but the patient became severely hypotensive. She was treated with a massive transfusion protocol and watched closely for several days in the hospital's intensive care unit (ICU).

Disposition:
The patient remained in the hospital for several days and received close care in the ICU. She eventually stabilized and improved, leading to her discharge. She received detailed instructions to care for her wound at home and was informed of her follow-up appointments. 

Overall, the patient's clinical presentation was indicative of significant trauma and required multiple invasive procedures and interventions to address the associated injuries. The patient's prognosis for recovery remains positive, though she requires close monitoring and follow-up care.

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted to our hospital with complaints of pain abdomen for the past 15 days. He was diagnosed with empyema of the gallbladder with an abscess in the left lobe of the liver. Considering the patient's age and comorbid conditions (essential hypertension and type 2 diabetes), laparoscopic cholecystectomy was planned.

During laparoscopy, dense adhesions were noted around the gallbladder. The adhesions could not be released, and the abdomen was opened. The gallbladder was found to be necrotic and friable and was removed in piecemeal. The other abdominal organs were normal. The patient developed atrial fibrillations and died of cardiogenic shock on the tenth postoperative day before histopathological diagnosis was made.

Histology revealed fragments of gallbladder tissue displaying infiltrating tumor composed mainly of spindle-shaped pleomorphic cells with occasional bizarre giant cells. Scattered inflammatory cells, congested capillaries, and dense fibrocollagenous tissues were also noted.

On immunohistochemistry, majority of the spindle-shaped tumor cells and bizarre giant cells were positive for cytokeratin, with C-11, and 1:100 dilution. Osteoclastic giant cells were CD68 positive. A diagnosis of carcinosarcoma of the gallbladder was made.

N/A

This patient has expired, and no further follow-up is required. 

Primary Diagnosis: 

Carcinosarcoma of the gallbladder.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 45
Gender: Female
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admission Diagnosis: Urticaria and Presyncope
Discharge Diagnosis: Carboxymethylcellulose Allergy with Oral Allergy Syndrome

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the emergency department with widespread urticaria and presyncope 30 minutes after receiving an intraarticular elbow injection of Kenalog and lidocaine local anesthetic. Physical examination demonstrated generalized urticaria, angioedema of her tongue and throat, and diaphoresis. The patient was hypotensive and tachycardic and was treated with 500 μg of 1/1000 intramuscular adrenaline, 10 mg of intravenous chlorphenamine, 200 mg of intravenous hydrocortisone, and 1 L of intravenous 0.9% saline salt, to good effect. She was monitored overnight, received further intravenous hydrocortisone the following morning and was discharged with a course of oral prednisolone 30 mg daily and chlorphenamine 4 mg three times daily for 5 days, to which she clinically responded well.

Three years later, the patient developed widespread urticaria, chest tightness, light-headedness, and swelling of the lips and tongue within 40 minutes of drinking a supermarket-bought white hot chocolate powdered drink. She again presented to the emergency department and was managed with 10 mg of intravenous chlorphenamine and 200 mg of intravenous hydrocortisone, with good response. The white hot chocolate was found to contain e-number E466, an alternative descriptor for carboxymethylcellulose. Skin prick testing was positive to hot chocolate powders containing E466/carboxymethylcellulose, and to Celluvisc carmellose 0.5% eye drops, which contains cross-linked carboxymethylcellulose as its active ingredient. The diagnosis was confirmed to be carboxymethylcellulose allergy.

Follow-up in the allergy clinic revealed that the patient has developed features of oral allergy syndrome with localized oral itching on eating raw apple, nectarines, peaches, pears, and cherries. Skin prick tests confirmed sensitization to mixed tree pollen, birch tree pollen, mixed weed pollen, and fresh apple on prick-to-prick testing. The patient has otherwise remained well, with no further food-induced systemic reactions for the subsequent 2 years.

Recommendations:
The patient was advised to avoid both triamcinolone acetonide and any substances containing carboxymethylcellulose, provided with an anaphylaxis management plan, and trained with and prescribed two adrenaline autoinjectors. She was also prescribed a 2-day course of prednisolone 40 mg for acute exacerbations of her symptoms. The patient should follow up with an allergist regularly and carry the prescribed adrenaline autoinjectors at all times.

Follow-up:
The patient should continue to avoid all foods and drinks containing carboxymethylcellulose and any substances that may contain it. The patient should continue the prescribed course of prednisolone for acute exacerbations of her symptoms. It is recommended that the patient follow up with an allergist regularly for further management of her carboxymethylcellulose allergy and oral allergy syndrome. The patient should carry the prescribed adrenaline autoinjectors at all times. If the patient develops any symptoms suggestive of an allergic reaction, she should use the adrenaline autoinjector and seek immediate medical attention.

Hospital Course Summary:
This is a summary of the hospital course of a 59-year-old Japanese man who was admitted with fever, appetite loss, dyspnea on exertion, and skin rash. Blood testing revealed anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and C-reactive protein (CRP). On admission, he was administered pulse steroid therapy and cyclophosphamide (CPA). Skin eruptions were observed on his back and lateral regions, and pancytopenia was seen with large atypical lymphocytes. Soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R) was elevated to 12,600 U/mL, and bone marrow aspiration demonstrated atypical lymphocytes and hemophagocytosis by macrophages, suggesting lymphoma-associated hemophagocytic syndrome. Bone marrow biopsy revealed hypercellular marrow with diffuse infiltration of large atypical lymphocytes, which were compatible with the hemophagocytic-syndrome associated variant of intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVLBCL). 

After the diagnosis of IVLBCL, the patient was treated with one course of CHOP and six courses of R-CHOP. While undergoing the sixth course of R-CHOP therapy, he developed issues with motor coordination. He was diagnosed with a fresh infarction in the white matter, which was possibly caused by IVLBCL. High-dose cytarabine and prednisolone therapy was administered for three days, and repeated intrathecal injections of cytarabine and prednisolone were administered. The patient had responded well to these treatments, but in May 2012, he suffered from staggering gait, headache, and dysesthesia. MRI showed that a mass in the infarction lesion in the white matter around the left lateral ventricle had relapsed. The patient was administered the second course of CHASER, followed by whole brain irradiation, and MRI revealed shrinkage of the mass.

In June 2012, the patient was diagnosed with CNS relapse of IVLBCL, and high fever, shock, and bilateral diffuse pneumonia developed. Autopsy revealed diffuse infiltration of IVLBCL in the brain and respiratory failure due to bilateral pan-lobular pneumonia. Lymphoma cells were observed in capillaries in the choroid plexus, bilateral adrenal glands, fatty tissue around them, ectopic adrenal cortex tissue around the spleen and transverse colon. The lymphoma cells were CD20 (+), CD79a (+), CD10(−), Bcl-6(−), MUM-1(+), CD5(−), CD3(−), and CD56(−), with no lymphoma infiltration observed in the thyroid gland, liver, spleen, heart, skin, or bone marrow. No lymphadenopathy was detected. Unfortunately, the patient died in August 2012, one year after diagnosis.

Summary:
A 59-year-old Japanese man with a history of methotrexate-induced interstitial pneumonia and rheumatoid arthritis was admitted with fever, appetite loss, dyspnea on exertion, and skin rash. Blood testing revealed anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase and C-reactive protein, and bone marrow aspiration demonstrated atypical lymphocytes and hemophagocytosis by macrophages, suggesting lymphoma-associated hemophagocytic syndrome. He was diagnosed with the hemophagocytic-syndrome associated variant of intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVLBCL) and was treated with pulse steroid therapy and cyclophosphamide (CPA), followed by one course of CHOP and six courses of R-CHOP. Unfortunately, he developed CNS relapse of IVLBCL and died from respiratory failure due to bilateral pan-lobular pneumonia.

Hospital Course:

Baby O C, a 6-hour-old female, was admitted for evaluation and treatment of upper abdominal and lower chest defects, bodily rashes, and limb abnormalities. Prenatal ultrasounds were unremarkable. Upon admission, her respiratory rate was 99 cycles/min, SpO2 was 97%, and she weighed 3.5 kg. A diagnosis of POC, multiple limb anomalies, and cutaneous vascular malformations was made. Echocardiography revealed a small-sized patent ductus arteriosus.

Treatment:

Repair of the defects was carried out on the 4th day of life. The lower chest membrane was excised, and the lower lip of the diaphragm was mobilized and sutured to the upper lip, thereby closing the heart. Both hemisterni were apposed, and the anterior abdominal wall was closed with nylon 3/0 suture. The patient recovered from anesthesia without the need for mechanical ventilation and was discharged 18 days later.

Follow-up:

Baby O C has been followed up for 3 years with no further complications reported.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission: Southern rockhopper penguin, 5-year-old female (Case 2)

Chief Complaint: Weakness, dyspnea, reduced appetite.

History of Present Illness: The patient presented with a significantly decreased appetite and was observed floating in water. During physical examination, severe dyspnea and generalized weakness were noted. The penguin was given oral itraconazole for aspergillosis prophylaxis for the duration of relocation.

Course of Treatment: Shortly after induction, the bird died. Post-mortem radiographs showed increased soft tissue opacity in the lungs. Necropsy revealed dark red, wet lungs, friable spleen, and edematous pericardial sac. A well-demarcated white to yellow, raised, coelomic plaque was seen on the inner surface of the ribs, and there was a moderate amount of green fecal staining around the cloacal orifice.

Admission: Southern rockhopper penguin, 32-year-old female, (Case 3)

Chief Complaint: Weakness, dyspnea, anorexia.

History of Present Illness: The patient presented with weakness, anorexia, and dyspnea. Auscultation revealed harsh lung sounds. The penguin was treated with ponazuril, enrofloxacin, meloxicam, and furosemide for presumed pulmonary edema.

Course of Treatment: The bird died one hour after treatment. Necropsy examination revealed dark red, wet lungs, an enlarged, nodular spleen, and a small, focal, tan to brown, firm area in the caudal aspect of the left lung. Cytologic examination of lung tissue imprints from case 3 showed crescent-shaped protozoal zoites, toxic heterophils, and multinucleated giant cells.

Following the deaths of both penguins, the remaining flock was moved to an indoor, chilled holding area.

Overall, both cases show symptoms of respiratory distress and systemic organ involvement. Further investigation is requested to determine the underlying etiology.

Hospital Course:
The 40-year-old male patient was referred to an endodontist by a general dentist for assistance in locating root canals of the mandibular first molar. After undergoing an extensive examination, patency of root canals was confirmed. The access preparations were appropriately modified, and orifice shapers were used to enlarge the coronal areas of the canals. To close the gaps between the canal orifices and the gutta-percha points, a hot plugger was used to soften the gutta-percha, which was then adapted to the canal walls using a cold plugger.

Treatment:
The pulp chamber was exposed, and acid etching of the entire area was executed using 37% phosphoric acid. After rinsing and drying were completed, dentin bonding was applied according to the manufacturer's recommendations and was light-cured. The initial layers were built using dual-cured flowable resin, followed by hybrid composite for subsequent layers. The occlusal surface was then Levelled with a high-speed diamond bur for ideal endodontic reference points.

Outcome:
A stable coronal structure was achieved with access to each canal being administered effectively. During subsequent follow-up visits, there was reliable rubber dam isolation, and the composite buildup integrity was preserved throughout treatment. No complications were encountered during or after treatment.

Hospital Course: The patient, a 9-year-old boy, was admitted due to a 2-year history of epileptic seizures. The boy presented with delayed development, poor speech and mathematical abilities, and poor cognitive function. Upon examination, he showed dysarthria and bilateral enlargement of gastrocnemius muscles, but no sensory disturbances or ataxia. 

Diagnostic Tests: An EEG showed interparoxysmal multifocal spike-slow complex waves and sharp-slow complex waves in bilateral central-parietal areas and frontal midline area, which is consistent with partial seizures. A skeletal muscle biopsy was performed which showed a few degenerative, necrotic, and regenerative muscle fibers and moderate connective tissue hyperplasia. Sarcolemma showed partly positivity for dystrophin-N. Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) showed a duplication mutation in exons 37-44 in the Dystrophin gene, and was confirmed to be novel through genetic testing. 

Diagnosis: Based on the clinical and genetic evidence, a definitive diagnosis of BMD was made. 

Treatment: The patient was prescribed oxcarbazepine and administered 10 mg per day coenzyme Q10 for approximately 2 years. Two years later his symptoms relieved and an EEG showed less spikes and slow waves than it had previously shown. The patient had no adverse events and his motor function remained stable. 

Discharge Condition: The patient was discharged in improved condition. 

Follow-up Care: The patient is recommended to continue follow-up care with his primary care provider and neurologist.

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 20-year-old female with a history of type I (von Gierke) glycogen storage disease, who was transferred to the referral hospital for liver transplant evaluation. She had recently undergone a living-related renal transplant which failed due to renal vein thrombosis. Following an allograft nephrectomy, she developed multi-organ biochemical derangement, fulminant hepatic failure, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, renal failure, and anemia. She was admitted with a diagnosis of hepatic coma, with investigations revealing elevated transaminase levels, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated serum amylase, and significantly elevated lactate levels.

Upon admission, a CT scan of her head and abdomen was performed. There was no evidence of intracranial bleeding, however, a lower chest infiltrate was identified, and there was suspicion of hepatic vein thrombosis. Blood cultures were drawn on admission and later found to be positive for gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains, specifically Enterococcus faecalis. The patient was started on cefotetan and vancomycin therapy.

The following day, although her lactate levels and transaminases levels decreased, her lipase levels increased, and bilirubin levels climbed. Blood and sputum cultures from the third day were positive for Enterococcus faecalis.

The patient was stable for a short period of time, but on the fourth day, she became unresponsive, had diffuse edema, and developed metabolic acidosis and shock. Blood and sputum cultures remained positive for Enterococcus faecalis. The decision was made to perform an emergency hepatectomy with portocaval shunt, as the patient's liver was suspected to be the source of her sepsis.

Unfortunately, during the surgery, the patient became bradycardic and started bleeding through her endotracheal tube. Despite cardiopulmonary resuscitation, she did not respond, and arterial blood showed a severe respiratory acidosis with decreased oxygen levels. The patient was pronounced dead and an autopsy was carried out.

Final Diagnosis:

The patient had a history of type I (von Gierke) glycogen storage disease and had recently undergone a living-related renal transplant. Following renal failure, she received a second living-related renal transplant which thrombosed and had to be removed. Subsequently, she developed multi-organ biochemical derangement, fulminant hepatic failure, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, renal failure, and anemia. Investigations revealed elevated transaminase levels, hyperbilirubinemia, and significantly elevated lactate levels. Blood cultures were positive for Enterococcus faecalis.

Discharge Condition:

The patient passed away during the emergency hepatectomy surgery, and an autopsy was conducted.
