Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 17 years
Gender: Male
Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]
Hospital: ENT OPD

Admission Diagnosis: Left-sided tonsillar enlargement with a large, pale polypoidal growth

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with a 2-month history of recurrent fever and difficulty in swallowing. He had received several courses of oral antibiotic therapy but had a persistent left-sided pharyngeal discomfort. Examination of the oropharynx revealed left-sided tonsillar enlargement with a large, pale polypoidal growth. A CT scan revealed a poorly circumscribed, multiloculated hypodense mass with fluid accumulation. The mass was clinically diagnosed as a tonsillar cyst and polyps, parapharyngeal masses were considered as close possible differential diagnoses. It was attached to the lower pole of the left tonsil by a narrow elongated stalk.

Treatment:

The left tonsil and the pedunculated mass were removed by surgery. The patient's surgical site was monitored and managed appropriately with medication and care. Pain and discomfort post the surgery were managed using analgesic medication. The patient was discharged in a stable condition and advised to follow-up with ENT for further evaluation.

Diagnostic Data:

Gross examination showed an exophytic polypoid nodule measuring by 3.7 cm × 2.6 cm × 0.8 cm. Microscopy showed tonsillar tissue with underlying multiple dilated lymphatic spaces. The cystic spaces lined by endothelial cells were filled with lymph and lymphocytes. The surrounding stroma was infiltrated by lymphocytic aggregates, fibrous tissue and mature adipocytes. 

Diagnosis on Discharge:

Left-sided tonsillar enlargement with a large, pale polypoidal growth

Follow-up:

The patient is advised to follow-up with ENT for further evaluation.

The 17-year old male patient was admitted to ENT OPD with a 2-month history of recurrent fever and difficulty in swallowing. Hospital Course:
The patient is a 16-year-old female who presented with a 12-month history of mid-lower back pain that was worse in the morning, after sitting, and after activity. A lumbar Computed Tomography (CT) scan with and without contrast revealed evidence of left facet joint synovial enhancement with erosion along both sides of the joint at level L3-L4. Initial laboratory findings were negative for ANA, RF, anti-CCP, and HLA-B27. Lyme serology was not performed. She was diagnosed with seronegative juvenile idiopathic arthritis and started on prednisone 50mg daily for 10 days with clinical improvement of pain. She was then prescribed Naproxen 500mg twice daily, with minimal relief. Adalimumab 40mg subcutaneous (SQ) every two weeks was initiated, which was increased to 40mg SQ every week, and resulted in significant improvement of pain. She was also started on vitamin D 50,000IU weekly and 1g of calcium carbonate daily for eight weeks for vitamin D deficiency. Repeat imaging six months after adalimumab therapy (40mg SQ every week) showed no significant new changes. The patient was discharged in stable condition with a follow-up scheduled with her primary care physician.

Attending Physicians: [REDACTED]
Consulting Physicians: Rheumatology, Cardiology

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted with right-sided hemiparesis and aphasia due to a history of stroke seven months prior. The patient had been previously diagnosed with lupus anticoagulant, beta2-glycoprotein Ab, antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-dsDNA, and low complement levels. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed bicuspid aortic valve leaflets with mild aortic stenosis (AS) and mild aortic insufficiency (AI) with two nonmobile small masses on the tip of right cusp and non-coronary cusp suggestive of non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (Libman-Sacks endocarditis). The patient's diagnosis was systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS).

The patient was treated with intravenous (IV) heparin, which was then bridged to oral warfarin to achieve an international normalized ratio (INR) goal of 2-3. At one-year follow-up, the patient remained symptom-free without any SLE flare-up or cardiovascular incident. Follow-up TEE indicated no vegetations.

During surgery, it was discovered that the patient had a bulky pleural empyema (approximately two liters), right lung's lower lobe necrosis, a portion of right diaphragm destruction, and a necrosed cavity in the right liver. The right lower lobectomy was executed, in addition to diaphragm suture and pleural space cleaning and drainage.

The patient presented a satisfactory recovery after surgery. The pleural drain was removed on the ninth day after the operation, and the patient was discharged from the hospital 18 days later. The histopathological analysis of the resected lung demonstrated pneumonitis with necrosis and fibro-anthracosis. Five months after surgery, CT images illustrated complete recovery of pulmonary lesions and almost complete disappearance of hepatic lesion. Nine months after surgery, the patient is well and asymptomatic.

An endometrial polypectomy was performed under hysteroscopy and a large ligule vegetation was found in the posterior uterine wall near the fundus of the uterus, which was completely resected and sent for pathological examination. The pathology diagnosis was endometrial polyp, and an adenomyoma was discovered during regular ultrasound scans post-operation, indicating thickened endometrium and an ill-defined mass with continuous enlargement in the myometrium of the posterior uterine wall. The patient refused further hysteroscopic exploration, other treatment, and follow-up for one year.

On December 27, 2018, the patient was re-admitted for lower abdominal distension for over one week. A gynecological examination revealed that the patient's uterus had enlarged to the size of eight weeks gestation. A mass in the right adnexal area was found, which extended across and attached to the uterine body with unclear boundaries and poor mobility. Serum levels of Carcinoma Antigen 125 and estradiol were elevated. Ultrasound scans showed a heterogeneous echo cluster in the right annex area and pelvis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis revealed an irregular mass shadow in the right annex area that had mixed high signal on T2WI, low signal shadow, and partial high signal on T1WI.

Exploratory laparotomy was performed with a clinical preoperative diagnosis of right ovarian cancer and adenomyoma. The surgery revealed a mass in the right ovary that closely adhered to the surrounding peritoneum and affected the surrounding intestine. A mass was found in the anterior rectum, densely adhered to the posterior uterine wall, and the posterior cervix lip. The patient received transperitoneal retroperitoneal pelvic surgery combined with total viscera resection, including the uterus, bilateral appendages and rectum, omentectomy, appendectomy, lymphadenectomy, and ileostomy.

The tumor had also invaded the whole rectal wall, the greater omentum, and had a tumor embolus in the vascular system. There was no metastasis in the lymph nodes and no tumor cells in the peritoneal wash. Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [redacted]

Medical Record Number: [redacted]

Date of Admission: [redacted]          Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Admitting Diagnosis: Wilson's disease

Hospital Course:

An 8-year-old girl weighing 29.9 kg was admitted for deceased-donor liver transplantation due to Wilson's disease. Two days of perioperative prophylactic antibiotics - ampicillin and cefotaxime - were administered. Immunosuppression therapy post-transplant consisted of tacrolimus and methylprednisolone. The patient developed massive ascites after transplantation, most likely due to small graft and/or hepatic vein stenosis. On the 43rd postoperative day, the patient presented with fever and abdominal pain. An elevated white blood cell count with 85% neutrophils was also observed. Renal function was normal, and an elevated ascites cell count with 75% neutrophils suggested bacterial peritonitis. Piperacillin/tazobactam was initiated. Two days later, exploratory laparotomy detected abdominal abscess, and intensive peritoneal lavage was performed. MDR Enterobacteriaceae was isolated from ascites, and the antibiotics were switched to meropenem and gentamicin. Gentamicin was eventually discontinued, leaving the patient with meropenem alone. Meropenem dosing was increased due to suspected underdosing caused by massive ascites. Gradual improvement was observed, but relapse of bacterial peritonitis occurred six days after the completion of the initial meropenem course. The relapse was successfully treated with a second course of meropenem-based antibiotic therapy. However, a third episode of peritonitis occurred even after completion of the second course of therapy. Meropenem dosing strategy was altered, and prolonged meropenem administration was started, but it did not help much. Antibiotic prophylaxis was switched to cefmetazole, and eventually, the abscess disappeared from the peritoneum. The patient was discharged after the successful management of peritonitis.

An eight-year-old girl was admitted with Wilson's disease. She underwent deceased-donor liver transplantation and subsequently developed massive ascites. Bacterial peritonitis was observed postoperatively, requiring antibiotic treatment. The patient relapsed twice despite the treatment of the first course of antibiotics, and finally discharged after successful management of bacterial peritonitis.

The patient, a previously healthy five-and-a-half-year-old boy, presented to our hospital with painless distension of the abdomen for three years. The resection specimen was a multilocular cystic mass weighing 1,000 g, filled with serohemorrhagic fluid, and covered with a thin transparent wall. The patient recovered well after the procedure, and postoperative follow-up examinations were uneventful. The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions for routine postoperative care. Further follow-up was recommended with his primary care physician.

Hospital Course:
A 65-year-old Japanese female patient was admitted to our hospital for retrieval of a fragment of Peeso reamer that had broken during a root canal enlargement and that was embedded in the canal of her right mandibular first premolar, extending beyond the apex (tooth number 44). A customized interocclusal splint was fabricated to maintain the mandible in a repeatable position, which would be vital for the accuracy required for retrieving the small foreign body. The imaging data were obtained in a Digital Imaging and Communication in Medicine format and transferred to a Medtronic StealthStation S7 workstation with Synergy Fusion Cranial 2.2.6 software. After data registration was complete, continuous three-dimensional tracking of the navigation probe was available to the surgeon in real time, allowing the surgeon to locate the foreign object and remove it successfully.

Postoperative radiographs confirmed the complete removal of the fractured segment. Our patient was discharged later that day. Follow-up after the prosthetic treatment was uneventful; her clinical course was good.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Migration of a broken endodontic instrument beyond the apical foramen into the mandible.

Discharge Instructions:
Our patient was advised to maintain good oral hygiene and follow up with her dentist regularly. No further action was required.

Discharge Summary:

Identification:

This is a discharge summary for a 27-year-old male who presented with floaters in his right eye and was diagnosed with Toxoplasma retinochorioditis.

Hospital Course:

The patient's medical history included CML on remission, chemoradiation, and allogenic bone marrow transplantation. He was on prophylactic medications along with several immunosuppressive agents. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed irregular, fluffy, white subretinal and intraretinal lesions with pigmentary changes, and a smaller similar lesion in the left eye. Differential diagnosis included viral retinochoroiditis vs. CML relapse vs. atypical toxoplasmosis. Serum IgM and IgG titers for CMV and toxoplasmosis were negative, and CSF analysis showed no evidence of CML relapse. MRI brain/orbits showed no abnormalities. Intravenous cidofovir had recently been started. Two weeks after presentation, visual acuity decreased, and examination revealed a progression of the retinal lesions with a mild vitritis. An anterior chamber paracentesis was performed, and the aqueous humor was sent for PCR. A more aggressive treatment of the CMV retinitis was also pursued with bilateral intravitreal injections of foscarnet in addition to intravenous route. Five days later, quantitative PCR analysis revealed Toxoplasma gondii, and a diagnosis of Toxoplasma retinochorioditis was made. Clindamycin was injected intravitreally OU twice at 4 days apart. Over the next month, the active areas of retinochoroiditis regressed followed by gliosis of the lesions with pigmentary changes. The vision subsequently improved.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Toxoplasma retinochorioditis.

Discharge Medications:

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Disposition:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with follow-up instructions.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 37-year-old female with a history of dyslipidemia, asthma, and fibroids, presented to the emergency room reporting two weeks of bilateral posterior neck pain and headaches. She initially presented with right-sided neck pain, which she attributed to various physical activities and sleeping in uncomfortable hotel beds.

Physical Exam:
The patient showed muscular tenderness but no midline or cervical spinous process tenderness. There was no rigidity, with full active and passive range of motion without pain. Neurological exam was within normal limits.

Diagnostic Results:
CT head/brain without IV contrast showed nonspecific left cerebellar hypodensities that may represent age-indeterminate embolic infarcts/injuries among other possible etiologies, with no acute intracranial hemorrhage. Head MRI without contrast (DWI sequence) showed large areas of acute ischemia in the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) territory with additional smaller areas of acute ischemia in the left superior parasagittal cerebellum. CT angiography of the head and neck with and without IV contrast demonstrated a relatively abrupt change in the caliber of the left V3 vertebral artery suggestive of dissection and a short segment high-grade narrowing of the right vertebral artery also highly suggestive of a dissection.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with bilateral cervical arterial dissection.

Treatment:
The patient was started on intravenous heparin at 1,000 units/hr without initial bolus and close monitoring. Additionally, aspirin and atorvastatin were also started. She was eventually bridged to warfarin with an international normalized ratio (INR) goal of 2–3.

Follow-Up:
The patient will follow up with neurology as an outpatient. INR was monitored biweekly and remained within therapeutic range throughout the 3 months. MR angiography after three months showed complete resolution of the dissection. The patient did not report any bleeding complications from dual therapy.

Hospital Course Summary:

This is a hospital course summary for a 71-year-old Japanese woman who was admitted to Toranomon hospital because of reduced consciousness. She had a history of a mastectomy for right breast cancer. Eight months before admission, she came to the hospital because of partial paralysis of her right hand. A chest computed tomography (CT) scan showed a mass in the left upper lobe, as well as lymphadenopathy. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed multiple brain metastases. The patient was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma using transbronchial lung biopsy. She received chemotherapy and radiotherapy but her state of consciousness rapidly worsened in the 2 weeks before admission. 

On admission, lumbar puncture was performed and cytological examination of her cerebrospinal fluid revealed adenocarcinoma cells. Erlotinib at 150 mg/day was dissolved in 15 mL of water, and was administered via a feeding tube because she could not swallow a tablet. At the same time, dexamethasone and glycerin administration were started via drip infusion. The patient’s state of consciousness gradually improved with this treatment. As a side effect of erlotinib, diarrhea of the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 4.0 grade 2 developed. Three weeks after receiving erlotinib and steroids, the patient started to vomit and suffered from grade 3 diarrhea. At that time, she was diagnosed with pneumatosis intestinalis (PI). 

PI was managed conservatively with a combination of antibiotics and inhalation of oxygen. Two weeks later, the CT findings of PI were improved. Erlotinib was re-administered without steroids, and PI relapsed 4 weeks later with diarrhea. After improving PI by discontinuation of erlotinib and conservative therapies, gefitinib was administered safely without PI and diarrhea for 3 months. At that time, the number of cells in the cerebral fluid decreased with erlotinib and gefitinib, although the cytology was still positive for adenocarcinoma. 

The patient died of worsening brain metastases 8 months after the diagnosis of LM.

Hospital course:
The patient, a 36-year-old female, presented to the outpatient otorhinolaryngology clinic with a 3-week history of headache in November 2005. She reported worsening symptoms despite ongoing antibiotic therapy, including nausea, vomiting, myalgia, and general weakness. A brain CT scan was initially performed, which showed no lesions. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was then performed, which revealed a 2.5-cm sellar and suprasellar mass with heterogeneous enhancement, suspicious invasion to both cavernous sinuses, and left maxillary sinusitis. The mass compressed the optic chiasm, and her serum prolactin level was 123.17 ng/mL before surgery. The patient underwent a gross-total resection based on the initial diagnosis of pituitary macroadenoma with 3rd and 6th nerve palsy. Following the surgery, a residual nodular enhancement was identified, which led to radiotherapy (total dose 5,040 Gy) being undertaken.
The patient was readmitted 6 months later with a one-month history of left cheek and periauricular pain, difficulty opening her mouth, and pain, swelling, and local heating. Radiologic assessment revealed a soft tissue mass with cortical destruction and a permeative osteolytic lesion at the left mandibular ramus. A partial mandibulectomy was performed, and the histologic features and immunohistochemical results were identical to those observed in the previous pituitary tumor. A primary pituitary carcinoma was confirmed from the histopathologic findings and a metastasis. The patient died approximately nine months after the initial diagnosis, in August 2006.

The patient received appropriate care and support and was educated on the importance of maintaining good oral hygiene and regular dental checkups. She was discharged with no reports of complications.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 13-year-old girl, was admitted to our hospital with a history of nocturnal enuresis and circular bald patches on her head. She had received previous treatment at a local hospital with corticosteroids and liquid nitrogen therapy, which had not completely cured her condition. 

Medical History:
The patient's medical history was significant for parental divorce 6 years prior, after which the bald patches on her head began to appear and grow. Her mother remarried 1 year later, after which the hair loss became more severe. Peripheral blood and biochemical tests revealed no aberrations, and autoantibodies and thyroid hormones were within the reference ranges. 

Psychological Evaluation:
The results of psychological testing showed moderate to high levels of depression and anxiety. The patient's basic interpersonal relationship stance was reported as 'I am not OK, You are OK', with a high score on the Nurturing Parent subscale and a low score on the Free Child subscale. The patient was encouraged to speak about interesting episodes in her daily life to promote a more proactive and positive ego state. 

Treatment:
The patient was provided with unconditional positive affirmations, including reassurance that she was important regardless of hair loss. Six months later, new hair growth was observed as the patient became more confident in talking about herself. Two years later, the bald patch had completely disappeared and there has been no recurrence of any bald patches during 5 years since her initial examination. 

Follow-Up:
Upon discharge, the patient was instructed to continue to maintain positive self-talk and to seek mental health counseling if needed. She was advised to follow up with her primary care physician on a regular basis for routine check-ups.

The patient presented with a progressive locoregional recurrence of previously treated luminal A breast cancer.

The patient was diagnosed with progressive locoregional recurrence of previously treated luminal A breast cancer, with metastases to the sternum, mediastinal LN, chest wall, and pleura.

Discharge Summary:
Patient Identification:
The patient is a 16-year-old female with dyspnoea on exertion that worsened in the supine position. She had productive cough, intermittent fever and dysphagia for solid food for 1 month and was referred to a pulmonologist for management of her condition. She underwent right lateral thoracotomy and excision of tumour for a benign mature teratoma. 

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with dyspnoea on exertion that worsened in the supine position. She was treated with antibiotics and bronchodilators to reduce breathlessness, and transfusion of 2 units of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) to improve haemoglobin levels. Her pulse rate was 110/min and her blood pressure was 110/60 mmHg. On physical examination, there was reduced air entry in the right supraclavicular, infraclavicular, mammary and subscapular areas and dullness on percussion. CT scan of the thorax revealed a lobulated heterogeneous solid cystic mass on the right side of the superior mediastinum, extending from the level of the inlet of the thorax to the upper part of the right atrium. She underwent fibreoptic bronchoscopy (FOB), which showed no extrinsic compression on the airway.

During induction of anaesthesia, the patient was initially intubated with a 26Fr left-sided double-lumen tube (DLT), which failed to achieve single lung ventilation. After the third attempt, the patient started desaturating, and ventilation with 100% O2 and intubation with a 6.00 mm cuffed oral endotracheal tube was performed. As the patient developed bradycardia, Inj. Atropine 0.02 mg/kg was administered, but there was no improvement; the patient responded to Inj adrenaline (1 mg/kg) I.V. and developed tachycardia (150-170 bpm). The patient finally achieved ventilation, although insufficiently, after the 6.0 mm tube was replaced with a 7.0 mm tube using a tube exchanger.

After excision of the tumour, the patient was ventilated in the ICU for 24 h. Inotropic support was tapered on the second day, and the patient was extubated on the third post-operative day. She had an uneventful course and got discharged after 10 days.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
The patient was diagnosed with a benign mature teratoma in the right side of the superior mediastinum. She underwent right lateral thoracotomy and excision of tumour for the same. During anaesthesia, there were multiple attempts to intubate the patient successfully, and the patient finally achieved ventilation after the 6.0 mm tube was replaced with a 7.0 mm tube using a tube exchanger.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to follow-up for a comprehensive evaluation to assess the adequacy of ventilation and monitor the pulmonary oedema.

Gender: Female
Diagnosis: Dilated Cardiomyopathy

Hospital Course: 
The patient underwent orthotropic cardiac transplantation by biatrial technique due to dilated cardiomyopathy. The thyroid hormone function tests of the donor were normal, and the patient's thyroid hormone levels were within normal range preoperatively. After the surgery, the patient's haemodynamic status was uneventful for the first 20 hours. However, in the 15th hour, the patient was extubated, and arterial blood pressure decreased with bradyarrhythmic episodes. Temporary pacing was initiated, and adrenalin was given to manage the patient's low blood pressure. Subsequently, dopamine infusion therapy was started to maintain haemodynamic stability. During this period, thyroid hormone levels were low and needed replacement therapy. The dopamine infusion therapy continued for six days, and the patient's pulse rate was adequate by the end of the sixth day. On the seventh day post-surgery, the patient's thyroid hormone levels returned to normal. The patient was discharged uneventfully on the 30th postoperative day.

The patient's thyroid hormone levels were low and needed replacement therapy. Hospital Course:

The 36-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital with jaundice and abdominal pain, which had persistently worsened for the past five days. Physical examination revealed a palpable liver and upper abdominal tenderness without rebound tenderness. Computer tomography scans indicated hepatosplenomegaly, splenic parenchymal and perisplenic hemorrhage, ascites, and enlarged lymph nodes of the peritoneal cavity. A diagnosis of splenic rupture was confirmed by CT scans. Splenectomy was performed shortly after admission with the biopsy of liver implemented simultaneously. 

Final Diagnosis:

Upon microscopic examination, the liver showed damage to its normal structure, while numerous monomorphic medium-sized cells with pale/amphophilic cytoplasm infiltrated the portal areas and sinusoids. The spleen showed an expansion of the red pulp and the presence of neoplastic cells in the cords and sinuses of red pulp, resembling the cells that infiltrated into the liver. The neoplastic cells were positive for CD3ε, CD56, CD16, CD43, Granzyme B, TIA-1 and showed a proliferation index of approximately 90% evaluated by Ki-67 staining. The EBER-ISH was positive for most of the abnormal cells. No cloned TCR-γ gene rearrangement was detected, ultimately leading to a diagnosis of aggressive natural killer cell leukemia/lymphoma (ANKL).

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient had a rapidly worsening clinical course leading to a diagnosis of ANKL with splenic rupture. Despite splenectomy and biopsy of the liver, the patient suffered from multiple organ dysfunction syndromes and eventually succumbed to multi-organ failure 14 days after hospitalization. The family did not provide consent for an autopsy.

Hospital Course Summary:

Chief Complaint:
The patient presented with a history of seizures for one year.

History:
The patient had focal dyscognitive seizures with secondary generalization. This was characterized by a transient sense of dizziness followed by a vacant blank stare, loss of contact with the surroundings, and deviation of eyes to the left side. There was then tonnic clonic movements in the left upper and lower limbs with a loss of consciousness that lasted between 3-4 minutes. Following the seizure, the patient had amnesia.

Past Medical History:
The patient was born out of a non-consanguineous marriage. Both the delivery and the developmental milestones were normal. The patient had multiple hyperpigmented lesions over the neck, abdomen, and back since birth. These lesions were progressive in nature and had become more pigmented and hyperkeratotic over the last 3-4 years. Lesions were not preceded by blistering or inflammatory changes. The patient had posterior subcapsular cataract in both eyes.

Physical Examination:
On examination, the patient had normal skeletal and mental development appropriate to her age. The patient had multiple hyperpigmented and hyperkeratotic verrucous plaques over the face, arms, legs, chest, back, and abdomen distributed in a blaschkoid pattern. The patient also had acanthocytosis nigricans over the nape of the neck. The patient was not hirsute or obese, had no hair or nail abnormality.

Investigations:
Electroencephalography revealed focal right temporal sharp and slow wave discharges, and magnetic resonance imaging of brain with contrast did not show any abnormality. All other routine investigations were normal including fasting glucose and insulin levels.

Diagnosis:
A diagnosis of epidermal nevus syndrome was considered, and patient was subjected to skin biopsy, which showed epidermal acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, orthokeratosis, papillomatosis, and finger-like papillary projections without any signs of epidermolysis, with variable pigmentation of basal layer of epidermis. The histopathologic findings were suggestive of non-epidermolytic, non-organoid keratinocytic type of epidermal nevus with associated acanthosis nigricans.

Management:
Anti-epileptic therapy with oxcarbazepine was titrated to a dose of 15 mg/kg/day leading to complete seizure control over the last one year. For skin lesions, she was treated with topical tretinoin cream 0.025 percent once daily for 6 months with not much improvement. Ablative CO2 laser treatment is planned as the next line of treatment for her skin lesions.

Patient Information:
- Name: (redacted)
- Age: 61
- Sex: Male
- Admitting Diagnosis: Ibogaine-Induced QT Prolongation, Cotriggered by Secondary Hypokalemia

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the clinic with a history of opioid dependency related to chronic pain. He was administered ibogaine capsules to address his opioid addiction symptoms and achieve an anticraving effect, which resulted in severe gastrointestinal symptoms including vomiting and diarrhea. The patient showed significant alterations in consciousness, and as a result, was urgently transferred to the nearest hospital.

Upon arrival, the patient was unresponsive, and his pulse was not palpable. Initially, a wide QRS complex tachycardia was revealed in the 12-lead ECG with a rate of 270 rpm. Emergent defibrillation was performed which converted the patient to a sinus rhythm, but the ECG revealed massive QT prolongation leading to ventricular bigeminy. The patient's hypokalemia was corrected aggressively, and his hemodynamics improved with supportive treatment. Laboratory testing for cointoxication was negative.

Despite extensive investigations, no evidence of significant heart disease was found. Serial ECGs demonstrated delayed recovery of corrected QT intervals, which took 7 days to recover completely. The patient underwent an exercise treadmill test to screen for hereditary long-QT syndrome in which he demonstrated normal QT dynamics during exercise and recovery.

Disposition:
The patient was diagnosed with ibogaine-induced QT prolongation triggered by secondary hypokalemia, which led to ventricular tachycardia. After successful recovery, he was discharged home. No genetic testing was performed due to the well-known cardiotoxic effects of ibogaine.

Hospital Course:
The 37-year-old male presented with sustained proptosis, fullness of the right upper eyelid, and inferior displacement of the right eye that had developed gradually over several months, without experiencing pain, loss of visual acuity, or diplopia. Upon examination, a slight limitation of supraduction was observed. The patient reported no prior episodes of inflammation, sinus infection, or trauma. 

Diagnostic Findings:
Contrast-enhanced coronal and sagittal CT scans disclosed a lytic lesion arising from the roof of the right orbit. The mass had a thinning effect on the superior wall of the roof, extended over the anterior cranial fossa, and had intratumoral foci of mineralization. The lesion was heterogeneously enhancing, hyperintense on T1-weighted MRI images, and with a lobulated, pseudonodular appearance, along with a markedly increased signal intensity on T2-weighted images.

Treatment:
An orbitotomy was performed, and the lesion was removed using an ultrasonic aspirator system. The mass was separated from the healthy tissue and fragments of bone tissue within the soft tissue removed. Following the procedure, a leak of cerebrospinal fluid originating in the innermost part of the cavity was observed, which was efficiently sealed using human fibrinogen/human thrombin. The capsule and the tissue attached to the cortical surface of bone were removed, and a curettage was performed. The patient was prescribed 1 week of oral antibiotics.

Follow-up:
After 18 months of follow-up, there were no signs of recurrence, and the patient's symptoms had resolved.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A

Medical Record Number: N/A

Date of Admission: N/A

Date of Discharge: N/A

Hospital Course:

This 8-year-old female patient presented to the oral and maxillofacial surgery department of Saint Rafaël hospital of Leuven, Belgium, for a maleruption of the left lower first molar. The patient did not have any complaints, besides the fact that the 3.6 was not erupting, and she did not mention any pain or tenderness to palpation. After clinical extra- and intraoral examination, a panoramic radiography was performed, and a cone beam CT was carried out, which presented the buccal localization of the lesion with an extended resorption of the vestibular cortical plate and a periosteal reaction.

Surgical treatment was performed under general anesthesia, creating a mucoperiosteal intrasulcular triangular flap prepared from the distal side of the lower left second premolar to the distal margin of the lower left second molar. The jaw bone was deperiostized, and an osteotomy was done in order to have access to the cyst. By finding the clivage plane, the lesion was enucleated, and a curettage of the residual bony cavity was performed. The residual surgical area was thoroughly rinsed with sterile 0.9% NaCl, and the flap was replaced by simple interrupted stitches suture with resorbable suture (Vicryl 3/0).

Anatomopathological analysis revealed a vestibular cyst, microscopically characterized by inflammatory infiltration of neutrophils, plasma cells, lymphocytes, and eosinophils. Based on clinical, radiographic, and histological examination, the diagnosis of MBBC was established.

After two years, a follow-up cone beam CT was carried out in order to evaluate the eruption pattern of the mandibular first molar. It was evident that the first molar erupted in the right place, still showing some minor buccal tilting. A slight bone defect was still noticed on the buccal area at the site of the bifurcation. Interestingly, the second mandibular molar was mesially tilted and was not able to erupt due to impaction at the distal edge of the first mandibular molar.

Summary:

This discharge summary is being provided for an 8-year-old female patient who was admitted to Saint Rafaël hospital of Leuven, Belgium, for a maleruption of the left lower first molar. Surgical treatment was performed under general anesthesia, and the patient was diagnosed with MBBC, which was subsequently treated by enucleation and curettage of the residual bony cavity. A follow-up CT scan was carried out after two years, and it showed that the first molar erupted in the right place with buccal tilting. A slight bone defect was still present on the buccal area, and the second mandibular molar was mesially tilted and was not able to erupt due to impaction at the distal edge of the first mandibular molar.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a 2-month history of mid-back pain and mild motor weakness of the lower extremities. The patient had tenderness over the left iliac bone, and a neurological examination revealed severe impairment of deep sensation and hypalgesia up to the level of T9.

Initial laboratory examination showed a normal white blood cell (WBC) count, C-reactive protein (CRP), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), but a QuantiFERON-TB test was negative. Radiographic imaging showed a T8 and T9 compression fracture with destruction of the anterior and mid vertebral bodies. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a collapsed T8 and T9 disc space with a paraspinal soft-tissue collection compressing the cord at the same level.

A T8 and T9 decompressive laminectomy and decompression of the soft-tissue component compressing the cord was performed. A specimen was sent for histopathological and culture sensitivity analysis. Postoperatively, the patient was relieved of mid-back pain, and the motor weakness was improved, but deep sensory impairment persisted. Six weeks later, M. tuberculosis was detected from the cultured specimen, and antitubercular treatment was started.

At the 3-month follow-up, the laboratory examination showed a mild increase in the CRP and ESR but no change in the size of bony destruction or the epidural soft-tissue lesion. The patient reported mild motor weakness of both lower limbs and was able to walk without support, with deep sensory impairment still persisting. Antitubercular treatment was continued for 6 months.

Six months postoperatively, the patient presented with recurrence of mid-back pain and moderate paraplegia. MRI showed an increase in the size of the epidural soft-tissue mass compressing the dural sac. The patient underwent a laminectomy of T6–7 and T10–11, removal of scar fibrous tissue around T8 and T9, and bilateral pedicle screws and rod fixation on T5–7 and T10–11.

Histopathological findings ruled out TB spondylitis, showing only chronic inflammatory changes. Two months after the second surgery, the patient reported improvement in back pain and motor weakness, with slight sensory improvement. Six months after the second surgery, bony fusion developed, with remodeling of the vertebral body, and CT showed no further progression of the kyphotic deformity. MRI showed that the paravertebral abscess was resolving and decreasing in size.

The antitubercular treatment was completed at 6 months, and the laboratory examination showed a mild increase in the CRP and ESR. The patient was discharged with the recommendation for further outpatient follow-up.

Diagnosis:
1. T8 and T9 spondylodiscitis
2. Pyogenic spondylodiscitis
3. Pott's spine
4. Metastatic tumor compression fracture

Condition at Discharge:
The patient's back pain and motor weakness were improving, with slight improvement in deep sensory impairment. The patient was discharged with instructions for further outpatient follow-up.

Follow-up Recommendations:
1. Follow-up with primary care physician for regular monitoring and management of comorbidities.
2. Follow-up with neurologist for monitoring of mid-back pain, motor weakness, and deep sensory impairment.
3. Follow-up with infectious disease specialist for ongoing management and treatment of T8 and T9 spondylodiscitis and mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
4. Follow-up with surgeon for regular monitoring of postoperative recovery and rehabilitation progress.

Admitting Diagnosis:
Metrorrhagia, Bilateral pelvic tumors, Myoma of uterus, Bilateral breast pain and swelling

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our department of gynecology with symptoms of metrorrhagia, bilateral pelvic tumors, and myoma of the uterus. A total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed to make a definitive diagnosis of the tumors. The patient was also referred to the breast cancer outpatient clinic for bilateral breast pain and swelling.

Physical examination revealed diffuse induration with uneven surface and tenderness in the bilateral breast. The density of the bilateral breast was high, but no mass or calcification was detected by mammography. Ultrasonography showed diffuse mottled hypoechoic lesions in the bilateral mammary glands. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the right breast showed an extensive enhanced area in the mammary gland with edema of retromammary adipose tissue and skin in the delayed phase. Axillary lymph node swelling was also detected by MRI.

Core needle biopsy of the right breast revealed diffuse infiltration of signet-ring cells in the mammary gland and intracytoplasmic lumens also were seen. The pathologic examinations of the resected pelvic tumors also revealed signet-ring cells in the bilateral ovaries, suggesting that the tumor metastasized from another site.

Further investigations were conducted, and it was discovered that the primary site of the metastasis was an ulcerative lesion similar to a Borrmann type 4 tumor in the lower part of the stomach. Pathologic examination of a biopsy specimen from the stomach revealed infiltration of signet-ring cells similar to the infiltration observed in the breasts and ovaries.

The breast lesions were diagnosed as metastases from the gastric carcinoma, and combination therapy of S-1 and cisplatin was administered after the diagnosis. The metastatic tumors in the breasts became impalpable after two cycles of therapy. Further, MRI of the right breast showed neither enhancement nor edematous changes.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Metastatic breast cancer, Gastric carcinoma

The patient is to follow up with their primary care physician for ongoing monitoring. They should continue their current regimen of medication as prescribed.

Chief Complaint: Penetrating injury with scissors.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 51-year-old woman, was admitted with a penetrating injury to the right upper eyelid caused by scissors. The injury caused subarachnoid hemorrhage, frontal lobe hemorrhage, and intraventricular hemorrhage, which affected the patient's mental state and caused neck stiffness.  The scissors entered the skull through the right orbital roof and crossed the midline of the brain, leading to TICA identified at the right CM-CA junction. The patient underwent surgery two days later and had a skull defect in the anterior cranial fossa, which was repaired with a galeal flap. After the hematoma adjacent to the TICA was removed, bleeding developed from the CM-CA junction due to two ruptured sites at the left side wall of the cortical artery and two injured sites at the right side wall of the cortical artery. The patient underwent a proximal and distal clip application, resulting in partial stenosis of the CM lumen and a small infarction in the left frontal lobe. The patient developed postoperative meningitis due to methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, which was treated with vancomycin and conservative therapy. Follow-up angiography performed two months later showed no residual aneurysm and a preserved right callosomarginal arterial flow, with no flow in one cortical artery.

Discharge Diagnosis: Penetrating injury with subarachnoid hemorrhage, frontal lobe hemorrhage, intraventricular hemorrhage, TICA, and postoperative meningitis.

Disposition: Discharged in stable condition.

Reason for Admission:
Patient presented with nausea, vomiting, and dyspnea, shortly after consuming liver and gonads of a fish that he had caught. He had perioral paraesthesia, limb muscle weakness, and acute respiratory failure with bradypnea, which quickly led to cardiac arrest. The patient was diagnosed with tetrodotoxin poisoning, due to the temporal proximity of clinical manifestations to the consumption of the fish.

Hospital Course:
The patient was transferred to the ICU, where he was provided with supportive treatment. The fish remnants were analyzed and identified as the poisonous Lagocephalus sceleratus. The patient had complete muscle paralysis, with no motor responses and a lack of pupil reactions, and deep coma (GCS of 3). Given his severe condition, and having assessed several possible treatment options and outcomes, the medical team decided to treat the patient with a cholinesterase inhibitor. Intravenous neostigmine (2.5 mg) was administered 4 times within the first 24 hours of admission. After the first dose, deep tendon reflexes were noted, and the comatose state was reversed. The patient completed a course of 4 doses of neostigmine over the next 24 hours. A significant improvement was observed with complete recovery of muscle strength and return to full consciousness.
 
Outcome:
The patient made an uneventful recovery over the next several days. He showed no signs of muscle weakness, and there was no recurrence of paraesthesia. All deep tendon reflexes were present and intact, and his level of consciousness was within normal range. The patient was discharged after 36 hours of admission. 

Recommendations:
The patient should avoid consuming fish that are potentially poisonous or toxic. It is recommended that the patient follow-up with his primary care provider to assess any potential long-term effects or implications of the toxin exposure.

Patient Information:
26-year-old female patient with a history of epigastric pain, night sweating, and weight loss.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Center with a 1-month history of epigastric pain. Examination revealed a palpable, slightly mobile, and tender epigastric mass. Barium meal study showed an ill-defined mass involving gastric fundus and extending into gastric cardia and lower gastroesophageal junction. A chest, abdominal, and pelvic contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scans showed a 3.8 × 7.2 × 8.7 cm ill-defined mass, involving gastric fundus and extending into gastric cardia and lower gastroesophageal junction. It was associated with multiple enlarged gastrohepatic lymph nodes; the largest measured 1.2 cm. A CT-guided tissue biopsy was obtained and revealed DSRCT. Positron emission tomography (PET) scans showed hypermetabolic fluorodeoxyglucose- (FDG-) avid mass lesion in gastric fundus, extending into gastric cardia and lower gastroesophageal junction. In addition, it was associated with a few hypermetabolic FDG-avid lesions in the gastrohepatic junction, indicating lymph node metastases. Patient then underwent total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy, splenectomy, and antecolic Roux-en-Y esophagojejunal anastomosis. All resection margins were free from tumor cells. Metastatic tumor was found in five out of eighteen gastrohepatic lymph nodes. The common hepatic artery lymph nodes and the porta-hepatis lymph nodes were all reactive and negative for malignancy. The lymph nodes around the celiac access, splenic artery, and splenic hilum were involved and enlarged. Spleen showed no significant pathology. No evidence of ascites or peritoneal carcinomatosis was detected. The resected specimen was analyzed by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) technique and confirmed the diagnosis of DSRCT of stomach by identifying the characteristic EWS-WT1 gene fusion protein. A postoperative 3-month followup failed to show any recurrence.

Diagnosis:
DSRCT of the stomach.

Treatment:
Total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy, splenectomy, and antecolic Roux-en-Y esophagojejunal anastomosis.

Follow-up Care:
Patient was discharged on the 10th postoperative day in a good condition and received no adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

Summary:
This is a case of a 26-year-old female patient with a diagnosis of DSRCT of the stomach, who underwent total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy, splenectomy, and antecolic Roux-en-Y esophagojejunal anastomosis. The resected specimen was analyzed by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) technique and confirmed the diagnosis of DSRCT of stomach by identifying the characteristic EWS-WT1 gene fusion protein. A postoperative 3-month followup failed to show any recurrence. The patient was discharged in a good condition and received no adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Primary Diagnosis: AA Amyloidosis

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with rising levels of serum creatinine, which were between 1.7 and 1.9 mg/dL. The patient had a history of ankylosing spondylitis and long-standing hypertension. A kidney transplant biopsy revealed 23% amorphous eosinophilic material around the hilum and focal mesangium and capillary walls. The patient was diagnosed with AA amyloidosis after Congo red staining revealed apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Electron microscopy revealed fibrillar deposits in mesangial areas.

The patient had a history of using long-term anti-inflammatory agents, which had caused tubulointerstitial nephritis. The patient received a living-related kidney transplant approximately 8 years prior to the biopsy. The patient's baseline immunosuppressive medications consisted of mycophenolate mofetil and tacrolimus. Physical examination findings revealed flexion deformity and decreased range of motion of the cervical spine.

Further tests revealed increased C-reactive protein and rheumatoid factor. Serologic tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody were negative. Anti-nuclear antibody and anti-SSA/SSB titers were within normal limits.

The patient underwent a left hip arthroplasty that revealed AA amyloidosis involving the arteries of the head of femur. The patient received colchicine and was started on adalimumab. Two months after initiation of adalimumab, the serum creatinine was 1.9 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 10 mm/h, and C-reactive protein was less than 3 mg/L. The urinary protein/creatinine ratio was 0.28.

Recommendations:

The patient's care was managed by a multidisciplinary team including a nephrologist, rheumatologist, and orthopedic surgeon. The patient will require regular follow-up visits to monitor the progression of AA amyloidosis and the effectiveness of treatment with colchicine and adalimumab. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Age: 65-year-old female

Brief Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with a 2-month history of progressive dysphagia and 5 kg weight loss. The upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed a 4 cm whitish firm mass in the middle esophagus along with a semi-circumferential deep ulcer with irregular borders on the opposite mucosa. A pedicle was not identified during handling a polypectomy snare around the esophageal mass. The upper gastrointestinal series showed an ovoid lacunar image at the distal part of the esophagus with inhomogeneous, calcifications and smooth contours. The esophageal lumen was enlarged with a diverticula development at the posterior wall. CT of the thorax excluded a pedunculated tumor, describing an intra-luminal calcified esophageal mass. Biopsies obtained from the esophageal ulcerated mucosa revealed inflammatory cells, without malignancy. Based on these results, a bezoar was supposed to have been developed in an esophageal diverticula, subsequently with ulcerated mucosa.

The esophageal mass was removed with an endoscopic snare in one piece, as the fragmentation was not physically possible. The macroscopic appearance revealed a 4 cm, globular mass, heterogeneous, dense, whitish, in places with harsh yellow foci, most likely dystrophic calcification. Microscopic examination revealed hyaline fibrous tissue with numerous crystalline basophils deposits of minerals, rare fibrocytes, and very few vessels. A definitive histological diagnosis was not possible as the pedicle was not identified, but the presence of the connective tissue suggested the previous presence of a pedicle into the lesion. 

One month later, the patient was asymptomatic. Endoscopy did not reveal an enlarged esophagus, the appearance of the esophageal mucosa was normal, and no diverticula was identified. No motility disturbances were found on esophageal manometry.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The final diagnosis was an esophageal benign mesenchymal originating mass (most probably a fibrovascular polyp) auto-amputated and calcified. The long term calcium tablets intake might explain the calcification process developed into the vascular-connective tissue. 

Disposition:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions for follow-up care.

A 62-year-old white male was admitted to our hospital with right abdominal and flank pain. Workup revealed a right adrenal mass, which led to suspicion for pheochromocytoma. Serum and urinary metanephrines were obtained, and the patient was started on phenoxybenzamine blockade prior to planned right adrenalectomy. The pituitary adenoma was treated with transsphenoidal resection, but the patient did not regain visual function in follow-up. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]

Hospital Course:
This is a summary of the hospital course for a 68-year-old male with a chief complaint of left thumb numbness with a palpable mass along the flexor surface of his thumb. The patient suffered from tingling in his left hand mainly at night for the last 3 years, weakened grip while bowling, difficulty performing daily living activities, along with mild arthritis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Clinical examination showed a left-thumb mass, decreased range of motion in the neck, positive Tinel's sign over the left-thumb mass and at the carpal tunnel bilaterally, and a positive carpal compression test on the left.

The patient underwent several tests, including electrodiagnostic testing which was negative for any compressive neuropathy or cervical radiculopathy. The diagnosis of bowler's thumb was made after a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of his left hand detected no definite abnormal signal or lesion at the region corresponding to the palpable mass. The patient underwent surgical intervention, which involved a Bruner incision marked out over the proximal aspect of the ulnar side of the thumb with an extension into the palm. The ulnar digital nerve of the left thumb was exposed, revealing extensive scar tissue and fibrosis surrounding approximately 3 cm of the nerve. Neurolysis of the ulnar digital nerve was completed, and the nerve was wrapped with an AxoGuard Nerve Protector placed in 2 different locations, both proximally and distally, and loosely sewn into place with 8-0 interrupted nylon sutures.

The patient's postoperative evaluation showed that he reported alleviation of his pain and numbness, with 2-point discrimination found to be 5 mm at the ulnar side of the thumb. Subsequent visits showed continued improvement in symptoms, with Tinel's sign at the thumb web space no longer present.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Bowler's Thumb

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition improved significantly post-surgery with alleviation of pain and numbness and improved range of motion. The patient was discharged in good condition.

Discharge Medications:
None

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with his primary care physician as needed. The patient should also avoid activities that could aggravate his hands and perform hand exercises provided by his physician as directed. This 27-year-old female patient was admitted to the hospital with a rapidly growing lump in the right chest wall for 3 months. The burns were not treated with skin grafting and were left to heal secondarily. Upon examination, the lump was located in the right mammary region and measured 10 × 8 × 6 cm. FNA smears showed moderate cellularity with round to oval cells forming a glandular pattern in some places. The cells showed moderate pleomorphism with high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, coarse chromatin, prominent 1-2 nucleoli and moderate amount of pale blue cytoplasm. The background was necrotic. Immunocytochemistry for HER-2/neu was performed which showed focal weak positivity for the marker. The cytological diagnosis was suggested as duct carcinoma breast.
A trucut biopsy from the lump revealed solid nests and tubular formations of atypical round to oval cells with moderate amount of cytoplasm, coarse chromatin with 1-2 prominent nucleoli and high mitotic activity (1-2/hpf). There was marked desmoplastic reaction in the surrounding stroma. On immunohistochemistry (IHC), few tumor cells stained positive for HER-2/neu. The histological features and IHC were compatible with high-grade IDC (NOS, grade 3).
The patient declined surgery and was lost to follow-up.

High-grade IDC (NOS, grade 3)

The patient was advised to continue follow-up care with an oncologist for further evaluation and management.

1. Patient Information:

The endoscopic ultrasound examination revealed a round mass in the intrapancreatic bile duct, with hypoechoic areas and heterogeneous echogenicity, which measured 21×16 mm in maximal cross-sectional diameter. Based on the findings, the patient is suspected to have a distal common bile duct mass.

The patient will require further evaluation and treatment to address the suspected distal common bile duct mass.

Chest CT had indicated interstitial changes accompanied by cystic lesions in the lung and pleural thickening. The patient had worked as a demolition worker and smoked approximately 30 cigarettes a day since he was 18 years old. Work- and smoking-related lung conditions were therefore considered to be the most likely causes of the pulmonary lesions. No mycobacterium species were detected by sputum culture tests that were repeatedly performed over a couple of years, although pleural thickening strongly suggested concomitant TB.

The patient was started on steroid therapy comprising of a 3-day intravenous infusion of 500 mg methylprednisolone followed by daily oral administration of 20 mg prednisolone (PSL) upon admission.

The patient has had no recurrence of hemoptysis since discharge and has undergone follow-up CT and serum MPO-ANCA level tests.

Patient 3, a 4-year-old male, presented to the clinic with a history of possible obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The patient had been insisting on things going his way since the age of three and if his desires were not met, he would throw tantrums and demand to turn back time. The patient's behavior had become more severe since he started attending kindergarten, demanding that routines be repeated and "played back." The patient was judged problematic in kindergarten and had repeatedly run away during tantrums. The mother reported being anxious, while the father denied any psychiatric symptoms. Patient 3 had a CY-BOCS score of 15.

The patient was referred to our clinic due to the mother's history of OCD and inpatient treatment. After evaluation, the clinical impression was possible OCD. Patient 3's parents were educated about the nature of OCD and reassured that this could be managed with appropriate treatments, including psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy if necessary.

The patient and his family were advised to follow up with a therapist, and the patient was recommended to continue attending kindergarten to improve his socialization skills. The family was advised to establish routines which should be adhered to, as this would help reduce the patient's anxiety levels.

Overall, the patient's condition would require ongoing multidisciplinary care and monitoring from a qualified therapist. The patient's prognosis could be favorable with appropriate treatments and committed follow-up.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Age: 33 years old

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia with maturation according to the WHO 2008 classification.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of dizziness and was found to be anemic with low-grade fever. The blood cell count showed hyperleukocytosis with increased number of blast cells. The bone marrow examination revealed the proliferation of myeloperoxidase-positive blasts and flow cytometry showed blasts were positive for CD13, CD33, CD34, and HLA-DR and negative for lymphoid antigens. Chromosomal analysis of BM cells showed normal karyotype.

Due to the patient's wishes to not receive blood transfusions, Azacitidine therapy (75 mg/m2/day for 7 days) was initiated on the fifth hospital day as an induction therapy followed by hydroxyurea (1500 mg/day) from day 2 to day 16th to control hyperleukocytosis. During the induction therapy, the patient developed a left axillary abscess on day 10 which was treated with antibiotics and drainage with a small incision. The patient's blood-cell nadir values were hemoglobin 2.5 g/dL, platelets 9 × 109/L, and granulocytes 0.18 × 109/L, and he experienced dizziness on walking, but bleeding tendency was mild and the axillary infection was well controlled.

The BM examination was carried out on day 20, which revealed the disappearance of blasts and the emergence of normal hematopoiesis. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (Filgrastim 75 μg, subcutaneous injection on days 26–30), erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (darbepoetin alfa 120 μg, subcutaneous injection on day 29), and an anabolic steroid (Primobolan 20 mg, oral administration on days 29–42) were used to enhance the recovery of normal hematopoiesis. The patient's blood cells recovered to the normal level, and the BM examination on day 43 confirmed complete remission.

The patient then received three cycles of conventional postremission chemotherapy (combination of idarubicin and enocitabine) and henever received any blood transfusions. The patient remained in remission with normal physical condition.

Hospital Course Summary:
This 6 8/12-year-old Hispanic girl presented with concerns of poor linear growth and possible precocious puberty. She had a history of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome and underwent kidney transplantation from her mother at age 3 9/12 years. She developed proteinuria immediately after transplantation, which persisted despite aggressive medical therapy. Treatment with an ACTH analog was initiated, resulting in gradual resolution of her proteinuria and edema. However, she developed obesity and generalized increase in body hair and a small amount of axillary hair.
Upon examination, the patient was Cushingoid and had generalized increase in body hair. She was Tanner 3 for breast development and Tanner 4 for pubic hair. Laboratory studies showed high concentrations of cortisol and adrenal androgens with elevated gonadotropins and estradiol levels. Bone age was mildly advanced, and pelvic ultrasound showed prepubertal uterus with imperceptible endometrial stripe, right ovarian volume 0.8cc, and left ovarian volume 1.3cc. Our impression was that ACTH treatment had resulted in hypersecretion of adrenal androgens, and breast development was the result of aromatization of androgens.
The patient's ACTH dose was slowly decreased, but two months later, she resumed breast development while still on treatment with aromatase inhibitors. Laboratory studies showed increasing concentrations of gonadotropins and estradiol, and a repeat pelvic ultrasound showed maturing ovaries and uterus, consistent with development of central precocious puberty. Treatment with an analog of luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) was initiated to suppress gonadotropin production, resulting in suppression of gonadotropins and resolution of breast development. Over one year after starting LHRH therapy, her puberty is still suppressed, both clinically and biochemically.
The patient's interval linear growth has been appropriate, and her nephrotic syndrome is still in remission.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a five-year-old male child, was admitted to the hospital due to acute pain abdomen and vomiting of two days duration. The pain was diffuse and severe with no palpable mass. Routine hematological examination of the patient was within normal limits except for mild leucocytosis and slightly raised C-reactive protein. On further examination through an ultrasonography and CT scan of the abdomen, evidence of intraperitoneal multiloculated cystic lesion measuring 7 cm × 4.10 cm was found in relation to the small intestine mesentery.

Surgical procedures performed:

Laparotomy was carried out, and a thin-walled dumbbell-shaped mesenteric cyst was seen attached to the ileal mesentery 15 cms proximal to the ileocecal junction. Surgical resection of the cyst along with a small part of the ileum was performed, followed by end-to-end anastomosis to restore the intestinal continuity. Postoperative period was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on the sixth post-operative day.

Pathological findings:

Grossly, the cyst was thin-walled, contained a pale straw-colored fluid, and was multiloculated. It measured 7.1 cm in its greatest dimensions. Cut surface revealed a small polyp measuring 1.4 cm in its greatest dimensions attached to the inner surface of the cyst wall through a small stalk. Microscopically, the cyst wall was composed of fibro-collagenous tissue lined by flattened to low cuboidal epithelial cells. The attached polyp was completely infarcted and showed congested blood vessels, a few hemosiderin laden macrophages and plenty of inflammatory cells near the stalk. Exact morphological categorization could not be done due to the complete infarction of the polyp.

Outcome:

The patient showed steady improvement post-surgery, and the hospital course was uneventful. The patient was discharged on the sixth post-operative day in a stable condition and advised to have regular follow-ups with the treating physician.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 64-year-old man with history of heart transplant and transient acantholytic dermatosis

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted to our institution due to a one-month history of mildly pruritic skin lesions on the abdomen and lower extremities.

Hospital Course:
Physical examination revealed numerous erythematous red-brown papulovesicles. The patient had undergone heart transplantation 22 years previously on account of a dilated cardiomyopathy. After the transplant, immunosuppression consisted of rabbit antithymocyte globulin for three days, cyclosporine A, azathioprine, and steroids. Eleven years after HTx, the patient developed a posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder which was treated with chemotherapy with CHOP regimen for six cycles. No relapse of NHL was observed. On admission to our center, the patient was on low-doses of cyclosporine A and prednisone.

Diagnostic Tests:
Autoimmunity, cryoglobulins, and PCR for EBV, CMV, HHV-8, HCV, and Parvovirus B19 were negative.

Hospital Outcome:
Punch biopsies from two different cutaneous lesions were performed and histological examination of both skin samples documented an acantholytic dermatosis, which exhibited a Darier disease-like pattern. The patient was diagnosed with transient acantholytic dermatosis and skin lesions began to improve during hospitalization. The patient was discharged to the outpatient-clinic to continue follow-up.

Follow-Up Recommendations:
Follow-up appointments are recommended to ensure continued improvement and to monitor for any potential recurrence of the condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male
Age: 39
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Abnormal chest computed tomography (CT) scan

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted due to an abnormal chest computed tomography (CT) scan showing a 35 × 25 × 25 mm tumor located in the right hilar region. This tumor was suspected to have invaded the right main bronchus and right main pulmonary artery. 18-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography showed moderate FDG uptake within the tumor. After a series of laboratory tests, including an endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA), the tumor was diagnosed as a suspected giant cell carcinoma. The patient underwent right upper sleeve lobectomy due to the tumor invading the base of the right upper lobe bronchus. The surgery was successful, with no major postoperative complications. After the surgery, the patient received three cycles of cisplatin and pemetrexed adjuvant chemotherapy. The patient remained in a healthy condition, and no sign of recurrence or complications was reported. The patient was discharged in good health after 10 days of recovery.

Clinical Course:
The patient had general fatigue, appetite loss, and a fever for about 3 weeks before admission. The patient's tumor marker levels were not elevated. Laboratory test results, including a panel of antibodies for autoimmune processes, and an immunohistochemical analysis for lymphoma were all negative. However, the patient's serum IL-6 levels were markedly high (28.2 pg/ml [<2.41]), but the serum G-CSF level was not.  The patient's post-surgery 9-day serum IL-6 level was 10.9 pg/ml, which was lower than that before the operation. 

Pathological Findings:
Pathologically, the tumor showed proliferation of atypical epithelial cells having pleomorphic nuclei and prominent nucleoli arranged in a lepidic, acinar, or solid growth fashion (adenocarcinoma component), mixed with bi- and multinucleated cells with occasional emperipolesis (giant cell carcinoma component) and stroma, findings which were consistent with a pleomorphic carcinoma. Immunohistochemically, the carcinoma cells were faintly or focally (50 % tumor cells positive) positive for IL-6 but negative for G-CSF. Giant cell proportions were 30 % in this tumor. IL-6 positive carcinoma cells were 50 % in these tumor cells, which include the adenocarcinoma component. There were no lung abscesses and inflammatory changes. The final pathological stage of this case was T2aN1M0 stage IIA pleomorphic carcinoma.

Discharge Medications:
The patient received three cycles of cisplatin and pemetrexed adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery.

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition was stable and improved. The patient was discharged in a healthy condition, with no sign of recurrence or complications reported.

Follow-up Instructions:
The patient should follow up with his physician regularly. He should continue to follow a healthy diet and lifestyle to maintain optimal health. Any unusual symptoms or signs should be reported immediately to the physician. The physician will monitor the patient's condition closely to ensure the patient's overall health.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [Name]

Admission Date: [Date]

Discharge Date: [Date]

Admission Diagnosis: Gingival Lesion

Admitting Provider: Department of Dermatology, Command Hospital Pune

Discharge Diagnosis: Pemphigus vulgaris

Discharge Provider: Department of dental surgery, AFMC, Pune

Hospital Course:

A 36-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital with a chief complaint of a burning sensation in the oral cavity. The patient had noticed ulcers in the mouth followed by vesicles on the gum. The vesicles on the gum ruptured to produce pain and severe itching in the mouth. Small eruptions were also noticed over the skin on the face and extremities. The patient was referred by the Department of Dermatology, Command Hospital Pune to the Division of Periodontics, Department of Dental Surgery, AFMC, Pune.

On general physical examination, the patient was moderately built and nourished, with vital signs within normal limits. Numerous flaccid vesicles and ruptured bullae of varying diameter were seen over the back and nose, which were mainly seen as ulcerated eroded surfaces. On extraoral examination, there were no relevant findings. On intraoral examination, denuded and spontaneously bleeding gingival zones were revealed.

After a routine hemogram, urine and blood sugar examination of the patient, incisional biopsy was taken for histopathological examination in normal saline. The sample was sent to the Department of Pathology. The patient was referred back to the Department of Dermatology, and a biopsy of skin was taken from the back for histopathological examination and for a direct immunofluorescence assay in Michel's solution.

On histopathological examination, acantholysis was revealed along areas of ulceration without dysplastic changes with polymorphonuclear leucocytes infiltration. Basal cells of epithelium remained attached to the basement membrane. Higher resolution showed perivesicular edema with loss of cohesiveness and hyperchromatic epithelial cells called “Tzank cells,” suggesting diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris. The direct immunofluorescence showed intercellular deposition of C3, IgG, and IgM in stratum spinosum, confirming the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris.

The oral lesions were treated with 0.1% Triamcinolone acetonide ointment and skin lesions with topical application of 0.05% Clobetasol with Soframycin twice daily. Prednisolone 20_mg twice daily with multivitamins was administered systemically. The patient is under control and still under review.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient has been discharged in stable condition. She has been instructed to continue the prescribed medications and visit the Department of Dermatology and the Division of Periodontics for follow-up and monitoring of the condition. The patient has been advised to maintain good oral hygiene habits and avoid hot and spicy foods.

Follow-Up:

The patient will follow up with the Department of Dermatology and the Division of Periodontics for further evaluation and monitoring of symptoms.

Signed,

[Discharging Provider Name and Credentials]

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient is a 67-year-old female with a history of scoliosis and early osteoporosis who presented with a non-productive cough, unintentional weight loss, and daytime fatigue. Chest radiograph showed possible right middle lobe pneumonia. Treatment with levofloxacin was initiated, but patient developed severe diarrhea due to Clostridium difficile colitis. A CT scan of the chest was performed, revealing right middle lobe and lingula bronchiectasis, nodularity, and mucus impaction. Patient was put on airborne isolation for pulmonary tuberculosis and an induced sputum sample was negative for MTB PCR probe. However, bronchoscopy with lavage showed smear positive for AFB, and eventually grew M. avium.

The patient was discharged from the hospital on a combination of ethambutol, rifampin, and azithromycin three times weekly to be continued for three months. Repeat CT imaging at 6 months showed an improvement with fewer lung nodules and less mucus impaction. 

Overall, the patient has responded well to treatment for M. avium infection with significant improvement in her respiratory symptoms and ability to gain weight. Follow-up care will be important to monitor her progress.

Admitting Diagnosis: Infrarenal saccular aneurysm

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 69-year-old male with a history of ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis, was admitted with complaints of generalized malaise, fevers, abdominal, and back pain. The initial suspicion was raised towards the progression of his primary sclerosing cholangitis. The magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatogram showed an infrarenal saccular aneurysm with associated periaortic soft tissue enhancement. A computed tomography angiography confirmed the presence of the aneurysm, which was further characterized by a high-resolution CT chest that identified a right middle lobe pulmonary nodule.

The management involved a combination of antibiotic therapy and semi-urgent surgical excision and reconstruction of the infected aorta. The IMA, left accessory RA and lumbar arteries were ligated and the infrarenal aorta excised. The end-to-end anastomosis with 4-0 prolene was performed in quadrants using the right superficial FV, ensuring alignment. The proximal aortic wall was gradually plicated, achieving the desired tapering effect.

Post-operative days were uneventful. The patient was discharged on post-operative Day 13 on IV ceftriaxone 2 g q24h for 6 weeks. The patient underwent routine follow-up and continued prophylactic enoxaparin for 30 days.

Final Diagnosis: Infrarenal saccular aneurysm

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was advised to attend scheduled follow-up appointments with his healthcare provider. Additionally, the patient continued prophylactic enoxaparin for 30 days and wore thigh-high class II compression stockings for prevention of right lower limb complications following FV harvesting.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with symptoms of acute hepatitis E, including general fatigue, anorexia, cough, mild jaundice and excretion of tea-colored urine. Liver function tests showed elevated levels of AST, ALT, total bilirubin and conjugated bilirubin. Serological study indicated positive for IgM antibodies for HEV. However, on the 4th day of admission, he developed progressive muscle weakness on his lower limbs, numbness, and abnormal pinprick sensation in his plantar, and was transferred to our hospital for further treatment.
General physical examination showed asthenia, jaundice, blepharoptosis and paresthesia. The cranial nerve examination showed unilateral facial nerve palsy, Romberg’s sign and the straight leg raising test were positive. Muscle weakness was present in all limbs, and the patient had dysphagia, choking, areflexia and labored breathing. The neurological examination showed unilateral cranial palsy with left blepharoptosis, flat nasolabial fold, and incomplete eyelid closure of the right side. Muscle weakness in his four limbs progressed rapidly.
Lumbar puncture was conducted, and CSF examination showed albuminocytologic dissociation, evidence of demyelinating neuropathy with dysfunction of motor and sensory nerve fibers. Serological studies for IgM and IgG anti-HEV were both positive. The patient was diagnosed with acute HEV-associated GBS and treated with intravenous immunoglobulin, steroid, glycyrrhizin, glutathione and ademetionine. During the next 2 weeks, the patient's clinical condition and muscle power improved gradually, and repeat CSF examination 2 weeks after admission revealed improvement in monocyte counts and protein level. At discharge, the patient had 5/5 power bilaterally in his arms and 4/5 power bilaterally in his legs. A month later, his liver function substantially improved, and his serum levels of AST and ALT were nearly normal. Serological study showed that IgM anti-HEV antibodies became negative, which suggested full recovery from the acute phase of hepatitis E. The patient responded well to treatment with muscle power returning to normal, but still felt weakness in his right arm.
 
Summary:
The patient was admitted with symptoms of acute hepatitis E, which progressed into GBS. The patient's clinical condition improved gradually after treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin, steroid, glycyrrhizin, glutathione and ademetionine. At discharge, the patient had regained muscle power in his arms and legs and showed no clinical signs of respiratory distress or malaise.
