Patient Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 43 years
Date of Admission: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted in November 2018 for an evaluation of transvaginal hemorrhage and waist pain, which led to the identification of a poorly differentiated, microinvasive, squamous cell carcinoma, stage IIB, originating in the cervix. She underwent five cycles of chemotherapy and radiotherapy. In July 2019, the tumor mass had increased, and the patient underwent further treatment with four applications of cisplatin and brachytherapy, completing in September 2019. In November 2019, the patient experienced a nonproductive cough, headache, and blurred vision in the left eye, which progressed rapidly.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with poorly differentiated, microinvasive, squamous cell carcinoma, stage IIB, which later progressed to stage IIIB with involvement of the pelvic wall and pelvic lymph nodes. The patient also had metastases to the lungs, liver, and spleen. Furthermore, the patient had a choroidal tumor projecting from the middle periphery to the macular area and serous retinal detachment in the upper temporal sector with abundant fluid involving the macular area.

Treatment:
The patient underwent five cycles of chemotherapy based on carboplatin and gemcitabine, in addition to radiotherapy (50.4 Gy in 28 fractions). Further treatment included four applications of cisplatin along with brachytherapy (30 Gy in five fractions).

Follow-Up:
The patient refused palliative chemotherapy and died from respiratory complications 2 months after the ocular symptoms were present.

Summary:
The patient was admitted for an evaluation of transvaginal hemorrhage and waist pain, which led to a diagnosis of poorly differentiated, microinvasive, squamous cell carcinoma, stage IIB. Hospital Course:

A 29-year-old female patient was admitted to the hospital due to hemoptysis. A CT scan showed an upper abdominal mass with a potential infiltration of the liver, as well as thrombosis of her portal vein and partial thrombosis of her superior mesenteric vein, splenomegaly, and varicose veins of her entire stomach wall. During surgery, the lesion was diagnosed as a non-resectable hemangiomatosis of the greater omentum, extending through the hepatoduodenal ligament to the left lobe of her liver, and a biopsy was performed. An end-to-end portacaval anastomosis was also created. The biopsy was examined by a pediatric pathologist and categorized as an angiomatosis, with the disease pattern classified as "KMS". The patient underwent corticosteroid therapy followed by interferon alpha for three months each. She survived without symptoms for 15 years before returning with hemoptysis. A lower left lobectomy was performed to treat hemoptysis and prevent life-threatening bleeding. The resected specimen showed focal vascular malformations with associated fresh and old residual hemorrhages of the neighboring tissue.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 68-year-old male with T3N3M1a stage IV lung adenocarcinoma

Hospital Course:

Admission Date: April 2017
Discharge Date: Ongoing

Admitted for: Exertional dyspnea and cough

History and Examination:
The patient presented with exertional dyspnea and cough in April 2017. CT scanning of the chest revealed a nodule in the right lower lobe, enlarged hilar lymph nodes, and pleural effusion. A cytological examination of the pleural effusion confirmed malignancy, i.e., lung adenocarcinoma. The patient was diagnosed with T3N3M1a stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with positive pleural effusion.

Diagnosis:
T3N3M1a stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with positive pleural effusion

Treatment and Progress:
Gefitinib therapy was chosen as first-line therapy. Within 6 months, the patient experienced a partial remission of the lung disease. After 16 months of follow-up, a CT scan showed that the lesion in the right lower lobe had grown. However, the overall RECIST evaluation was still within the stable disease boundaries. A re-biopsy was performed, which confirmed solid type lung adenocarcinoma. The patient underwent pleural drainage and pleurodesis of the right-sided effusion. Treatment started with osimertinib, and after 3 months, a CT scan showed partial remission of the lung disease. Currently, 28 months after the diagnosis, the patient is doing well without any side effects and continues with osimertinib treatment.

Summary:
The patient presented with exertional dyspnea and cough, and was diagnosed with T3N3M1a stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with positive pleural effusion. After undergoing various treatments, including gefitinib therapy and osimertinib treatment, the patient has shown significant improvement and is currently doing well. Follow-up appointments are recommended to monitor the patient's ongoing recovery.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 69-year-old female with a history of a ruptured appendix (AA) and right lower abdominal pain. CT examination revealed an appendiceal mass and irregular wall thickness of the cecum, which aroused suspicion of colon cancer. Moreover, the CT scan uncovered mediastinal and para-aortic lymph node swelling, which led physicians to suspect malignant lymphoma or lymph node metastases. Serum blood tests showed elevated levels of soluble IL-2R, CEA, and CA19-9, which further supported the suspicion of malignant lymphoma or an epithelial neoplasm. The patient underwent conservative therapy with intravenous antibiotics for AA.

Hospital Course Summary:
After seven days of conservative therapy, the patient's general condition and inflammatory signs improved significantly. The patient was discharged from the hospital with no complications after undergoing ileocolectomy (i.e. extended appendectomy because of strong suspicions of malignancy) for making a pathological diagnosis. Pathological findings confirmed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with peripheral lymph node metastases, and genetic testing revealed a right-colon BRAF mutation. The patient received chemotherapy (bevacizumab, 5-FU, folinate, oxaliplatin, CPT-11), and three months later, both mediastinal and para-aortic lymph node swelling, as well as all metastatic lesions, had completely disappeared. The patient was kept on complete response (CR) at the final visit, which took place one year and two months after the operation.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: Not provided, 84-year-old Japanese Female
Medical Record Number: Not provided
Date of Admission: Not provided
Date of Discharge: Not provided

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient was referred to our hospital for further examination due to elevated α-fetoprotein (AFP) in a routine blood test. The patient was negative for a history of alcohol consumption, smoking, excessive weight loss and medications including herbs. The patient had hepatitis C virus (HCV)-associated chronic hepatitis and diabetes mellitus.

HOSPITAL COURSE
During the hospital course, abdominal ultrasonography revealed a 3.4-cm solid tumor in liver segment 8 (S8), with a heterogeneous irregular center but no fibrous capsule. A tumor 3 cm in size was observed in S8 on abdominal contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) performed at the time of admission, which showed heterogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase and washed out insufficiently in the portal and equilibrium phase. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) also revealed a tumor in S8. The enhanced pattern was not typical, but hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) was considered the most probable diagnosis. As a result, liver resection (S8) was performed, and the surgically resected specimen contained a tumor 2.5 cm at the largest diameter without fibrous capsule.

FINDINGS
The histological examination showed that the tumor had several different components. Within the nodule of well-differentiated HCC, an area accompanied by marked lymphocyte infiltration in the tumor stroma was noted and the tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) were predominantly CD8+ T cells. The other half of the tumor was replaced by fibrotic tissue accompanied by infiltration of lymphocytes and foamy macrophages; the histologic picture of this area closely resembled inflammatory pseudotumor of the fibrohistiocytic type. Small nodules that grossly showed pale yellow color were scattered within the nodule of well-differentiated HCC and inflammatory pseudotumor-like lesion, and the small nodules were entirely composed of necrotic tissue, indicating moderately differentiated HCC.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS
The final diagnosis was hepatic tumor with multiple components, including well-differentiated HCC with TILs, inflammatory pseudotumor-like lesion, and moderately differentiated HCC with extensive coagulative necrosis.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS
The patient was discharged 27 days after surgery. The patient has visited the hospital regularly for more than 6 years, with no signs of HCC recurrence on CT scan. No further discharge instructions were provided.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS
Not provided.

FOLLOW-UP APPOINTMENTS
The patient has been visiting the hospital regularly for more than 6 years, with no signs of HCC recurrence on CT scan.

Patient: 64-year-old male

Medical History:
- Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the lung
- Chemoradiotherapy
- Endoscopic metallic stent insertion
- BEI therapy (balloon-assisted endoscopic injection therapy)
- Recurrent tumour

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of cough and dyspnoea. Chest computed tomography revealed a narrowed airway in the left main bronchus and bronchoscopy showed stenosis of the left main bronchus. Histological examination revealed adenoid cystic carcinoma of the lung.

Chemoradiotherapy was administered as the first-line treatment, followed by endoscopic metallic stent insertion to prevent restenosis. However, the distal portion of the left main bronchus gradually stenosed 2 years and 3 months after stent insertion. Bronchoscopic examination revealed a polypoid mass lesion at the distal end of the inserted stent, which could not be passed through.

BEI therapy was performed to reduce tumour size, with a dose of 0.1-0.8 ml of absolute ethanol injected four times with aspiration needle over 8 months, along with one-time balloon dilatation. The polypoid mass size decreased and the bronchoscope could pass through, but the proximal left main bronchus became constricted again due to recurrence 1 year after the first BEI therapy.

Chemotherapy was then administered as the next treatment and continued for approximately 2 years. After disease recurrence, BEI therapy was performed again with concurrent chemotherapy, resulting in a reduction in airway obstruction. No clinically meaningful treatment complications were experienced, except for mild cough during the procedure.

Four months after the last BEI therapy was performed, bronchoscopy showed tumour recurrence. Another round of chemotherapy was done as the next treatment, and tumour progression was controlled for approximately 1.5 years with multiple BEI therapy through the assistance of balloon dilatation and chemotherapy.

Final Diagnosis: Recurrent adenoid cystic carcinoma of the lung

Disposition: Discharged with physician follow-up and close monitoring.

Hospital Course Summary:

This document outlines the hospital course of a 69-year old female patient who presented to the eye casualty at the Sussex Eye Hospital with red, sore and itchy right eye. Upon examination, severe scleritis was diagnosed which was inflammatory in nature and was treated with intensive preservative free lubricants and oral Prednisolone 60 mg tapering over 6 weeks with antacids cover. The patient settled with no evidence of thinning or recurrence of melanoma. She was noted to have a large patch of scleromalacia with significant scleral thinning and conjunctival blebs in the inferonasal quadrant of the right eyeball a year later. She is currently under 6 weekly observations in the clinic to look out for signs of perforation. 

History:

The patient had no past ocular history. Her past medical history included hypertension, pulmonary embolism and diverticulitis. She took regular amlodipine, losartan and apixaban with no relevant family history. The patient worked as a farmer, which predisposed her to ultraviolet light exposure.

Initial Findings:

Visual acuity was 20/200 (corrected 20/60) in the right eye, and 20/10 in the left eye. The left eye was structurally normal. Intraocular pressures were normal. Fundus examination was normal. Ultrasound B-scan and a gentle ultrasound biomicroscopy showed no intraocular mass lesion.

Diagnosis and Treatment:

Upon examination, severe scleritis was diagnosed which was inflammatory in nature and treated with intensive preservative free lubricants and oral Prednisolone 60 mg tapering over 6 weeks with antacids cover. Following the treatment, the patient settled with no evidence of thinning or recurrence of melanoma. 

Follow-up:

A year later, the patient was noted to have a large patch of scleromalacia with significant scleral thinning and conjunctival blebs in the inferonasal quadrant of the right eyeball. She remains under 6 weekly observations in the clinic to look out for signs of perforation.

The patient, a 25-year-old male with no significant medical history, was admitted to the liver surgery department due to right upper quadrant swelling pain. There were no accompanying symptoms. The physical examination and laboratory tests were unremarkable.

Abdominal color ultrasound, contrast-enhanced color ultrasound, and dynamic contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) imaging revealed a heteroechoic mass in the right trisegment of the liver. Histological and immunohistochemical staining suggested a diagnosis of myofibroblastic sarcoma that was further classified as grade 3 according to the French Federation of Cancer Centers Sarcoma Group (FNCLCC) system[]. The patient refused postoperative chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

The patient tolerated the procedure well and was discharged with good general condition.

Diagnosis:
Myofibroblastic Sarcoma - Grade 3 according to the French Federation of Cancer Centers Sarcoma Group (FNCLCC) system.

Treatment:
Right hepatic trisegmentectomy.

The patient was stable, and no evidence of recurrence was noted.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A

Medical Record Number: N/A

Date of Admission: N/A

Date of Discharge: N/A

Admitting Diagnosis: Triplet pregnancy with threatened abortion at 15 weeks of gestation

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our maternal and fetal unit for detailed ultrasonographic examination due to triplet pregnancy with threatened abortion at 15 weeks of gestation. An inquiry into the family history revealed that her mother had delivered triplet babies all of whom died in the early neonatal period. Detailed ultrasonography at our maternal and fetal unit revealed a monochorionic triamniotic triplet pregnancy. After three days' hospitalization, the vaginal bleeding ceased and the patient was discharged to follow-up.

At 24 weeks of gestation, one of the triplet fetuses was diagnosed with a multicystic lung lesion suggestive of CCAM. Until 30 weeks of gestation, the fetuses had appropriate growth, and the follow-up of the pregnancy was uneventful except that the fetus with CCAM developed mild polyhydramnios. At 30 weeks, the patient presented with preterm uterine contractions that ceased after tocolysis with nifedipine 60 mg per day. Betamethasone (12 mg × 2 doses in 24 hours) was administered intramuscularly to the mother to promote fetal lung maturation.

The patient was readmitted to our unit at 34 weeks for uterine contractions and impaired fetal growth. At 35 weeks of gestation, the patient underwent a low-transverse caesarean section and delivered three live male babies. Apgar scores were 7/9, 6/8 and 7/9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. One of the triplets died due to sepsis on day 7 postpartum. Computerized tomography (CT) of one of the surviving infants at 3 months and 6 months showed cystic lesions in the right lung.

Discharge Diagnosis: Monochorionic triamniotic triplet pregnancy

Discharge Condition: Stable

Discharge Medications: N/A

Plan: The patient and her family were educated on the risks of multiple pregnancy and monochorionic placentation. Follow-up appointments were scheduled to monitor the health of the infants who were discharged and manage any complications that arise.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [redacted]
Date of Admission: 22/02/2017
Date of Discharge: [redacted]
Length of Stay: 2 days

Admission Diagnosis:

35-year-old multiparous female at 8 months of pregnancy presented with absent fetal movements since the last 2 days. IUFD confirmed by ultrasound and labor induction was done.

Hospital Course:

The patient delivered a macerated female baby of 1.8 kg vaginally. Active management of the third stage of labor was done and thereafter labor events were uneventful. On clinical examination after delivery, the baby did not have any gross congenital malformation. Postpartum period was uneventful and she was discharged in good health on the second day of puerperium.

Clinical Findings:

On general examination, the patient was not pale, icterus, oedema, cyanosis and dehydration were all absent, temperature was 980F, pulse rate 88/min, and B.P was 160/90 mmHg. The CNS, CVS and respiratory tract examination were within normal limits. On obstetric examination, fundal height corresponded to 34 weeks of gestation, uterine tone was normal and fetus in cephalic presentation and fetal heart sound could not be localized. Pervaginal examination revealed that the cervix was 1.5 cm dilated and 50% effaced with intact membranes and adequate pelvis. Her urine albumin was 2+ on dipstick.

Investigations:

All relevant investigations were sent and IUFD was confirmed by ultrasound. There was no congenital malformation in the fetus by ultrasound. Her blood group was B positive, Hb 10.6 g/dl, TLC 10,600/cumm, DLC N76L16 M6E2, platelet count was 3.3 lacs/cumm, RBS 77 mg/dl, LFT-Total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dl, SGOT 23 U/L, SGPT 24 U/L, total protein 6.2 mg/dl, blood urea 28 mg/dl, Sr. creatinine 1.0 mg/dl, Prothrombin time 15 secs, APTT 40.1 secs, INR 1.15, VDRL nonreactive, HbsAg negative, HIV nonreactive.

Final Diagnosis:

IUFD secondary to placental abnormalities with chorangiosis due to chronic hypoxia confirmed by histopathological examination.

Discharge condition:

The patient is discharged in good health with adequate health counselling and advice regarding future pregnancies.

Follow up:

The patient is advised to attend regular antenatal follow-up for future pregnancies. She is also advised to adopt a healthy lifestyle and manage her hypertension to prevent future complications. Discharge Summary:

This is a summary of the patient's episode of care at our hospital. The patient was a 40-year-old male who was involved in a road traffic accident as a motorbike driver. He presented with a left dorso-lateral tibial head impression fracture, a left middle foot fracture, and a closed, displaced comminuted fracture of the distal lower right leg with C3-fracture of the tibial pilon and luxation fracture of the ankle including a fracture of the distal fibula.

After the decompression of the compartments of the lower leg and temporary wound coverage with artificial skin coverage, the tibia was reconstructed using small fragment screws and secondary wound closure.

At 61 months follow-up, mobilization in the right ankle joint was actively possible with a range of pain-free movement of 10 – 0 – 30 degrees (left 20 – 0 – 35 degrees). The AOFAS score was 82 points.

Overall, the patient's recovery has been satisfactory, and we recommend continued follow-up with the treating clinicians.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Patient ID: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: Infertility due to polycystic ovary (PCO)

Hospital Course: The patient, a 32-year-old female with a history of PCO, underwent a third intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) attempt. She had achieved biochemical pregnancy on the first ICSI cycle and had a first-trimester miscarriage in the second cycle. Before starting the third cycle, elevated prolactin was corrected with Dostinex and she received 50 micrograms thyroxine daily. The ovarian stimulation was initiated with Gonal-F; the dose was adjusted from 150 IU to 225 IU. Cetrotide was administered for four days. The final oocyte maturation was achieved with a single injection of hCG. Thirteen oocytes were collected, and three MII oocytes were injected. On day three post-retrieval, two embryos were transferred, and luteal support was provided. The first pregnancy test revealed positive hCG values, and four intrauterine gestational sacs were observed on an ultrasound at 5 weeks. After discussions regarding monozygotic pregnancies, medical abortion, and selective embryo reduction, the couple accepted fetal reduction, and cervical cerclage was performed at 10 weeks and two days. At 12 weeks and six days, a final ultrasound scan showed two healthy twin boys, who were vaginally delivered after 36 weeks gestation.

Hospital Course Summary:

- Third intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) attempt for infertility due to polycystic ovary (PCO)

- Elevated prolactin was corrected with Dostinex; 50 micrograms thyroxine provided daily

- Ovarian stimulation: Gonal-F (150-225 IU), Cetrotide (four days), hCG for final oocyte maturation

- Thirteen oocytes collected; three MII oocytes injected; two embryos transferred on day three post-retrieval with luteal support

- Positive hCG values and four intrauterine gestational sacs observed on ultrasound at 5 week

- Fetal reduction and cervical cerclage performed at 10 weeks and two days after discussions about monozygotic pregnancies, medical abortion, and selective embryo reduction

- Final ultrasound scan confirmed two healthy twin boys, who were vaginally delivered after 36 weeks gestation.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: [patient name]
Age: 8 years
Gender: Male
Diagnosis: Acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau (ACH)

Medical History:
An otherwise healthy 8-year-old Saudi boy with no known family history of psoriasis presented to the dermatology clinic with a pustular eruption of the fingers and toes associated with burning sensation, dryness, and scaling for 8 months. Nail changes ensued during the course of the illness, leading to nail detachment of all fingernails and numerous toenails. The patient did not report any history of joint pain, lower limb edema, or jaundice.

Hospital Course:
Physical examination revealed scaly erythematous plaques with overlying pus and crust formation involving all distal digits and multiple areas on the palms and soles. Nails showed severe onychodystrophy with confluent pustules covering the nail bed. A skin punch biopsy was taken, and histological examination was consistent with subacute psoriasiform dermatitis/pustular psoriasis. Radiological examination showed focal soft tissue swelling at the tips of fingers of both hands with irregular outline and fissure-like indentation. Underlying terminal tufts showed focal areas of bone resorption, particularly over the fourth and fifth left digits. X-ray of the feet did not show any remarkable joint or osseous abnormalities. Based on the clinical and histological findings, a diagnosis of ACH was made. The patient was started on etanercept 25 mg subcutaneously twice weekly.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was successfully treated for Acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau (ACH) and was discharged in stable condition. The patient was advised to follow up with the dermatology clinic to monitor his progress and delivery of ongoing care. Further course of treatment will be determined by the dermatologist based on the previously documented case report.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [Insert name]
Medical Record Number: [Insert number]
Date of Admission: [Insert date]
Date of Discharge: [Insert date]

HOSPITAL COURSE
The patient was admitted with a diagnosis of malignant melanoma and underwent wide excision which resulted in a 7.5x7.5 cm defect. An 8.0x8.0 cm flap was raised, containing two perforators from the lateral middle third of the right lower limb, along with some peroneal vessels to obtain a longer pedicle. Anastomosis was performed on the peroneal artery and two venous comitantes in the flap to the palmar carpal branch of the radial artery, and to the comitant and superficial veins at the recipient site. The donor site was then treated with split-thickness skin grafting.

FINDINGS
The patient underwent surgery that involved flap elevation and grafting, and now has incisions from these procedures.

DIAGNOSIS
Malignant melanoma.

TREATMENT
The patient underwent wide excision and flap elevation, followed by anastomosis of the peroneal artery and two comitant veins in the flap to the palmar carpal branch of the radial artery, and to the comitant and superficial veins at the recipient site. The donor site was then treated with split-thickness skin grafting.

CONDITION ON DISCHARGE
The patient is stable and has been discharged. They are instructed to follow up with their physician for any necessary care related to their diagnosis and treatment.

OUTPATIENT PLAN
The patient is to schedule follow-up appointments with their physician.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS
The patient is advised to rest, avoid strenuous activity, and care for the incision sites as instructed. They should also monitor their incision sites for signs of infection and report any concerning symptoms or changes to their physician. It is also recommended that the patient maintain a healthy lifestyle and practice sun safety to prevent any future occurrences of malignant melanoma.

None.

Hospital Course: 

A 72-year-old female presented with a history of burning feet that began one year earlier. On examination, she exhibited red discoloration on the soles of the feet. Her medical history was significant for Polycythemia Vera (PV), a blood disorder. Routine laboratory investigation showed normal blood glucose, transaminases, creatinine, thyroid hormones, and folate but elevated hematocrit, leukocyte, thrombocytes, and serum vitamin B12 levels. Paraproteinemia was excluded by electrophoresis. Vibratory testing with a tuning fork at 128 Hz was slightly decreased symmetrically on the distal part of the legs in a stocking-like pattern. Pinprick and proprioception were also decreased distally. The Achilles tendon reflex was absent. Dorsiflexion of the feet was weak, but the patellar reflexes were present, and muscle hypotrophy was not significant. The patient had received antithrombotic drugs, acetylsalicylic acid and angrelide, and the cytoreductive compound hydroxycarbamide in the past, after which all medical treatments had stopped due to noncompliance. The diagnosis of erythromelalgia, combined with peripheral sensorimotor axonal neuropathy of the legs, was suspected, and the patient was referred for further diagnosis to the neurologist. 

Hospital Course Summary:

A 72-year-old woman was admitted with a history of burning feet that started approximately one year ago. On examination, the patient had red discoloration on the soles of the feet, which led to the diagnosis of PV in April 2011. The hematocrit was significantly elevated, along with leukocyte and thrombocyte levels. Vibratory testing showed decreased sensation distally, and the Achilles tendon reflex was absent. Electro diagnostic studies showed peripheral sensorimotor axonal neuropathy in the legs. After receiving antithrombotic drugs, acetylsalicylic acid and angrelide, and the cytoreductive compound hydroxycarbamide, the patient discontinued all treatments due to noncompliance. Further diagnosis required referral to a neurologist.

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Sex: Male
Age: 34 years

Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) due to a single parathyroid adenoma which was causing elevated levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH) and hypercalcemia.

Medical History:
The patient's medical history was unremarkable with no prior medical conditions.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with a six-month history of nausea and vomiting, which had worsened over the last two weeks. During the clinical assessment, the patient's physical examination was normal except the elevated levels of hemoglobin, alkaline phosphatase, creatinine, calcium, PTH, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. The patient's laboratory test findings showed no abnormalities in liver, coagulation, thyroid, and other markers. Imaging techniques such as technetium-99m-sestamibi (99mTc-MIBI) scintigraphy and enhanced CT described an abnormal right inferior parathyroid gland that was diagnosed as PHPT due to a single parathyroid adenoma. However, on the second day after admission, the patient developed a dry cough with no fever. Subsequently, a chest CT scan showed diffuse ground-glass-like appearance in both lungs. Based on the clinical findings, the patient was prescribed antibiotics, antifungals, corticosteroids, and other supportive medications. After 14 days, the patient's dry cough did not improve, and a whole-body scan using technetium-99m-diphosphonate (99mTc-MDP) indicated increased accumulation of radioactivity diffused throughout the lungs and stomach. A follow-up SPECT/CT fused image revealed that the radioactive uptake was heterogeneously distributed within the pulmonary parenchyma and stomach. Furthermore, gastroscopy without biopsy yielded normal results, indicating a metastatic pulmonary and gastric microcalcification due to the parathyroid adenoma. The patient underwent right parathyroidectomy, where the pathology report showed nest-like distribution of chief cells, confirming the diagnosis of a parathyroid adenoma. One day after surgery, the patient's PTH level decreased to 9.6 pg/ml, and calcium levels returned to within normal levels. The patient's dry cough gradually improved, and he regained health. At the six-month follow-up visit, the patient's calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels were within normal limits, but PTH levels were mildly elevated. Subsequently, a repeat 99mTc-MDP SPECT/CT showed no radioactive distribution in the stomach and significantly reduced radioactive distribution with slight, uniform ground-glass features in the pulmonary parenchyma.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions for follow-up visits with his assigned healthcare provider.

Disposition:
The patient was discharged home.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 58-year-old female

History of Present Illness: The patient presented to a local emergency room with a constant headache, mild left-sided hemiparesis and a history of back pain during stretching exercises. The physician diagnosed migraine and prescribed triptans. However, her headache worsened, and she became stuporous and was transferred to another facility for treatment. CT scans revealed a right chronic subdural hematoma with a marked right-to-left midline shift. The patient underwent a small craniotomy to evacuate the hematoma, but her condition continued to deteriorate. She was then transferred to our institution for further evaluation and treatment.

Hospital Course:

Workup: A lack of neurologic and radiographic improvement after hematoma evacuation suggested the presence of underlying intracranial hypotension. Further testing, including MRI with gadolinium, revealed diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement and downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsil, which verified the diagnosis of SIH. A lumbar puncture was performed, and a CSF leak was detected.

Treatment: An intrathecal saline infusion was performed to temporarily ameliorate neurologic deficits, and a blood patch was urgently performed to seal the CSF leak. The patient showed improvement in consciousness level and left-sided hemiparesis after the blood patch therapy and was discharged free of symptoms 20 days after admission to our institution.

Follow Up: The patient has not sustained a recurrence of SIH for more than 6 months. A brain MRI obtained 30 days after blood patch therapy revealed the disappearance of contrast enhancement, subdural hematoma, and the return of the brainstem to the normal position.

Diagnosis: Chronic subdural hematoma with a right-to-left midline shift and subsequent intracranial hypotension.

Recommendations: The patient is advised to follow up with her primary care physician and neurosurgeon for further evaluation and management.

Appropriate antibiotics and analgesics were given for the initial 3 days of treatment. The patient was also instructed to consume a diet which included green vegetables, fruits, rice, roti (bread), and plenty of water, and to avoid non-vegetarian, spicy food, oily food, junk foods, and alcohol. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]
Admission Date: [Redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: Malignant melanoma of the left lower lid, skin, and bulbar conjunctiva
Discharge Diagnosis: Successfully treated left lower lid malignant melanoma

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to clinic with a rapidly growing pigmented left lower eyelid lesion that was diagnosed as malignant melanoma of the left lower lid, skin, and bulbar conjunctiva. Due to the patient's refusal of orbital exenteration, tumor excision surgery was performed in the form of a left lower eyelid resection with the use of a TPF reconstruction. 

During the procedure, a full-thickness defect was created using a no.15 blade to excise the lower lid from the sidewall of the nose, down to the level of the inferior orbital rim and across the entire horizontal length of the infraorbital rim and to the lateral canthus area. A composite nasal cartilage-mucosa graft was harvested from the left septum of the patient and was placed into the defect as a tarsus with the mucosa facing the eyelid. The fornix was first reformed by suturing the remnants of the bulbar conjunctiva to the sutures. The medial canthus was reformed by placing two sutures through the remnants of the medial canthal tendon. These sutures were then placed through the medial edge of the cartilage mucosal graft in a mattress fashion and then tied. Sutures were placed through the periosteum of the lateral orbital rim slightly above the original insertion site of the lateral orbital tubercle and used to secure the lateral edge of the composite graft.

To begin the TPF reconstruction, the superficial temporal artery was palpated approximately a centimeter anterior to the root of the helix. Local anesthesia with epinephrine was infiltrated along the course of the skin incision from the tragus of the ear along the course of a hemicoronal scalp incision. The incision was made to the level just deep to the hair follicles of the scalp. The fascial flap was then elevated off the underlying deep temporal fascia and pedicled entirely on the superficial temporal artery and vein. 

Using endoscopic visualization and endoscopic instruments, a tunnel in a plane deep to the TPF, just above the true temporalis fascia was created approximately 2 cm above the zygomatic arch to the level of the lateral orbital rim. At the level of the orbital rim, the flap was retrieved and pulled across the lower lid defect and sutured into the medial canthus area over the composite nasal cartilage-mucosa graft. The TPF was then secured to the rest of the lower lid defect using several sutures.

Once the TPF had been anchored into position overlying the defect, attention was then turned to the skin graft. An elliptical skin graft approximately 5 × 8 cm was removed from the forearm and was placed over the TPF and secured at the cardinal points using buried sutures. The remainder of the closure was completed using a combination of interrupted and running sutures.

Postoperatively, the patient healed well without any complications. The patient's pain was well controlled, and there were no signs of hematoma formation. The flap was edematous in the immediate postoperative period, but the edema resolved and the flap was successful.

The patient was discharged following successful treatment of the left lower lid malignant melanoma. The patient was advised to follow-up with their healthcare provider for regular check-ups and to report any concerning symptoms promptly. 

Signed,

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 81-year-old female with a history of hypertension, high cholesterol, hyperlipidemia, and osteoporosis, presented with a cystic mass on her right ankle that had been gradually increasing in size for 5 years. Physical examination revealed a cystic mass of approximately 45 × 30 mm at the tip of the right lateral malleolus. A needle aspiration of the mass revealed accumulation of approximately 10 mL of yellowish white homogeneous fluid that contained accumulated neutrophils and Gram-negative branching hyphae.

Diagnostic Findings:
X-ray images revealed osteoarthritis of the ankle joint, and MRI scan with contrast revealed a well-defined, T1 iso−/T2 high-intensity mass with strong marginal enhancement on contrast imaging. White blood cell count and serum C-reactive protein levels were within the normal limits. There were no organisms or crystals detected upon microscopic analysis of the fluid. After the initial visit, the patient discontinued the follow-up visits.

Course in Hospital:
One year after the initial visit, the patient returned to our hospital because of pain in the right ankle joint, and a recurring accumulation of fluid was detected. A repeated needle aspiration revealed growth of black colonies, and microscopic analysis detected blackish hyphae. The fungus was classified as a branching group of Kirschsteiniothelia by sequencing the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) regions. A second aspiration performed 1 month later showed the same results on morphological and molecular biological examinations. The patient refused further treatment, such as antimycotics or surgical debridement, and is currently under careful observation.

Disposition:
The patient was discharged from the hospital.

Hospital Course:
The 44-year-old female patient presented to our clinic with a two-year history of posterior neck pain, left-sided shoulder radiating arm pain, paraesthesia, and persisting ipsilateral arm weakness. On physical examination, a small round mass was palpable in the C6-7 nerve root area of the left brachial plexus. The patient showed grade 3 motor weakness and paresthesia of her left arm. The tumor was enucleated and emerged from the nerve roots during surgery, but a gross total resection could not be achieved. 

The patient underwent a second operation after a recurrence of the tumor and a histological examination showed a malignant transformation which resulted in complete monoplegia. The patient received concurrent chemotherapy and rehabilitation and showed no evidence of re-growth until one year after the second operation. 

Discharge Summary:
The 44-year-old female patient was discharged after a prolonged hospital stay due to a granular cell tumor with malignant transformation in the C6-7 nerve root area of the left brachial plexus. The patient underwent two surgeries with a subtotal resection of the tumor in each operation. The patient experienced significant deterioration in neurologic function after the second surgery and complete monoplegia developed. The patient received concurrent chemotherapy and rehabilitation and showed no evidence of re-growth until one year after the second operation. Close monitoring and follow-up treatment plan were recommended.

Admitted Diagnosis: Glossitis secondary to Pasteurella multocida infection and systolic heart failure.

Hospital Course: The 56-year-old male with a past medical history of hypertension, high cholesterol, gastroesophageal reflux disease, hearing impairment, tonsillectomy, and recurrent otitis media presented to the Emergency Department with tongue swelling, dysphagia, drooling, and shortness of breath. He presented to the same ENT specialist who found tongue edema, enlargement, and tenderness suggestive of glossitis. The patient was admitted to the ICU for glossitis or possible Ludwig's angina. Blood cultures were obtained, revealing Gram-negative rods which were later identified as Pasteurella multocida. Aztreonam and Metronidazole were discontinued, and the patient was started on Imipenem. Laboratory work showed improving leukocytosis and repeat blood cultures were negative the next day. Echocardiogram showed normal valves and normal right ventricular size and function, but moderate to severe global left ventricular dysfunction. The patient was diagnosed with systolic heart failure.

The patient's symptoms gradually resolved, and he was discharged home with Ertapenem via PICC line for a total of 14 days. Ten days after discharge, the patient presented again with a milder swelling of the tongue. Blood cultures were negative, and laboratory work was within normal limits. The course of Ertapenem was completed, and the patient was discharged home. He did not report any further episodes of tongue or throat swelling.

Discharge Medications: None

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 51-year-old man with perineal congenital hypospadias

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery of China Medical University Hospital with recurrent episodes of urinary retention, urethral stricture, and a ventral scar. He had undergone Bracka orthourethroplasty and staged Nesbit plication with correction of penile shaft chordae, as well as several failed urethroplasty procedures. Urethral augmentation using local options was contraindicated, and substitution urethroplasty was performed using a free ileum flap after resecting the urethra distal to the stricture. A ventral skin resurfacing and split-thickness skin graft were also performed to reconstruct the urethra, penis, and scrotum. The patient underwent a successful normal voiding and reported good sexual function during 3 years of follow-up. However, a ventral skin scar contracture prevented the penile shaft from achieving a full-length erection, and the ileum prolapsed through the penile tip. Scar contracture release, gracilis muscle debulking, and a local rotational flap were performed to increase the amount of longitudinal penile ventral skin. Normal voiding and satisfactory aesthetics were maintained for 1 year. Nevertheless, the patient requested a peno-urethral separation, and the "accessory penis" method was applied to satisfy his request. The patient underwent a further surgical separation procedure involving the division of the distal neo-urethra from the penile shaft and ventral-circumferential enterolysis dissection. A local fasciocutaneous rotation flap and split-thickness skin graft were used to provide skin coverage at the base of the penis and scrotum. The patient was discharged after a 6-month follow-up.

Summary of Care:
The patient presented with recurrent episodes of urinary retention, urethral stricture, and a ventral scar following several failed urethroplasty procedures. A substitution urethroplasty was performed using a free ileum flap after resecting the urethra distal to the stricture, and a ventral skin resurfacing and split-thickness skin graft were also performed to reconstruct the urethra, penis, and scrotum. The patient underwent a successful normal voiding and reported good sexual function during 3 years of follow-up, but eventually requested a peno-urethral separation, which was performed using the "accessory penis" method. The patient underwent a further surgical separation procedure and was discharged after a 6-month follow-up. The patient reported satisfactory aesthetics and sexual function.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient was a 21-year-old female who was initially diagnosed with relapsing-remitting MS in December 1993. The patient received glatiramer acetate treatment and later switched to interferon β-1a (Rebif® 44 μg three times a week) in April 2007 after suffering from several relapses. In May 2007, the patient developed numbness on the left side of her face. MRI revealed a contrast-enhancing lesion in the right paracentral lobule and 23 supratentorial and 1 infratentorial lesion on T2-weighted scans. A relapse was suspected, and the patient was treated with prednisone. The patient was admitted to the hospital with progressive disturbance of consciousness while traveling.

The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit, and CT showed hypodensities in the basal ganglia, frontal lobe, and mesencephalon. Internal venous thrombosis was ruled out, and MRI showed hyperintense lesions in the basal ganglia on T1-weighted scans and punctate hemorrhages on T2-weighted images. CSF analysis showed an elevated protein levels indicating a severe dysfunction of the blood-CSF barrier. The patient developed seizures, and EEG showed diffuse, severe encephalopathy. The patient underwent a diagnostic brain biopsy of the parenchyma, and the predominant findings were perivascular hemorrhagic necrosis and severe edema of the CNS tissue with an inflammatory infiltrate principally composed of neutrophils.

Despite treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by intravenous immunoglobulins, the patient remained in a severe spastic tetraparesis state. The patient experienced a relapse in August 2014 with internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The most recent MRI examination displayed a new lesion located paramedian in the medulla oblongata. Intravenous methylprednisolone therapy led to a considerable improvement of the lateral gaze.

The patient was discharged after a lengthy hospital course and had a stable clinical course without MS-specific therapy for the following 7 years. Given the high EDSS of 9.5, disease-modifying therapy was not initiated. The patient will require long-term follow-up and care to monitor the progression of her MS symptoms.

Hospital Course:

A 27-year-old man was transferred to our center for clinical review and further treatment due to spinal injuries after being involved in a road traffic accident as a passenger. He was diagnosed with posterior rib fractures and a haemothorax upon initial examination at the Emergency Department, and imaging revealed a posterior element fracture at the level of T8.

Treatment and Management:

The orthopaedic team reviewed his imaging and suspected a possible combined bony and soft tissue Chance fracture with a rupture of the ligamentum flavum at T7/8 and a hyperintense signal in the intervertebral disc at T8/9 on MRI. The patient was counselled regarding the unstable nature of this type of fracture and the risk and benefits of surgical and conservative management. After much discussion with the surgical team and family members, the patient opted for conservative management.

A thoracic brace was fitted, and the patient was mobilized after seven days of injury. Follow-up appointments, including x-rays of the thoracic spine, were arranged to monitor his progress, and the patient was discharged with appropriate analgesic medications, including paracetamol and dihydrocodeine, to manage any pain. After four days, the patient developed pleuritic chest pain, which was investigated by CTPA to exclude pulmonary embolism. CTPA concluded negative for PE and confirmed that there was still no displacement of the thoracic spine.

Follow-up and Outcome:

The patient did not show any displacement of the vertebrae, and there was no change to thoracic alignment during the follow-up appointments. However, he experienced increased thoracic back pain ten weeks after initial presentation, and MRI confirmed traumatic spondylolisthesis of T8 on T9. As the risks of surgery outweighed the risks of continuing conservative management, the patient underwent instrumented posterior stabilisation and fusion with allograft bone from T7 to T10 eight weeks later, wherein the surgery was successful.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was discharged and instructed to maintain proper wound care and continue wearing his thoracic brace for six weeks, except when taking a shower, for the surgical site's protection. He was advised to restrict himself from doing any strenuous and heavy lifting activities for at least 12 weeks and restart physical activities slowly and gradually thereafter. Appropriate analgesic medications, including regular paracetamol, were prescribed for any pain. A follow-up appointment with the consultant was arranged.

The patient was discharged from the hospital in stable condition with appropriate follow-up and management of symptoms.

Hospital Course: 
The patient, a 23-year-old Caucasian female, was admitted with complaints of abdominal pain, diarrhoea, dyspnoea on exertion, bilateral lower extremity oedema, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and orthopnoea. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Date of Admission: N/A
Date of Discharge: N/A

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 46-year-old woman with a history of hepatitis B and liver cirrhosis, presented to the ER with hematemesis and hematochezia. She had previously undergone a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure for gastroesophageal varix bleeding. Initial laboratory results showed a decrease in blood pressure, a decrease in hemoglobin, a decrease in platelet count, and an increase in prothrombin time/international normalized ratio. Endoscopy showed esophageal varices and a polypoid mass on the stomach fundus. Computed tomography showed liver cirrhosis with splenomegaly, umbilical varix, and gastroesophageal varices. The previously inserted TIPS stent was occluded by a thrombus.

The patient was transferred to the angiography suite for TIPS revision, but this was not possible because of the severity of the stent obstruction. Because the patient had a gastrocaval shunt instead of a gastrorenal shunt, PARTO was not possible, but a gastrocaval shunt was considered as an alternative treatment option. A 12 mm Amplatzer vascular plug II was placed in the gastrocaval shunt, and coils were used to embolize collateral vessels. Gelatin sponges were injected through the catheter toward the gastrocaval shunt and gastric varix until the afferent veins were opacified. After embolization, the patient's vital signs were stable. The patient experienced additional melena the day after the procedure and was discharged after there were no additional bleeding events.

Follow-up CT after 9 months showed an Amplatzer vascular plug, coils in the embolized gastrocaval shunt, and disappearance of gastric varix.

1. Liver cirrhosis with splenomegaly, umbilical varix, and gastroesophageal varices
2. History of hepatitis B
3. Polypoid mass on stomach fundus
4. Partially occluded TIPS shunt

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Diagnosis: Constitutional Symptoms

Hospital Course:

This is a summary of the hospital course of a 62-year-old male admitted with constitutional symptoms of asthenia, anorexia, low grade fever, night sweats and weight loss progressing over 5 months. On admission, the patient was hemodynamically stable, but subfebrile with pale mucous membranes. Cardiac and pulmonary auscultations were normal but there was tenderness on abdominal palpation on the flanks suggesting ascites. The neurological examination was normal.

Investigations:

The hemogram showed a normal blood count, elevated sedimentation velocity and C-reactive protein, with normal renal, thyroid and hepatic function tests, negative viral serology and normal levels of immunoglobulins. The X-ray and chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a bilateral micronodular pattern and evidenced multiple adenopathies. During hospitalization, abdominal-pelvic CT showed high-volume ascites with heterogeneity and densification of the peritoneum. Adenosine deaminase (ADA) in the ascites was 2.5 times higher than normal on diagnostic paracentesis.

Treatment and Progress:

The patient was admitted to the ward and adalimumab therapy suspended. He underwent a videobronchofibroscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and bronchial lavage showed a negative direct test for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) on both. At day 4, we were notified that an IGRA screening test performed a few weeks earlier was positive. He was started on isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol.

Seven days later, the BAL cultural exam revealed AFB and DNA testing was positive for MB. As of such, we related the abdominal CT findings to peritoneal TB involvement. At day 17, the patient started complaining of memory loss and mental slowing. Neurological examination was unremarkable, but brain contrast CT revealed multiple small rounded scattered contrast-enhancing lesions. Lumbar puncture showed 23 leukocytes/µL, with predominance of mononuclear cells, 84 mg/dL proteinorachie, with normal glucose levels. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) ADA, MB DNA and AFB were negative. Assuming central nervous system disseminated TB, corticosteroid therapy was initiated.

The patient began to improve, maintaining apyrexia after day 18. The remaining study showed a negative rifampin resistance test. He completed a 12-month treatment with the anti-TB drugs with weaning corticosteroid therapy. The clinical outcome was good and the patient did not restart adalimumab therapy.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Confidential

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Clinical History: 
The patient, a 24-year-old male with a history of congenital membranous ventricular septal defect (VSD), developed tricuspid valve endocarditis following a dental procedure in 2007 and subsequently underwent VSD closure and bioprosthetic tricuspid valve replacement. In 2009, he presented with heart failure symptoms and was found to have severe left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction. Since LV dysfunction persisted despite optimal medical therapy, he was referred to electrophysiology for consideration of a primary prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) in 2010. 

Hospital Course: 
A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with a QRS pattern consistent with ventricular pre-excitation over a right free wall accessory pathway (AP). A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed normal LV size with evidence of abnormal septal wall motion and an LV ejection fraction of 35%. The bioprosthetic tricuspid valve showed normal function and there was no evidence of residual VSD. A cardiac CT revealed normal coronary arteries and a cardiac MRI showed no evidence of delayed enhancement. The patient underwent electrophysiology study with a plan for catheter ablation of the AP. Mapping along the atrial aspect of the tricuspid annulus was performed using a 4 mm solid tip ablation catheter. RF lesions deployed at this location resulted in permanent abolition of accessory pathway conduction. In view of significant LV dysfunction with heart failure symptoms and complete AV block, the patient underwent implantation of a biventricular ICD the following day. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showing sinus rhythm with biventricular pacing was noted. At a 2-week follow-up visit, significant improvement in heart failure symptoms and exercise tolerance was seen. Serial echocardiograms done at 3-month and 1-year follow up visits showed complete normalization of LV systolic function and wall motion with an estimated LV ejection fraction of 55%.

Diagnoses:
1. Congenital membranous VSD 
2. Tricuspid valve endocarditis 
3. Severe LV systolic dysfunction 
4. Ventricular preexcitation pattern 

Treatment:
1. VSD closure and bioprosthetic tricuspid valve replacement

3. Catheter ablation of the AP 
4. Implantation of a biventricular ICD

The patient was discharged in good health with no acute complaints.

2. Continue on optimal medical therapy for heart failure

Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: N/A
Gender: Female
Age: 49 years old
Admission date: N/A
Discharge date: N/A

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted to our institute for the management of an incidentally detected brain tumor during the routine medical checkup of the brain with MRI. All serum tumor markers were within the normal range.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent tumor resection by bilateral suboccipital approach. By opening the arachnoid membrane between the vermis and left biventral lobule, the tumor was identified using a navigation system, and the well-margined tumor bulk was totally resected after dissecting the feeding artery from the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) peripheral branch and the draining vein into the left inferior vermian vein. An intraoperative pathological examination was performed, which showed that polygonal cells proliferated in nests and cords with many blood vessels. The findings appeared compatible with hemangioblastoma.

The formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue revealed proliferation of vacuolated sheeted tumor cells with clear and eosinophilic cytoplasm and numerous thin-walled vessels. A thyroid follicle-like pattern including eosinophilic liquid was partially present. Irregular nuclear contours and nuclear grooves were focally observed. Immunohistochemical findings were positive for CD31, CD34, vimentin, and thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1), and negative for GFAP. The final diagnosis was Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC).

Postoperative MRI showed total resection of the tumor bulk and no ischemic complications. Therefore, postoperative radiotherapy and adjuvant therapy were not administered.

Outcome:
At 2 years postoperatively, the patient has no symptoms and no recurrence on follow-up MRI. Thyroglobulin (Tg) and anti-thyroglobulin antibody 2 months and 2 years after operation were under 0.1 ng/mL and under 6.0 IU/mL, 0.11 ng/mL and under 6.0 IU/mL, respectively, which all were within normal range.

Discharge Disposition:
The patient was discharged in good condition.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to follow-up with our institute for regular check-ups according to the advised schedule.

The patient presented with intermittent abdominal distension, which was slightly under no obvious inducement. Given that it was uncertain whether it was a benign or a malignant tumor of the spleen, a laparoscopic total splenectomy was performed for the purpose of diagnosis and treatment. Histopathologically, the tumor was characterized by multiple cystic structures with anastomosing vascular channels. Immunohistochemistry showed that the cells compromising the tumor were positive for CD21, CD31, CD68, and CD163. According to the histology and immunohistochemistry findings, the diagnosis of LCA of the spleen was established.

The patient was discharged 6 days after the splenectomy. One month after discharge, the patient's blood routine and clotting routine were normal, and Aspirin was stopped to use. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]
Diagnosis: Low-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma of the left upper femur

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 38-year-old Indian woman, was admitted to our hospital with a two-year history of swelling and pain in her left thigh and hip. The swelling was progressive in nature, and the patient had no history of trauma prior to the swelling. On examination, a 20 × 10 cm soft tissue swelling involving the anterolateral aspect of the left thigh and extending to the left hip was detected, with mild tenderness over the swelling and painful restrictions in movement at the hip joint. Results of systemic examination were unremarkable.

Routine haematological and biochemical investigations, including alkaline phosphatase, were within reference ranges. Radiological investigations, such as computed tomography (CT) scan and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), revealed a diffuse, irregular, ill-defined heterogeneous altered marrow signals in the patient's left upper femoral metaphysis and extending into the epiphysis and diaphysis. The altered marrow signals were seen to extend up to the lower shaft diaphysis and metaphysis. Similar signals were also noted in the patient's left pelvic bone (acetabulum and pubic). There was anterior and posterior cortical disruption in the patient's upper femoral metaphysis with extension into the adjacent soft tissues. The bone scan confirmed these findings, and the radiological features were suggestive of a malignant neoplasm.

A core biopsy from the soft tissue swelling was performed, and it was reviewed at our institute. The biopsy showed a spindle cell tumour with focal nuclear pleomorphism, intercellular collagenous stroma, and occasional mitotic figures. With an initial diagnosis of malignant mesenchymal tumour, the patient underwent proximal femoral resection and prosthesis reconstruction.

The patient's proximal femur measuring 13 × 9 × 7 cm with a fusiform swelling, with 8 × 7 × 4 cm of the femur involving metaphysis was received, and it was seen to destroy the cortex and was extending into the soft tissue. Multiple sections from the tumour showed a spindle cell lesion composed of hypercellular fascicular and hypocellular fibrous areas. The spindle cells were found to be positive for vimentin and smooth muscle actin and negative for desmin, S-100 protein, myogenin and CD68 on immunohistochemistry. MIB-1 labeling index was low at 1% to 2%.

The histomorphological, immunohistochemical and ultrastructural features suggested a final diagnosis of low-grade myofibroblastic sarcoma of the left upper femur. The patient is currently on follow-up with no appreciable increase in the residual tumour.

Recommendations:
The patient is advised to follow-up with her oncologist to monitor any residual tumour growth over the next few months. In case of any pain and discomfort, she should seek medical attention immediately. Further treatment options will be discussed during follow-up appointments with the oncologist.

The patient underwent total colonoscopy due to a positive fecal occult blood test, which revealed a 30 mm LST-G lesion in the lower rectum adjacent to the dentate line consisting of both aggregated small and large nodules and hardly elevated flat parts. Magnifying chromoendoscopy and narrow-band imaging were performed, which revealed MC vessels in nodular areas and no MC vessel in flat areas, leading to the diagnosis of adenoma.

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of hematuria, and laboratory studies showed an increased blood urea nitrogen/creatinine ratio. A review of sediment showed numerous RBCs and hyaline casts without any dysmorphic RBCs. Warfarin was held due to supratherapeutic INR, and treatment was initiated with intravenous fluids and antibiotics for possible urinary tract infection. Secondary workup for the etiology of AKI revealed 2.8 g of proteinuria on a 24-hour sample and a positive antinuclear antibody. A renal biopsy was performed, which demonstrated sclerotic glomeruli with mesangial expansion and accumulation of red cells within Bowman’s space. The patient was diagnosed with ARN superimposed on sclerosing IgA nephropathy. He required 5 sessions of hemodialysis and was later discharged after his creatinine stabilized.

Diagnostic Assessment:
The renal ultrasound revealed mildly increased echogenicity bilaterally, and renal biopsy showed mesangial expansion with segmental sclerosis. Immunofluorescence revealed the immune complexes to be mesangial and along the capillary loops. Electron microscopy demonstrated scattered mesangial and subendothelial immune complex deposits staining positive for IgA. Serum protein electrophoresis and serum immunofixation demonstrated a polyclonal IgA.

Treatment and Management:
The patient was put under conservative measures and received intravenous fluids and antibiotics for possible urinary tract infection. Hemodialysis was required and performed for 5 sessions before discharge.

Follow-up Care:
The patient had a follow-up visit in the clinic, and his creatinine stabilized at 2.5 mg/dL with a proteinuria level of 1.1 g.

Hospital Course Summary:
Patient was an 81-year-old male who presented with presyncope secondary to anemia and hematoma. Past medical history was significant for blood hypertension and Whipple's operation for carcinoma of the ampulla of Vater, which had been staged as pT2N1M0, two months prior to admission. The patient was on prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin treatment. Clinical examination revealed ecchymosis and edema of the right shin and the right and left forearms. Laboratory results showed normocytic normochromic anemia, slightly elevated lactate dehydrogenase, and a prolonged aPTT with a normal prothrombin time, and fibrinogen with absence of schistocytes on a blood film. An ultrasound and workup excluded thrombosis but confirmed the presence of hematoma and a differential diagnosis was put in place, which included an adverse reaction due to heparin use, antiphospholipid syndrome, and bleeding disorder due to the presence of an acquired inhibitor in the clotting cascade. Following the discontinuation of Heparin and a mixing study, it was determined that the patient had acquired hemophilia, and an immunosuppressive treatment was initiated. The patient was also successfully discharged for further outpatient care.

An erect chest and abdominal X-ray showed gaseous distension of the colon as far as the mid-descending colon with very little gas distal to this. Consequently, a computed tomography (CT) scan of her abdomen and pelvis was obtained which confirmed the plain X-ray findings and showed gaseous distension of the transverse colon with a transition point in the mid-descending colon where a colo-colic intussusception was demonstrated due to a large descending colon lipoma.

An urgent flexible sigmoidoscopy was arranged which showed a large mid-descending submucosal colonic mass with a smooth surface and mucosal ulceration, confirming the radiological impression of a submucosal lipoma. 

Rather than subject the patient to a left hemicolectomy, a minimally invasive laparoscopy assisted transcolonic resection of the lipoma was performed. Post-operatively, the patient made an uneventful recovery and was discharged on Day 4. 

Follow-up six weeks later showed the patient was totally asymptomatic, and she was discharged from surgical care. The histopathology of the specimen confirmed a benign submucosal lipoma.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: Dry cough

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 68-year old woman, was admitted to our department with a 2-month history of a dry cough that was unresponsive to administered antibiotics and antimycotics. She was also treated for rheumatoid arthritis (using methotrexate) for the last 5 years. The initial diagnosis suggested malignant mesothelioma or metastatic lesions based on the presence of two homogeneous pleural nodules (diameters of 2 and 4 cm) in the left upper lung field, according to computed tomography (CT) of the chest. Two CT-assisted transthoracic core-cut biopsies were performed, but the histopathology examination was inconclusive. The patient was later referred to our department of thoracic surgery for further evaluation. A minimally invasive revision (thoracoscopy) of the left pleural cavity was performed, during which both pleural nodules were confirmed. The nodules were resected (standard thoracoscopic resection) and removed via a protective bag. Postoperative recovery was uneventful, and the patient was discharged after a few days. The histopathology examination of the specimen showed normal splenic tissue.

Discharge Diagnosis: Thoracic splenosis

Indication for Hospitalization: Surgical resection of pleural nodules

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient suffered from a dry cough for 2 months before being referred to our department. At the time of referral, CT scans revealed two homogeneous pleural nodules in the left upper lung field, and two consequent CT-assisted transthoracic core-cut biopsies were inconclusive in diagnosis. Therefore, a minimally invasive revision (thoracoscopy) of the left pleural cavity was performed. Both pleural nodules were resected, and the histopathology examination of the specimen showed normal splenic tissue. The patient's symptoms disappeared after surgery. Upon taking a detailed medical history and thorough physical examination, the patient confirmed a gunshot injury requiring splenectomy (without known diaphragm or lung injury) 44 years ago. 

The diagnosis of thoracic splenosis was confirmed with the histopathology report and published data. According to available literature, intrathoracic splenosis is always located in the left hemithorax and occurs after simultaneous splenic and diaphragmatic injury. Asymptomatic thoracic splenosis usually presents as an incidental finding of pleural masses on chest radiograph or CT scans. A solitary nodule or multiple nodules are detected on CT scans. CT or MRI images demonstrate exact localization, topographic relationships, and dimensions of the lesions. 

The patient was discharged after an uneventful postoperative recovery. Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of proptosis of the right eye, along with double vision, pain around the right eye, epiphora, positional headache, and painful eye movements. The ear, nose, and throat examination showed only nasal and post-nasal discharge, while ophthalmologic examinations showed severe proptosis of the right eye anterolaterally (approximately 3 mm), mild diplopia, and painful motility.

Diagnostic workup revealed a radiopaque mass in the right ethmoidal air cells with protrusion to the right orbit arising from the anterior ethmoid sinus. As the tumor was too large, it was approached with a right-side Lynch incision. The tumor was divided into two halves by drilling at the narrowest segment in an orbital and ethmoidal portion. The ethmoidal portion was excavated by drilling, while the remaining eggshell of the tumor was separated from the ethmoid roof to prevent damage to the skull base and possible cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea. The orbital portion had an irregular surface and the superior oblique and medial rectus muscles were trapped in the tumor. The orbital portion was divided into pieces by drilling and freeing the entrapped muscles before removing the tumor.

Post-operatively, the patient’s proptosis disappeared completely, but suffered some limitations of inward eye movement, as well as decreased vision due to macular edema. The patient was started on oral prednisolone therapy (1 mg/kg daily) for one week and was observed at follow-up. The patient’s condition improved to normal over the course of 4 weeks. The patient was symptom-free even after 1 year follow-up.

Radiopaque mass in the right ethmoidal air cells with protrusion to the right orbit.

None.

Hospital Course:

An 80-year-old male was admitted with a 10-year history of a breast mass and rapid growth over the previous 3 months. Mammography showed a well-defined mass in right breast with ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasonography of the abdomen and computerized tomography of thorax showed no abnormalities. Fine-needle aspiration cytology confirmed a diagnosis of NE carcinoma of the breast. The patient underwent a right radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection.

Gross examination of the breast tumor revealed a solid, grey-white mass measuring 10 cm x 8 cm x 8 cm with a focal cystic area. Histopathological examination revealed a malignant tumor with cells in solid nests, trabecular and organoid patterns, separated by delicate fibro-vascular connective tissue stroma. The tumor cells contained moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm and nuclear pleomorphism. The nuclei were round to oval with occasional grooving and irregular outlines. Many nuclei contained large prominent nucleoli and atypical mitoses ranging from 6 to 10/10 hpf were seen. A tiny focus showed a mucin pool with floating small nests of tumor cells. A focal area also showed features of invasive papillary carcinoma. Four out of the six resected lymph nodes showed metastatic deposits from the primary breast tumor.

Immunohistochemical staining revealed cytoplasmic positivity for chromogranin confirming the NE nature of the tumor. The chest, abdomen, and pelvis were thoroughly examined for abnormalities to exclude a non-mammary primary site, but none was detected. Final diagnosis of primary pure solid NE carcinoma of the breast with a minor component of papillary carcinoma and metastasis to ipsilateral axillary lymph node was made.

The patient underwent adjuvant chemotherapy and was later discharged in a stable condition.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Primary pure solid NE carcinoma of the breast with a minor component of papillary carcinoma and metastasis to ipsilateral axillary lymph node.

Discharged to home. Follow-up with oncology department for further management.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital due to recurrent acute kidney injury despite prior hospitalization for the same condition. The patient had a known history of Crohn's disease and chronic kidney disease stage III. The patient had undergone multiple surgical procedures in the past, including subtotal colectomy, resections of the small intestine, and rectum extirpation, resulting in the placement of a terminal ileostoma.

Physical Examination:
The patient presented with cachexia, malnutrition, and severe dehydration. Skin pallor and nasolabial dermatitis were noted. Initial laboratory tests revealed normochrome and normocytic anemia, acute kidney injury, and electrolyte imbalances.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with short bowel syndrome, secondary hyperaldosteronism due to renal potassium wasting, and extrarenal chloride loss leading to hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

Treatment:
The patient was rehydrated with physiologic saline solution and received potassium chloride supplementation. To suppress gastric proton and chloride secretion, the patient was treated with a high dose of proton pump inhibition. The diagnosis of short bowel syndrome was confirmed through an oral enema with gastrografin. Port implantation and nocturnal parenteral nutrition were initiated due to excessive stomal fluid losses.

Follow-up:
Upon fluid replacement, electrolyte imbalances markedly improved, and creatinine rapidly declined to the known range. The patient was discharged after 11 days in good condition and advised to present at an intestine transplantation center for evaluation of future combined intestinal and renal transplantation.

Conclusion:
The patient's electrolyte and acid-base imbalances have markedly improved since initial admission to our hospital. Further evaluation of the patient's intestinal and renal function is suggested to assess eligibility for combined transplantation.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: Confidential
DOB: Confidential
Admission Date: July 13th, 2017
Discharge Date: August 12th, 2017
Length of Stay: 30 days

Medical History:
The patient was a 32-year-old man with a known history of ankylosing spondylitis, HLA-B27 positive. He was initially treated with corticosteroids, sulfasalazine, and indomethacin but due to the incomplete therapeutic response, his regimen was changed to anti-TNF-α (Etanercept) from September 15th, 2016.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with raised liver transaminases and poly gammopathy on February 12th, 2017, which were detected in his routine follow-up laboratory tests without any obvious clinical symptoms. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasounds had normal findings. His anti-TNF-α regimen was discontinued and after 2 months, his liver enzymes returned to the normal level.

On May 13th, 2017, the anti-TNF-α regimen started again with the same dosage as the beginning. After 2 months in July 2017, the patient was admitted to the emergency department of Tehran Imam-Khomeini Hospital Complex with icterus, fatigue, and weakness. His laboratory tests showed high liver transaminases and high bilirubin levels. His serologic markers had negative results for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, human immunodeficiency viruses or cytomegalovirus infections. The patient weight was 76 Kg (BMI=25.39kg/m2).

In the next two weeks, his liver enzymes did not change significantly, also his level of consciousness dramatically decreased and after 15 days, a grade II liver encephalopathy occurred. Therefore, he received emergent liver transplantation from a deceased donor with the clinical impression of fulminant hepatitis.

Pathologic Findings:
The explanted liver of the patient was received in the pathology department. The microscopic examination of prepared sections showed extensive confluent necrosis in all liver segments. In portal tracts, prominent infiltration of a mixed population of inflammatory cells composed of lymphoplasma cells, eosinophils and neutrophils were noticed. Also, a moderate to severe cholangiolar reaction was prominent. No significant fibrosis was identified on trichrome staining.

Summary:
The patient was diagnosed with anti-TNF-α induced liver injury. He received emergent liver transplantation due to the development of fulminant hepatitis. Pathologic findings showed extensive confluent necrosis in all liver segments. During hospitalization, the patient's level of consciousness gradually decreased and he received liver transplantation which was successful.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Sex: Female
Age: 24 years
Chief Complaint: Painless reddish swollen mass in lower right anterior region with gums which bleed profusely on mild manipulation

Hospital Course:

The patient reported to the Periodontics Department of Saveetha Dental College and Hospital, Chennai, with the chief complaint of painless reddish swollen mass in lower right anterior region with gums which bleed profusely on mild manipulation which had been present for 4 months. The patient's medical history revealed no debilitating systemic diseases except unusual asymptomatic patchy skin lesions since birth. The examination revealed generalized reddish pink gingiva which easily bled on mild provocation. Enlargement of 1 × 1 ×1.5 in respect to lower right canine and first premolar the lesion showed desquamative surface changes. Radiographs showed a localized horizontal bone loss of 2–3 mm in relation to 15.23 and angular bone loss in respect to 36. Blood investigations did not show any abnormality. Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, a provisional diagnosis of chronic gingivitis with inflammatory enlargement was made. 

The patient underwent Phase 1 periodontal therapy which included scaling and root planing along with 0.2% chlorhexidine mouthwash twice daily; however, the patient failed to respond appropriately to initial periodontal therapy. An excisional biopsy of the lesion present in lower right anterior gingival mass was taken after acquiring patient consent and was sent for histopathological examination. 

Histopathological examination revealed the presence of Fibrocellular connective tissue stroma with sheets of plasma cells admixed with neutrophils in the superficial layers along with areas of endothelial cell proliferation and numerous capillary-sized blood vessels.
