Subsequently, the diagnosis was confirmed as PCG. Further examination of K 13 and K 5 along with laminin was suggested to rule out possible mutations of epidermolysis bullosa and Cockayne syndrome.

After the histopathological confirmation of PCG, a comprehensive treatment plan was discussed with the patient. The patient was instructed to maintain good oral hygiene with regular visits to the Periodontics Department of the hospital for follow-up and monitoring of the condition. 

Condition at Discharge:

The patient was discharged from the hospital in stable condition, with no significant complications reported.

HCF Dental Centre, Sydney Discharge Summary

Patient: 40-year-old male with a chronic ulcer in the right buccal mucosa adjacent to tooth number 18.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient presented with a chronic ulcer in the right buccal mucosa adjacent to tooth number 18. The ulcer was diagnosed to have been present for 6 months and had increased in size. The patient initially sought treatment for pain and discomfort. However, after 5 months of non-resolution, he was diagnosed with a chronic ulcer and was referred to oral surgery for opinion and treatment.

Clinical examination revealed a large ulcer in the right buccal mucosa adjacent to tooth number 18, with indurated margins and a grayish-pink base. Tooth number 18 was buccally inclined and difficult to clean. There were no palpable lymph nodes.

An excisional/incisional biopsy was decided, and the removal of tooth number 18 was performed to remove a possible causative factor for the ulcer. After the removal of tooth number 18, the exposure of the ulcer was good, and an excisional biopsy was performed with safety margins. The area was sutured primarily. The postoperative period was uneventful, and the wound healed within 3 weeks without any complications.

Microscopic examination revealed the extent of ulceration, and all sections presented similar histologic features. The surrounding epithelium was intact and well differentiated, though slightly hyperplastic. The cellular infiltrate within the submucosal tissue consisted predominantly of eosinophils with a few scattered lymphocytes, plasma cells, and lymphocytes. The inflamed tissue included numerous mast cells, particularly in the corium adjacent to the hyperplastic epithelium. The inflamed tissue was well-vascularized. No atypical cells or signs of granulomatous infiltration were seen.

A follow-up of a year showed no recurrence or abnormalities. The patient was discharged without any further treatment needed.

Hospital course summary:

Patient is a 47-year-old female with a history of systolic heart failure, hypertension, and multiple sclerosis who was admitted for repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm (TAAA) secondary to aortic dissection. The patient's medical history was extensively reviewed, and further imaging demonstrated aneurysmal disease throughout the arch and into the three great vessels. The aortic dissection extended from the ascending aorta through the arch down into the left iliac. All visceral vessels and iliacs were fed by true lumen. A max diameter of 58 mm was noted just distal to the left subclavian artery with progressive back pain. The patient underwent a complex surgical repair which included two PAEGs: a double barrel and a manifold. The thoracic double barrel stent graft and thoracic manifold were positioned and deployed via right subclavian, left carotid, left brachial, and bilateral femoral accesses. Before we brought up the arch and descending thoracic graft, we established retrograde wire access in the other two limbs of the thoracic manifold. It is to be noted that access to the innominate was via our delivery wire from the right subclavian artery. Completion angiography demonstrated a patent aortic arch and patent great vessels. Flow was retained in the innominate, right- and left-common carotids, and bilateral subclavian arteries. The procedure required 147 cc of contrast and 105 min of fluoroscopy. Post-operative imaging showed no endoleaks. The patient experienced significant pulmonary issues and required two additional days on the ventilator. She was discharged to home on post-op day 13, and has been followed at 1 month, 6 months, and 12 months.

Patient Name: [Name]
Gender: Female  
Admission Date: [date]

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient was admitted to our Liver Surgical Unit with the history of flushing, diarrhea, vomiting and low grade fever. There were multiple hypoechoic lesions detected in both lobes of liver on Ultrasound (US). Computed Tomography (CT) revealed heterogeneous hypodense lesions invading most of the hepatic parenchyma. The lesions showed mild gradual enhancement during the arterial and portal phases, while cystic areas were also demonstrated. The larger lesions showed extrahepatic extension compressing and dislocating the duodenum.

DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT: A 24-hour urine test showed high 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) levels, while the tumor markers CEA and Ca 19-9 were within their normal range. The patient underwent a CT-guided biopsy of the larger lesion which confirmed the presence of a well differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. Based on the biochemical and radiological investigation, the diagnosis of PHCT was made. Due to the extended liver invasion, resection wasn't feasible and palliation was performed with TACE and administration of lanreotide. TACE included streptozotocin combined with lipiodol. 

RESULT: The patient is currently free of symptoms with no radiologic disease progression after two years of treatment.

HOSPITAL COURSE: During the hospital course, the patient underwent various diagnostic modalities along with TACE and the administration of lanreotide. During this period, the patient was kept under close observation.

Clinical History: The patient presented to the hospital with right flank pain, hematuria, and dysuria. He had a history of indwelling ureteral J stent and extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) for 1 cm right ureteral stone one year ago. The patient developed an anal abscess and left out the ESWL therapy after two sessions, and the ureteral J stent was not removed. He had pyuria in his urine test and urine culture revealed Enterococcus faecalis infection sensitive to ampicillin.

The patient had an uneventful postoperative period. The percutaneous nephrostomy tube was removed on the postoperative 1st day, and the patient was discharged on the postoperative 2nd day.
Discharge Diagnosis: Ureteral J stent fragmentation with stone formation around it.
Discharge Plan: The patient was discharged with instructions to follow up with the urologist and undergo imaging to ensure there are no residual fragments. He was advised to maintain good hydration and to report any signs of infection or recurrent symptoms. The patient was discharged on oral antibiotics and pain medication as needed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 20-year-old woman

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital for a chalazion of the left lower eyelid. The patient had undergone three surgical procedures in the past four years for this condition, but no tissues had been submitted for histopathological examination. The ocular examination was normal except for the presence of a firm, non-tender, painless nodule measuring 13 × 8 × 8mm located in the middle of the left lower eyelid, independent of the lid margin. No clinical findings were indicative of neurofibromatosis.

Treatment:

The patient underwent full-thickness resection of the lid around the tumor, and the lesion was removed under local anesthesia. The nodule was well-circumscribed, non-encapsulated, measuring 10mm in diameter with yellow appearance on cut sections. Microscopic examination revealed fascicules and bundles of non-pigmented spindle cells with elongated bland nuclei, and abundant extracellular collagen with adipocytes and squamous cells displaying an Antoni A pattern. There was no mitotic activity. Immunochemistry for S-100 protein was strongly positive, but tumor cells did not react with HMB45.

Outcome:

The final diagnosis was benign schwannoma of the eyelid. The patient is currently stable and has been discharged with appropriate post-operative instructions. Further treatment is not required at this time.

Follow-Up:

The patient is advised to follow up as directed by her healthcare provider and if there is a recurrence of the chalazion. The patient should also monitor for any signs of neurofibromatosis and report any new symptoms to her healthcare provider immediately.

Hospital Course:
The 1-year-old male infant, diagnosed with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS), was admitted to the Oral and Maxillofacial Department at the faculty of dentistry of King Abdul Aziz University due to macroglossia leading to an inability to close his mouth, interference with occlusion, feeding and swallowing difficulties, and drooling. The patient also presented with hemihypertrophy of the left side of the body. Ultrasonography showed mild hepatomegaly and mild bilateral nephromegaly with no other detectable abnormalities. Liver and kidney functions were assessed including the alpha-fetoprotein level for tumor screening, and all values were within the normal limit. No molecular confirmation was performed for this case so far.

Treatment:
The patient underwent full assessment by a multidisciplinary team comprising pediatrician, genetic specialists, oral and maxillofacial surgeons, pathologists, pedodontists, and orthodontists to assess his condition and treatment options. Surgical debulking of the enlarged tongue was performed by oral and maxillofacial surgeons under general anesthesia. The patient was placed in the supine position and a modified reduction glossectomy was performed using the stellate anterior wedge procedure. A specimen of the tongue was submitted to the Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology Department. Histopathology using hematoxylin and eosin staining revealed muscular hyperplasia.

Outcome:
The patient was discharged after 7 days of follow-up, and he was well. During the follow-up at age 2 years (1 year after the surgery), difficulties in airway and speech were not observed. The patient undergoes periodic follow-up with his pediatrician to assess enlargement of visceral organs and liver and kidney functions.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of fever, abdominal pain, watery diarrhea, and general malaise. Laboratory results indicated leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and low potassium levels. The patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy without complication. Postoperatively, the patient had positive cytomegalovirus antibody immunoglobulin M positive and blood cultures were positive for LM.

The patient was successfully treated for cholecystitis and listeriosis and remained hospitalized for workup of leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with chief complaints of lower abdominal pain, subjective fevers, chills, decreased appetite, and diarrhea. The patient had previously visited another hospital where a CT scan of abdomen and pelvis reportedly showed no abnormality. However, on admission, a CT of abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast revealed a mantle of low density surrounding the middle aorta with surrounding stranding and adjacent aortic calcification. A follow-up CTA abdomen and pelvis found an irregular saccular aneurysm involving the anterior infrarenal abdominal aorta below the level of the inferior mesenteric artery with periaortic low density concerning for inflammatory or infectious aneurysm. The patient was diagnosed with an infected aortic aneurysm and scheduled for surgery.

Treatment:
The patient was initially placed on broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage with vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam. Vascular surgery was consulted and the patient underwent excision of the infected aortic aneurysm, and reconstruction with homograft was performed. The patient was found to have salmonella bacteremia. The infectious disease was consulted and antibiotic coverage was changed to cefepime and later ceftriaxone based on the sensitivities. The patient was continued on six weeks of ceftriaxone through a peripherally inserted central catheter.

Outcome:
The patient's postoperative course was unremarkable, and recovery was satisfactory. The patient responded well to the antibiotic therapy and completed the prescribed course of treatment. The patient had a negative rheumatologic workup, and no complications were reported during the follow-up period. The patient was discharged from the hospital in good condition with a recommendation for medical follow-up.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was advised to complete the full course of antibiotics prescribed by the infectious disease specialist. The patient was also advised to schedule follow-up appointments with their primary care physician and vascular surgeon to monitor their condition. The patient was informed about the potential complications associated with the disease and advised to seek medical attention immediately if they experienced any symptoms. The patient was also instructed to maintain good hygiene practices and a healthy lifestyle.

Patient Summary:
A 21-year-old male presented with a slowly progressive weakness, thinning, and tremulousness of the left hand and forearm for 3 years. Neurological examination revealed moderate degree of wasting of forearm and small muscles of hand involving C7, C8, and D1 myotomes and weak thenar, hypothenar, and introsseous muscles. Deep tendon reflexes were normal in the upper limbs and brisk in the lower limbs with flexor plantar response. The patient was diagnosed with Hirayama disease.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent electromyography (EMG) of affected muscles and plain spinal radiograms which showed abnormal straightening of cervical vertebrae. Cervical MR images in the neutral position demonstrated focal atrophy of the cervical cord at the C5 and C6 vertebral levels along with loss of dural attachment from subjacent lamina on the left side. Dynamic flexion MRI showed the cervical cord to be displaced anteriorly and compressed over the posterior surface of the C 5-6 vertebral bodies with a prominent crescent-shaped epidural mass with flow voids.

The patient was treated for Hirayama disease and malingering with a team of physicians that included a neurologist, radiologist, and anesthesiologist. The patient was observed in the hospital for the duration of his treatment.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was discharged in a stable condition with instructions to follow up with his physician. The patient was prescribed necessary medications as per the physician's recommendations. The patient was advised to follow healthy lifestyle habits and a balanced diet. The patient's family was informed about the patient's condition and necessary follow-ups.

Patient Name: [CONFIDENTIAL]

Hospital Course:

The patient was a 38-year-old Caucasian woman with ulcerative colitis who had extra-intestinal manifestations (polyarthritis) and mitral valve prolapse. She presented to the emergency department with 10 days of bloody diarrhoea and lower abdominal cramping pain. She was admitted to the hospital for intravenous hydration and symptomatic treatment for presumed infectious enterocolitis. After 48 hours with minimal response to therapy, she was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis and started on mesalazine 2.4 g daily with oral prednisone 40 mg daily.

Due to persistent rectal urgency, the patient underwent an ileocolonoscopy which revealed diffuse crypt architectural distortion. A daily mesalazine suppository (1 g) was added with improvement, and at three months she remained in clinical remission on mesalazine monotherapy. Later onset of fatigue, palpitations, chest pain, anxiety and headaches led to echocardiography which disclosed mitral valve prolapse associated with moderate mitral regurgitation.

An eight-week course of tapering steroids was started with clinical remission occurring after three weeks. Continuing immunosuppressive and biologic therapy were considered excessively high-risk options given her predisposition to infective endocarditis. She was referred to the inflammatory bowel disease clinic of Parma University Hospital and soon after stopping steroids, there was another exacerbation of the colitis.

Withdrawal of the budesonide precipitated a further relapse comprising diarrhoea and bleeding. Omega-3 unsaturated fatty acid therapy was commenced at 1 g twice daily, while mesalazine was maintained at 2.4 g daily. At 2 weeks, complete clinical and endoscopic remission had been accomplished, with a Mayo Clinic score of 0.

The patient was discharged and will continue her Omega-3 unsaturated fatty acid therapy at 1 g twice daily and mesalazine therapy at 1.6 g daily for the succeeding 18 months. Surgical work-up for mitral valve replacement was commenced. She was advised to avoid anti-inflammatory drugs and to follow a diet low in fat and high in fiber.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Gender: Male
Age: 2

Hospital course:
The patient was admitted with a prenatal diagnosis of left MCDK and right hydronephrosis. The patient underwent surgery for the right PUJO to prevent renal dysfunction. The post-operative course was uneventful, and the patient showed improvement in the right hydronephrosis.

Diagnosis and treatment:
The patient had left MCDK and right hydronephrosis. Surgery was performed for right PUJO to prevent renal dysfunction. Three right renal vessels were independently branching from the abdominal aorta. The middle renal vessels (renal artery 2) were located at the ventral side of the pelvis and were coincident with the site of PUJO. The CVs were dissected and taped with vessel tape. An intraoperative diuretic test was performed by an anesthesiologist using furosemide loading. Extrinsic PUJO owing to the CVs was definitively confirmed. Transposition for the CVs (VH) was performed instead of AHDP. The CVs were mobilized in the cranial direction and those were loosely wrapped by dilated pelvic anterior wall using three interrupted sutures of 4–0 non-absorbable monofilament.

Follow-up:
MRU showed improvement of the right hydronephrosis. The renal scintigraphy findings improved and showed a favorable response of furosemide loading.

Recommendations:
The patient should follow up regularly with the physician to monitor the improvement of right hydronephrosis. Further testing may be needed to ensure proper and adequate renal function.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A

Admitting Diagnosis: Mobile battery blast injury to the face

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 10-year-old male child, was admitted to the Pediatric emergency department with an injury to the right side of the face caused by a mobile battery explosion. Upon examination, the patient was found to have a circular injury on the right cheek. The injury was found to be communicating intraorally to the oral cavity. There was herniation of the buccal pad of fat, blood clots, and superficial burn around the wound.

The patient's parotid gland appeared to be injured, but there was no damage to the facial and trigeminal nerve functions. The patient was diagnosed with a soft tissue injury and treated with antibiotics and pain relievers. The patient also received a booster dose of tetanus toxoid immunoglobulin.

The patient underwent an emergency operation for wound closure under general anesthesia. Cleansing and rinsing of the wound were done using povidone-iodine and normal saline solution, followed by marginal necrosectomy and debridement. Suturing of the oral mucosa, parotid gland, parotid capsule, and sub-dermal layer was done with 4-0 polyglactin suture while 5-0 prolene suture was used on the superficial skin layer.

Post-operatively, the patient was supported with antibiotics, analgesics, and fluid supplements. The dressing was done twice a day for 1 week. On the fourth post-operative day, the patient developed salivary leakage from the extraoral margins of the sutured wound. Despite the re-evaluation of Stenson's duct which was found to be intact, the conservative approach was opted, and pressure packing was used. Finally, on the fourteenth post-operative day, sutures were removed, and the patient was discharged in a healthy state.

Conclusion:
The patient was diagnosed and treated for mobile battery blast injury to the face. The patient underwent an operation for wound closure and was prescribed antibiotics, analgesics, and fluid supplements. The patient developed salivary leakage from the extraoral margins of the sutured wound on the fourth post-operative day, which was successfully managed by pressure packing. The patient was discharged on the fourteenth post-operative day in good condition.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Patient Name: Anonymous
DOB: Anonymous
Hospital ID: Anonymous

OVERVIEW:
This is an 18-year-old female patient diagnosed with Adult-onset Still's Disease (AOSD), who was admitted in January 2013 with complaints of nausea, abdominal discomfort, and pruritus. The patient had a history of recurrent fever, polyarthritis, abdominal lymphadenopathy, liver and spleen enlargement, and hyperferritinemia and had previously been treated with oral corticoids and methotrexate. Tocilizumab was started in June 2011 and, in December 2011, corticoids and methotrexate were discontinued. The patient had no symptoms and normal liver function tests under tocilizumab once every 3 weeks in 2012. But, in January 2013, the patient presented with acute liver failure, which was found to be drug-induced. Hepatocytes suffered from extensive centrilobular necrosis with collapse, ballooning, and clear cytoplasm, which were consistent with DILI. The patient received a 3-day course of intravenous N-acetylcysteine and liver function tests were monitored until normalization 6 weeks later. Causality assessment by the Naranjo score and the Liverpool Adverse Drug Reaction Causality Assessment Tool indicated tocilizumab as a probable cause of the acute liver failure.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was admitted to the hospital on January 24, 2013, with complaints of nausea, abdominal discomfort, and pruritus that persisted for two days despite taking a daily dose of 1 gram of paracetamol. On admission, the patient's physical examination revealed a slightly tender liver, but no signs of chronic liver disease were observed. Laboratory investigations showed low white blood cells and platelets counts, elevated AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, and total bilirubin with decreased prothrombin time suggestive of liver injury. However, kidney function tests were normal, and blood paracetamol concentration was not measured at admission due to minor exposure. Imaging studies showed mild liver and spleen enlargement despite no abnormality in abdominal imaging. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, and E) as well as HIV, CMV, EBV, and herpes simplex virus tested negative. Autoimmune testing (total IgG, antinuclear, antiactin, and anti-LKM1 antibodies) was negative, and ceruloplasmin was normal. A transjugular liver biopsy was performed with a portosushepatic venous pressure gradient of 8 mmHg, which showed extensive centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis with collapse and ballooning with clear cytoplasm. Mild inflammatory periportal cell infiltrations as well as rare areas of micro- and macrovesicular steatosis were also observed, which were consistent with DILI.

DISCHARGE STATUS:
The patient was discharged after a 6-week hospital stay, after receiving a 3-day course of intravenous N-acetylcysteine, which resulted in transplant-free survival in acute severe nonacetaminophen liver injury. Liver function tests were monitored until normalization. The patient and her rheumatologist were instructed not to be reexposed to tocilizumab as it was the probable cause of the acute liver failure.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient was advised to follow up with her rheumatologist regularly for her AOSD. Liver function tests were to be monitored for the next few months to ensure complete recovery from DILI. Any new symptoms or medication changes must be reported immediately to the healthcare provider. 

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
Acute liver failure due to Drug-Induced Liver Injury (tocilizumab)

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
None documented.

Discharge Summary for Patient with Fetal Growth Restriction and Uteroplacental Insufficiency

Patient Information:
Name: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 32 years
Date of Admission: January 2013
Date of Discharge: April 2013

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to our Out Patient Department (OPD) in January 2013 with 12 weeks of pregnancy. At 14 weeks, she required an emergency cerclage for cervical incompetence. She had a normal anomaly scan with no other co-morbid conditions. At 26 weeks and 3 days, she was admitted to the hospital due to clinical suspicion of oligohydramnios. Ultrasound with Doppler indicated reduced amniotic flow index with reduced umbilical artery diastolic flow, middle cerebral artery brain sparing effect, and estimated fetal weight of around 600 grams.

Sildenafil citrate 50 mg BD was used for the patient initially and gradually increased to 50 mg TDS with continuous fetal surveillance. Doppler showed improved uteroplacental blood flow with estimated fetal weight of around 800 grams and hence pregnancy could be continued to another 3 weeks. With the diagnosis of FGR with uteroplacental insufficiency, surveillance continued with ultrasonography and Doppler. However, Doppler again showed absent end diastolic flow after a few days, and 2 doses of 12 mg betamethasone injection were administered for her 24 hr apart. Repeat Doppler after 3 days showed reversed end diastolic flow. 

At a gestational age of 30 weeks, the patient and her husband were counseled regarding the need for emergency Caesarean section and the associated risks of perinatal morbidity and mortality. A live male baby of 800 grams was delivered and shifted to Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) for further management. After 80 days of NICU care, the baby was finally discharged healthy with a weight of 2.3 kg. 

Follow-up:
After 1 month of discharge, the mother and infant came for follow up and both were doing perfectly well. The infant was checked by the pediatrician and was found healthy. No further issues were reported by the patient at the follow-up visit. 

Diagnosis: 
Fetal growth restriction with uteroplacental insufficiency

Hospital Management:
- Sildenafil citrate 50 mg BD was used and gradually increased to 50 mg TDS.
- Continuous fetal surveillance was performed.
- 2 doses of 12 mg betamethasone injection were administered 24 hours apart.
- Emergency Caesarean section was performed at 30 weeks.

Prognosis:
The patient delivered a live, healthy male baby after emergency Caesarean section at 30 weeks. The infant received NICU care for 80 days and was ultimately discharged with a healthy weight of 2.3 kg. The patient and infant attended a follow-up visit one month after discharge and both were doing well. No further issues were reported by the patient at the follow-up visit.

Admitting Diagnosis: GI bleeding

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 92-year-old female with a history of SMM, was admitted with symptoms of progressive weakness, orthostatic dizziness, and melena. She had a bone marrow biopsy three months earlier that revealed a variably cellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis. A complete bone survey showed no lytic lesions in the bones. On admission, the patient had a soft and nontender abdomen and was found to have melena on rectal examination. She was diagnosed with GI bleeding and was found to have an 11 × 6 cm adherent blood clot attached to the gastric body during EGD. Despite vigorous endoscopic irrigation and aspiration, the clot could not be detached. The patient was administered intravenous pantoprazole at 8 mg/hr after an 80 mg loading dose and transfused 2 units of packed erythrocytes. Repeat EGD performed one day later revealed that the clot had mostly dissolved exposing a not actively bleeding, 2.5 × 2 cm ulcerated mass mostly covered by clot in the midgastric body along the lesser curvature. Histologic staining with Congo red stain revealed positively staining deposits in the lamina propria that exhibited apple-green birefringence under polarized light, consistent with gastric amyloidosis. Peptides extracted from Congo red-positive areas after microdissection of paraffin-embedded stomach biopsy specimens were consistent with AL- (lambda-) type amyloidosis.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient, a 92-year-old female with a history of SMM, was admitted with GI bleeding and diagnosed with gastric amyloidosis with AL- (lambda-) type amyloidosis. She was found to have an 11 × 6 cm adherent blood clot attached to the gastric body and was administered intravenous pantoprazole and transfused 2 units of packed erythrocytes. The clot was dissolved during a repeat EGD, and the patient had no further episodes of GI bleeding. She was discharged home after 17 days in the hospital while receiving omeprazole 40 mg orally once daily. No bleeding has been noted during one-month follow-up.

Discharge Diagnosis: Gastric amyloidosis with AL- (lambda-) type amyloidosis

Discharge Treatment: Omeprazole 40 mg orally once daily

Discharge Condition: Stable

Follow-up Instructions: Require one-month follow-up.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Gender: Male
Age: 62
Hospital Admission: Outpatient 

History of Present Illness:
The patient is a 62-year-old male with a history of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, diagnosed eight years ago, with inadequate glycemic control. Over the past two years, he had complained of pruritus predominantly over the lower limbs, soles, palms, and upper arms, which worsened over the past eight months with the development of nodular erythematous skin lesions over the areas of intense pruritus. The patient had a history of acute variceal bleed for which he underwent endoscopic band ligation six months prior and was controlled on secondary prophylaxis with beta-blocker therapy. He was diagnosed at that time with cirrhosis of the liver secondary to non-alcoholic fatty liver disease with skin changes suggestive of diabetic dermopathy and was advised strict glycemic control, emollients, and anti-histamines.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the outpatient department after the pruritus gradually worsened, and new crops of lesions developed over the lower back and thighs with new onset fatigue developing over the past two months. On physical examination, bilateral mild pedal pitting edema was evident, and multiple erythematous nodular lesions were observed over the thighs, legs, upper arms, and lower back. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, and E were negative, and HbA1c was 6.8%. Blood investigations for antibodies to nuclear, liver-kidney-microsomal type one, soluble liver, smooth muscle, Smith, and double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid were negative and total serum immunoglobulin G levels were within normal limits. However, the anti-mitochondrial antibody was positive at 1:80 titer by enzyme immunoassay test. Abdominal ultrasound, computer tomography, and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatogram scans showed the cirrhotic architecture of the liver with splenomegaly without ascites, focal liver lesions, portal vein thrombosis, intrahepatic biliary radicle dilatation, and normal common bile and pancreatic ducts. Bone densitometry was suggestive of osteopenia. 

The patient was diagnosed with primary biliary cholangitis or PBC and started on Ursodeoxycholic acid at 13 mg/kg per day in divided doses. However, the skin lesions were not classical of PBC. Skin biopsies were taken from inactive and active lesions, revealing histopathological features typical of dermatitis herpetiformis with its differentials. To confirm the diagnosis, the patient was advised gluten-free diet and 100 milligrams of oral dapsone was added. In three days’ time, the skin lesions started showing resolution in activity and pruritus reduced substantially. 

Hospital Outcome:
Dapsone was stopped, and dietary gluten was restarted, but the patient developed severe itching with new active lesions after four days of rechallenge, confirming the diagnosis of dermatitis herpetiformis and gluten sensitivity. The patient was advised to continue Ursodeoxycholic acid and the low dose of naltrexone with fat-soluble vitamin replacement and the short course of dapsone for symptomatic relief. At one-month follow-up, the patient is keeping well, and symptoms are abating. 

Diagnosis:
-Diabetes Mellitus
-Cirrhosis of the liver secondary to non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
-Primary biliary cholangitis 
-Dermatitis herpetiformis with gluten sensitivity 

Recommendations:
-The patient should continue Ursodeoxycholic acid 
-Fat-soluble vitamin replacement 
-Dapsone can be administered for symptomatic relief 
-Avoidance of gluten in the diet

Chief Complaint:
Patient presented in cardiac arrest likely due to hypoxia from refractory status epilepticus. Further evaluation revealed a febrile state of unknown origin and duration.

The patient was treated with several antiseizure medications, high dose steroids, IVIG, interleukin-1 inhibitor Anakinra, and plasmapheresis. After 42 days of hospitalization, the patient was discharged home where she has regained her ability to speak, feed herself, and continues to improve.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 61-year-old male with hepatitis B virus and a history of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with metastasis to the iliac bone

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital for the excision of a massive metastatic HCC tumor at the right iliac bone that had invaded the soft tissue and caused significant compression of the adjacent sciatic nerve. The surgery was successful in removing the tumor and relieving the patient's symptoms of right low back pain and radiation to the right lower extremity. The patient's recovery was uneventful, and he was able to walk with a stick. No further radiotherapy was arranged since the patient had prior radiotherapy.

A repeat surgery was performed due to tumor recurrence, and a biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of a hepatic metastatic HCC with sarcomatous change. The tumor pathology showed the transition from the differentiation of hepatocytic carcinomatous characters to spindle cell, chondroid and osteoid components. The serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level remained within normal limits despite the progression of the disease and absence of viable liver tumors.

The patient was discharged on October 30th, 2009, and instructed to continue follow-up with appropriate specialists.

A 73-year-old male smoker presented for the evaluation of a cardiac mass that was diagnosed incidentally during the workup for unintentional weight loss. The patient was found to have a large papillary fibroelastoma (PFE) attached to the non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve, along with several mobile echo densities which may represent multiple Lambl's or a sessile type of PFE. During the surgery, one large mass attached to the non-coronary cusp and a medium-sized mass were removed. There were numerous small frond-like masses attached to the aortic surface of all three cusps. Valve preservation was attained by the meticulous removal of each of the described masses. The patient had an uneventful recovery, and the dismissal echo showed a well-functioning aortic valve.

Papillary fibroelastoma (PFE)

Stable

Not applicable

No specific discharge instructions were provided.

A 63-year-old man was admitted to the hospital due to miosis, ptosis, hypohidrosis of his left side, polydipsia and polyuria. Computed tomography (CT) showed multiple lesions involving the pituitary gland, the apex of the left lung, and the left adrenal gland. 18F-fluorodeoxy glucose positron emission tomography / CT (18F-FDG PET/CT) imaging indicated high 18F-FDG uptake in the pituitary gland, bilateral adrenal glands and the lesion at the apex of his left lung. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed an enhanced suprasellar lesion and thickening of the pituitary stalk. Surgical biopsy of the pituitary lesion showed that the pituitary gland was almost completely replaced by large abnormal lymphocytes which were positive for B-cell markers (CD20), but negative for T-cell markers (CD3).

The patient was diagnosed with DLBCL with pituitary and adrenal involvement and panhypopituitarism and adrenal insufficiency. The patient was treated with hormone replacement therapy and six cycles of chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, and prednisolone (R-CHOP), followed by planned autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (auto-HSCT). To prevent infiltration of DLBCL into the central nervous system, the patient was also given two cycles of intravenous high-dose methotrexate (HD-MTX) therapy and two cycles of intrathecal injection of MTX, cytarabine, and dexamethasone.

The patient's pituitary and bilateral adrenal lesions disappeared on MRI, CT, and 18F-FDG PET/CT after chemotherapy, and the symptoms of diabetes insipidus decreased. The desmopressin dose was gradually decreased, and the requirement of hydrocortisone was also decreased. Under this replacement regimen, basal hormone levels of cortisol, TSH, and f-T4 improved. The patient is to undergo testosterone replacement therapy during the next follow-up visit.

According to the patient's diagnostics, he was assessed to have poor prognosis, but the treatments were successful, and the patient was discharged in a stable condition.

The patient is to follow up with his physician for regular monitoring of his medical condition. Hospital Course:
The patient is a 63-year-old male admitted with intermittent gross hematuria and anemia. He had undergone a Y-graft surgery for an abdominal aortic aneurysm 3 years earlier. Imaging revealed that the right ureter was extrinsically compressed by fibrosis at the site of its crossing over the Y-graft and a ureteral stent was placed at another hospital, 7 months before presentation. Cystoscopy revealed hematuria from the right ureteric orifice, suggesting the possibility of AUF. Laboratory data showed anemia with an elevated serum creatinine level and a slightly elevated C-reactive protein concentration. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a possible fistula between the right common iliac artery and the ureter. The patient was diagnosed with AUF associated with the Y-graft. An elective endovascular surgery was performed by vascular surgeons following embolization of the right internal iliac artery to prevent endoleak caused by backflow from the right internal iliac artery. A stent was placed via the right femoral artery. Extrinsic obstruction caused by inflammatory fibrotic change was considered to be so dense that it was impossible to treat the ureteral stricture. Neither antiplatelet nor anticoagulation drugs were prescribed. Two weeks after treatment, imaging showed disappearance of the fistula and improvement of right hydronephrosis. Six months after the endovascular surgery, severe right hydronephrosis was observed with an elevated serum creatinine level. Retroperitoneoscopic nephrectomy was performed because of concern about the recurrence of the fistula. No bleeding from the right residual ureter has been observed. 

Hospital Course Summary:
- Admission for intermittent gross hematuria and anemia.
- History of Y-graft surgery and extrinsic ureteral compression.
- Imaging revealed a possible AUF, and a stent was placed at another hospital.
- Diagnosis of AUF associated with Y-graft made at our hospital.
- Endovascular surgery performed with successful disappearance of fistula and improvement of hydronephrosis.
- Retroperitoneoscopic nephrectomy performed due to concern for fistula recurrence.
- No bleeding from the right residual ureter observed.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient presented to the emergency department with left-sided pleuritic chest pain, and imaging demonstrated left-sided pleural effusion with basilar consolidation. The patient was treated with oral levofloxacin for presumed community-acquired pneumonia, but failed empiric treatment.

The patient underwent ultrasound-guided thoracentesis that confirmed exudative pleural effusion. Following thoracentesis, the patient had ongoing evidence of effusion and underwent CT-guided left-sided 12 French chest tube placement with interventional radiology. Despite conservative management and attempts for drainage, the patient continued to be symptomatic and had ongoing evidence of effusion.

Due to persistent evidence of loculated collections on imaging and minimal output via chest tubes, the patient underwent thoracoscopic total lung decortication. Cytology from fluid collected from thoracoscopy was consistent with pneumonia and negative for malignant cells. Delayed intraoperative cultures identified growth from pleural fluid with Fusobacterium nucleatum. The patient clinically improved during this hospitalization on levofloxacin and was later discharged home after an eleven-day stay.

The patient completed her antibiotic course and was recovering well up until 3 weeks after the initial pneumonia presentation when she developed intractable back pain and associated leg weakness. The patient returned to the emergency room for evaluation of her symptoms that also included feet numbness and tingling, vague pain in her legs, especially her thighs, and finally, tightness and tingling sensation in her hands and wrists. Emergency room evaluation included thoracic and lumbar spine MRI.

The patient was started on steroids and gabapentin in addition to pain medications. After neurology consultation, the patient was diagnosed with Guillain–Barré syndrome based on mild symmetric weakness of small hand muscles, hip flexion, hip adductors, hip abductors, big toe extensors, quadriceps, foot dorsiflexion, and foot eversion. Additional testing included CSF analysis showing WBC of 0 and protein 199. Based on minor deficits and stability of her symptoms, the patient was discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility on a steroid taper.

On the patient's 3-month follow-up, her examination showed normal strength to all muscle groups and recovery of deep tendon reflexes.

Hospital Course:

This 13-year-old Korean male presented with a two-year history of painless exophthalmos of the left eye and facial swelling. Ophthalmologic examination revealed conjunctival hyperemia, proptosis, and no visible or palpable mass lesion. CT and MRI scans identified a 1.5x1.5 cm2 homogeneous mass with high signal intensity and relatively well-defined margins. Exophthalmos of the left eye was noted, with diffuse thickening of the left extraocular muscles. Blood studies documented a peripheral eosinophilia of about 26%. 

The patient underwent a lateral rectus muscle incisional biopsy of the left eye, which revealed abnormal vascular proliferation with marked eosinophilic infiltration in hypertrophied collagenous tissue. Oral steroid therapy was initiated for four days and gradually tapered for two months. As a result, exophthalmos of the left eye and facial swelling had substantially subsided but the size of the soft tissue mass increased again following steroid withdrawal. 

A trans-oral facial mass excision biopsy was performed by the otolaryngologist which resulted in histologic findings of follicular hyperplasia with perifollicular fibrosis and massive infiltration by mature eosinophils, which were the same histologic findings seen in the incisional biopsy of the patient's left lateral rectus muscle. 

As the patient responded well to oral steroid therapy and trans-oral facial mass excision biopsy, the patient was discharged for follow-up observation.

Admitting Diagnosis: Open Grade 3C Gustilo-Anderson fracture with the right floating knee


Hospital Course:

The patient presented to the hospital with an open Grade 3C Gustilo-Anderson fracture with the right floating knee following an injury. The patient was initially treated with debridement and external fixator elsewhere and advised amputation above knee before presenting to our hospital. 


Physical examination revealed a lacerated wound extending from distal third of thigh to middle third of leg anteriorly and exposed both femoral condyle fractured fragments and proximal tibial fractured fragments, with patella and lateral tibial condyle absent. The patient had feeble dorsalis pedis artery pulsation and absent posterior tibial artery pulsation. 

A CT angiogram revealed posterior tibial vessel under spasm and anterior tibial sluggish blood flow. Vascular surgeon advised conservative treatment since the injury was type II C as per modified Fraser’s classification. 

After discussion and obtaining consent from the patient and his relatives, the patient underwent a combined procedure under orthopedic and plastic surgery team. The procedure involved wound debridement, reconstruction with Ilizarov fixator, and soft-tissue repair. Intraoperatively, patella and lateral tibial condyle were absent, and patella tendon was sutured to quadriceps tendon. The patient was shifted to the ICU postoperatively and received cardiology consultation due to raised serum myoglobin and CPK levels. 

One week later, he underwent right leg Ilizarov realignment and wound debridement with medial gastrocnemius flap + split skin grafting + vacuum-assisted closure. The patient remained hemodynamically stable throughout their care and was discharged home after regular wound inspections and dressing changes. 

The patient was started on rehabilitative care on discharge, which included strict non-weight-bearing walking with walker support and quadriceps and hamstring muscle strengthening exercises. The treatment was deemed successful, and the patient was discharged. 

Follow-up X-ray radiography after 8 and 12 months showed fracture union for the distal femur and tibia, respectively, and the patient reported symptom improvement. 

Recommendations:
1. Continue to follow up with orthopedic and vascular physicians. 
2. Follow physical therapy recommendations for strengthening and mobility exercises.

4. Follow-up with cardiology if myoglobin and CPK levels rise again.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 42-year-old male
Date of Admission: [DATE]
Date of Discharge: [DATE]

Hospital Course: 
The patient presented with right progressive visual disturbance and was diagnosed with a tumor adjacent to the anterior clinoid process (ACP). The modified encephaloduroarteriosynangiosis (EDTPA) with standard frontotemporal craniotomy was performed. The falciform ligament was completely incised to facilitate optic nerve mobilization. Tumor adjacent to the anterior clinoid process (ACP)

Discharge Instructions: 
Please take all medications as prescribed by your physician. Follow-up with your primary care provider within 7 days of discharge. Please schedule a follow-up appointment with your neurosurgeon in 4 weeks for further evaluation.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]
Date of Admission: [Date]
Date of Discharge: [Date]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 53-year-old Caucasian female, was admitted with a one-month history of lower back pain radiating to the right lower limb, accompanied by weight loss, tiredness, and weakness. A week before admission, she reported petechiae in the lower limbs, a fever of 39°C, and palpable purpura.

Laboratory work-up showed leukocytosis and high levels of C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, and gamma-glutamyl transferase. The platelet count was low, and there were no signs of venous flow disturbance on Doppler ultrasonography.

The lumbar spine MRI showed vertebral disc degeneration with a hernia at L5-S1 space, and the physical examination revealed jaundice, palpable purpura, and hepatomegaly.

During the observation period, the patient developed pain in the left leg and was re-examined. Over the next few hours, her condition progressively worsened, with increasing heart rate, pericardial friction bruit on auscultation, and right bundle block, supraventricular tachycardia, and deviation of the electrical axis to the right on the ECG. Her serum troponin I was high, and she ultimately had cardiac arrest in asystole. Despite advanced cardiac life support, the patient passed away.

Autopsy findings and cause of death:

The patient was referred for autopsy, which showed acute myocardial infarction (MI) and acute pericarditis. Multiple foci of recent myocardial infarction were found, with one infarct involving the right bundle branch. Acute fibrinous pericarditis was also noted, with large areas of fibrin deposition on the outer surface of the heart.

Hospital Discharge:

The patient was discharged to the pathology service for autopsy. Communication was made with the patient's family to provide them with the necessary support and further information. The patient's death was attributed to acute myocardial infarction and acute pericarditis. The discharge summary and autopsy report were provided to the family for their records.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Patient: [NAME], Chinese man, 42 years old, with a history of chronic tophaceous gout.

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted with complaints of severe back pain radiating to his left lower limb and weakness of the left lower limb. The pain had persisted for 2 years, and he had experienced several episodes of similar back pain over the preceding 18 months. In addition, he had a history of gout for the past 4 years, which he had self-medicated with NSAIDs.

Hospital Course:
On admission, the patient was found to have tophi over the dorsum of bilateral hands, bilateral elbows, bilateral ankles, and toes. A neurological examination showed reduced power for left thigh flexion and extension and left knee flexion, and reduced reflexes in the left knee and left ankle. Sensation was reduced at left L4 and L5 dermatomes.
Further investigations revealed an elevated white cell count and C-reactive protein. Radiographs of his lumbosacral spine showed irregularities of the L4/L5 and L5/S1 endplate. An MRI of his spine demonstrated hyperintensity within the intervertebral discs spaces of L4/L5 and L5/S1, in keeping with fluid within.

A diagnosis of epidural abscess with spondylodiscitis was initially suspected, and the patient was started on intravenous cloxacillin. Blood cultures and investigations for tuberculosis were negative. A percutaneous biopsy was not performed due to the high clinical suspicion of epidural abscess and spondylodiscitis. The patient underwent surgery to drain the abscess and laminectomy and posterolateral fusion.

Operative findings showed chalky white non-adherent material over the facet joints resembling gouty tophi, with a small mass lesion with bony erosion noted over the left L4/L5 facet joint. There was no pus or slough at the operative site. Pedicle screws were inserted at the desired lumbar and sacral levels, mainly from L3 to S1. Laminectomy was performed at the L4 and L5 levels. Pre-contoured rods were inserted on both sides followed by posterolateral fusion.

The vertebral disc was submitted for histopathological examination, which revealed necrotic tissue only. Tissue cultures were negative, acid-fast bacilli smears were negative, and tuberculosis culture was negative.

During the hospital course, the patient experienced a gouty arthritis flare of his right wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints, for which he was treated with colchicine and a course of steroids. His back pain improved, and he was started on allopurinol for urate-lowering therapy.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Spondylodiscitis with gouty tophi of the lumbar spine.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with improved back pain and continued treatment with allopurinol for urate-lowering therapy. He will require close follow-up with his primary care physician to monitor his gout and spinal condition.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient was a 56-year-old male with a medical history significant for diabetes and psoriasis who was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma in the right lung. He was treated with pembrolizumab but had to discontinue it after developing a grade 2 colitis which worsened his psoriasis. Shortly after receiving the third cycle, he was admitted with worsening dyspnea and acute confusional state. Imaging studies showed pneumonitis adjacent to his lung lesion, acute pulmonary thromboembolism, renal and splenic infarctions, bilateral deep vein thrombosis and multiple signal changes involving the white matter of parietal, temporal and occipital lobe suggestive of an embolic event.
He underwent multiple diagnostic tests including transesophageal echocardiogram, transcranial Doppler, and brain magnetic resonance angiography, none of which showed any active embolism. Rheumatological markers were not reactive, and cerebrospinal fluid was normal and negative for malignant cells. It was suspected that he developed pneumonitis and vasculitis in response to pembrolizumab. Patient was treated with high dose of corticosteroids and enoxaparin, with progressive improvement of his symptoms, and after 10 days, he was discharged from the hospital.
Pembrolizumab was permanently discontinued. No other significant medical issues were encountered during the hospital stay. Follow-up appointments were scheduled with his primary care physician and his oncologist.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Date of Admission: N/A
Date of Discharge: N/A
Admitting Diagnosis: worsening depressive symptoms, mood-congruent psychosis, and vague suicidal ideation.
Discharge Diagnosis: Stable

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 57-year-old Caucasian male, was admitted on a Temporary Detention Order for two days following the worsening of his depressive symptoms, which included low mood, hopelessness, feelings of guilt and nihilism, and vague suicidal ideation. Concurrent mood-congruent psychosis with auditory hallucinations encouraging self-harm and delusions of impending personal health catastrophe, personal financial bankruptcy, and outstanding criminal charges were observed. The patient had a significant past medical history of ESRD and a psychiatric history notable for bipolar-type schizoaffective disorder, with sporadic inpatient psychiatric hospitalizations dating back to 2005.

The patient has been on multiple treatment regimens, including antidepressants, antipsychotics, and benzodiazepines. The patient's renal function had also been progressively worsening since 2016, requiring hemodialysis three times a week for renal failure. In 2019, a living donor renal allograft of the right kidney was performed without acute complications, and the patient has been stable with good kidney function since.

Due to the lack of efficacy in medication management, the patient underwent bifrontal ultra-brief-pulse ECT treatments three times per week. Bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) was used after the first two treatments due to acute respiratory distress, and the induction agent was changed from methohexital to etomidate after the fifth treatment due to a lack of adequate seizure activity. Also, a clevidipine drip was used for some treatments to manage posttreatment hypertension. The patient experienced no headache, memory loss, or other acute neurological complications, and his renal function remained stable.

The patient showed improvement in his psychosis as early as three treatments, and noticeable improvement in his mood after the eighth session. He continued ECT for a total of twelve treatments, during which he exhibited significant improvement, with little to no reports of hallucinations, paranoia, or delusions, and denied suicidal or homicidal thoughts. Upon discharge, the patient reported feeling "happy" and "back on the right track," and was visibly brighter, more social, and actively participating in group therapy sessions.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient has been discharged with instructions to continue long-term psychiatric counseling. Communication was maintained with the patient's out-of-state renal transplant surgeon, who was pleased with the status of his kidney transplant, antirejection medication levels, and blood pressures. The patient was advised to follow up with his psychiatrist for ongoing medication management and to continue his hemodialysis and regular monitoring of his renal function.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Conjoined twins (not named)
Age: 9 hours old
Sex: Female
Hospital course: 

The conjoined twins were brought into the sick babies unit by their mother. The pregnancy was carried to term and she had limited antenatal care. The delivery had been completed vaginally at home without any obstruction to labor. One twin presented with a well-formed head and cried after several minutes of stimulation. The other twin presented with an anencephalic head and was unresponsive to painful stimulus with dilated and unreactive pupils. The twins shared a single thorax, single abdomen, one complement of genitalia, and two neurologically independent lower limbs. 

The normal twin experienced repeated apneic attacks with cyanosed extremities and died within 9 hours of birth from cardiopulmonary failure. The anencephalic twin was unresponsive to painful stimulus and an orogastric tube was inserted that ended in the neck of the twin.

Post-mortem plain X-ray findings revealed a fully developed cranium with normal facial structures continuous with the main body for the head with a well-formed brain. The other head was devoid of a cranium. The twins each had neck organs and vertebral columns. The single pelvis and lower limbs are clearly defined. The ribs on the medial side of each twin were fused with each other creating 12 instead of 24 posterior ribs.

Two pairs of great vessels, two aortic and two superior vena cavae entered the single heart. There were two atria, two auricular appendages, and two ventricles. The lungs and heart were not demonstrable.

The twins were unable to be thoroughly investigated due to their unstable condition and the short duration of life. No diagnoses, treatments, or medications were given. 

Care was terminated due to the death of the normal twin.

Discharge Summary:
This 23-year-old Chinese male presented with progressive left upper limb and facial nerve palsy, impaired left upper limb movement, and mild dysphasia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a cystic-solid mass, sized 35*25*20 mm, located in the brainstem. A total surgical resection of the tumor mass via a right subtemporal approach was performed under general anesthesia. The lesion was purely intraparenchymal, and no dural or leptmeninges attachment was observed during the operation. The histological examination revealed a tumor tissue composed of sheets of cells arranged in a predominantly papillary pattern with perivascular pseudo-rosettes, consistent with papillary meningioma (WHO III). The patient was recommended for radiotherapy, but he refused further treatment. Nine months later, he was re-admitted with facial palsy and left upper limb weakness again, and brain MRI showed local tumor recurrence. He was re-operated on through the previous approach, with a total tumor resection. One month later, he received local external radiotherapy. Over the more than 2 years follow-up, brain MRI revealed no residual or recurred tumor. However, his left upper limb weakness remained grade IV despite rehabilitation therapy.

Hospital Course:
The 55-year-old male patient had a history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, which was treated with various medications but with no success. The patient was enrolled in a clinical trial that involved the use of an anti-interleukin 17A (IL-17A) monoclonal antibody, secukinumab, and was under observation. However, the patient's renal function started to worsen with rising serum creatinine levels associated with microhematuria and proteinuria. Additionally, the patient had active arthritis in the elbows and wrists. 

Diagnosis:
The patient was referred to the nephrology clinic where an evaluation showed hypocomplementemia, positive titers for anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (CCP) and MPO-ANCA. A renal biopsy was performed, revealing that the patient had pauci-immune necrotizing GN.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with three consecutive pulses of methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone and rituximab in accordance with RA's scheme. The patient had an important clinical improvement with full remission of joint pain and improved renal function. 

Outcome:
Two months later, the patient's renal function stabilized, proteinuria improved, and MPO-ANCA titer normalized. At the last evaluation, 10 months later, the patient's arthritis remains well-controlled, the patient had a prednisolone dose taper, and MPO-ANCA titer continued to normalize. 

Overall, the patient had improvement in joint pain, renal function, and MPO-ANCA titer following treatment for pauci-immune necrotizing GN.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 24-year-old Yoruba Nigerian female, was admitted with a four-month history of hypertension, intermittent bilateral frontal headache, and associated symptoms such as photophobia, tinnitus, palpitation, and diaphoresis. The physical examination showed an anxious patient, a pulse rate of 100 per minute, regular, and the blood pressure was 190/100 mmHg. A tentative diagnosis of pheochromocytoma was made, and the patient was commenced on antihypertensive medications while she was investigated.

Diagnosis:

Investigations revealed a normal thyroid function test, an elevated serum cholesterol level (296 mg/dl), and a left suprarenal mass displacing the left kidney postero-laterally, suggestive of a left adrenal mass. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen revealed a rounded bilobed left suprarenal mass of mixed density, and the twenty-hour urine metanephrine estimations were markedly elevated. A diagnosis of pheochromocytoma was subsequently confirmed.

Treatment:

The patient was commenced on Prazocin 0.5 mg p.o t.d.s, Atenolol 100 mg b.i.d, and Nifedipine 20 mg b.i.d. The blood pressure was maintained at 120/80 mmHg. She subsequently had surgery for excision of the tumor using a transperitoneal approach. There was a transient episode of intraoperative hypotension for which she was commenced on dopamine infusion. Anti-hypertensive medications were discontinued, and she was discharged home on the ninth post-operative day with a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg.

Postoperative Phase:

She is being seen in the surgical out-patient clinic and has remained free of symptoms. The histopathology report of the two resected specimens revealed a crescent-shaped normal intact adrenal gland grossly and on histology. The mass measured 8 × 6 × 4.5 cm in size and weighed 100 gm. The surface was lobulated with sparsely attached adipose tissue on its intact capsular surface. Cut surface revealed a bilobulated yellowish-brown surface. The histology showed a rim of atrophic cortical adrenal tissue and deep to this rim were nests and sheets of small to intermediately sized cells with moderate pleomorphic nuclei with occasional bizarre ones and with moderate amphophilic to eosinophilic cytoplasm. The cells were arranged around delicate vasculature. The chief cells in the tumor were strongly positive for Neuron-Specific Enolase, synaptophysin, and Chromogranin A. The surrounding sustentacular network of cells stained positively for the S-100 protein. These findings are suggestive of a pheochromocytoma in an accessory adrenal gland.

Discharge Summary:

Patient 1 (II-2, a), a 15-year-old boy, was admitted to our hospital due to slowly progressive weakness of his lower limbs. He had a history of frequent falls since infancy, with a fracture of his ankle at 10 years old, resulting in an awkward gait. Examination revealed muscle wasting of both distal leg and foot muscles, with inverted champagne bottle appearance of bilateral legs and foot drop. He walked with a high stepping gait. 

Examination of his upper limbs showed mild thenar and hypothenar muscle wasting with normal power. The peripheral reflexes and sensation were normal. He had no facial weakness, ptosis, or respiratory problem. Nerve conduction studies (NCS) showed absent compound muscle action potential upon supra-maximal stimulation of both peroneal and tibial nerves. The nerve conduction velocities of the median and ulnar nerves and the sensory nerve action potential of both sural nerves were normal. The result was suggestive of axonal degenerative motor neuropathy.

Patient 1's parents are cousins, and there is a history of consanguineous marriage in the last three generations of the family. Upon inquiry, the 17-year-old sister of Patient 1 was noted to have similar symptoms but remained ambulatory. Examination revealed muscle wasting of distal lower limb muscles and bilateral foot drop. She also walked with a high stepping gait. Nerve conduction studies also revealed similar findings to that in Patient 1.

Based on the observations and results, Patient 1 and Patient 1's sister (II-1, b) were diagnosed with axonal degenerative motor neuropathy. Further genetic testing was recommended due to the consanguineous marriage in the family.

Patient 1 and Patient 1's sister were discharged with instructions to continue with current treatments and were advised to follow up with their primary care physician and genetics specialist.

Patient Information:
The patient is a 61-year-old male who was admitted to our hospital due to asthenia, diffuse bone pain, fever, and cutaneous hemorrhagic diathesis.

Medical History:
The patient had a medical history of chronic bronchitis, obesity, alcohol abuse, and smoking.

Hospital Course:
Upon admittance, laboratory tests revealed mild anemia, leukocytosis, and severe thrombocytopenia. Further bone marrow analysis confirmed an atypical granular lymphoblastic infiltration and a B-cell lymphoid BC of CML diagnosis was made. The patient was treated with imatinib but had to discontinue due to intolerance. Dasatinib was started, and hematological response was observed. However, three months later, a relapse of BC-CML was seen. Ponatinib was then initiated, and chemotherapy was added as per ELN recommendations 2013. After six months of treatment, the patient achieved deep molecular response. Notably, in about a year from ponatinib initiation, the patient experienced BC-CML relapse. A new course of vincristine and prednisone was started, but the patient showed new neurological symptoms, prompting further testing. A cerebrospinal fluid evaluation showed no leukemic cells, but a CT scan revealed an ischemic stroke. Anticoagulant therapy was added, along with statins and antihypertensive drugs. Active treatments with ponatinib and vincristine were continued, and normalization of blood cell count was achieved. However, the patient passed away due to septic shock caused by an unresponsive pulmonary infection.

Summary:
This hospital course summary involves a 61-year-old male diagnosed with B-cell lymphoid BC of CML, treated with different drugs such as imatinib, dasatinib, and ponatinib. The patient's condition deteriorated, and he passed away due to septic shock from a pulmonary infection.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 41-year-old nulligravida Japanese woman who was referred to Kawakita General Hospital due to the presence of a large cervical mass. The patient had undergone myomectomy 13 years ago for the treatment of multiple uterine fibroids. Penetration beyond the endocervical gland had occurred during resection, and the anterior endocervical canal had been opened during the surgery. The patient had been following up at another hospital where cancer screening was performed once a year. Eight years after the original surgery, she had undergone pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which did not detect any abnormal masses in the uterine body or cervix. Twelve years after the original surgery, she underwent transvaginal ultrasonography, and no abnormal masses were detected. However, a pelvic examination performed in the current hospitalization indicated marked enlargement of the cervix, which was suspected to be a cervical malignancy. 

Diagnostic Assessment:

The patient underwent transvaginal ultrasonography, which indicated that the mass contained multilocular, hypoechoic lesions, with heterogeneous internal echogenicity. Furthermore, MRI confirmed the presence of a multilocular, irregularly shaped cystic mass (overall diameter, >15 cm) in the upper anterior cervix. Computed tomography (CT) did not show any evidence of enlarged lymph nodes, ascites, or a distant tumor. Blood tests did not show elevated levels of inflammation or tumor markers. The patient’s white blood cell count was 6,000/mL, and C-reactive protein level was <0.3 mg/dL. Levels of CA125, CA19-9, and squamous cell carcinoma antigen (SCC) were 32.4 U/mL, 6.4 U/mL, and 1.4 U/mL, respectively. Results from cytological examination of both the cervix and endometrium were negative for cancer. 

Treatment:

A total abdominal hysterectomy was performed, and dense adhesions were observed in the pelvis, particularly around the cervical mass. Moreover, the cervix was markedly enlarged, given the mass in the anterior wall. However, no additional abscesses or ascites were detected in the abdomen. The cystic mass originated from the upper anterior cervix, which was one of the sites involved in the original myomectomy. The mass consisted of 2 components, one containing an abscess within the soft solid tissue, and another that was filled with old blood (similar to an endometrial cyst). Following culture of the abscess tissue, Escherichia coli was identified as the causative bacteria. Microscopic examination revealed the coexistence of endometriosis, and an abscess was confirmed within the cyst, although malignant cells were not identified. An additional pathological review was performed at the University of Tokyo, which confirmed the absence of atypical or malignant cells. 

Diagnosis:

The patient's cervical mass was diagnosed as a pyogenic cyst, with endometriosis, which most likely occurred at the site of the uterine scar. 

Disposition:

The patient's care at Kawakita General Hospital has been successfully completed, and the patient has been discharged. The patient has been informed of their diagnosis and treatment plan and advised to schedule follow-up appointments with their primary care physician.

Open removal of 27 loose bodies from the anterior gutter was performed, with the larger bodies sent for analysis. The procedure was successful having obtained complete clearance with no intraoperative complications. The patient was discharged home on the same day with simple analgesia. A postoperative review at two weeks showed no interval complications, good functional outcome, and benign histology.

A repeat x-ray of the affected joint showed the reaccumulation of loose bodies, however to a much lesser extent. The management options were discussed, and the patient agreed to opt for a trial of conservative management, until the symptoms worsen. One year later, at the time of writing, his condition is clinically stable.

Hospital Course Summary:

This summary details the hospital course of a 68-year-old male, who presented to the emergency department with progressive dyspnea and weakness over the past two weeks. He had a past medical history significant for multiple comorbidities including end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, hypertension, high cholesterol, diabetes mellitus type 2, cirrhosis, hepatitis C, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and benign prostate hyperplasia.

Initial blood tests showed no abnormalities in renal function, electrolytes, or complete blood count. The patient had a normal AST and ALT, low albumin levels, high total bilirubin levels, and prolonged prothrombin time. Further investigations showed negative HBV surface antigen and HIV 1&2 antibodies. A chest X-ray revealed a large pleural effusion on the left side, which was confirmed by diagnostic thoracentesis to be an exudative pleural fluid per Light's criteria.

During physical examination, the patient also had abdominal pain, and ascites was noted. Diagnostic paracentesis revealed normal cell counts and negative culture. Repeat paracentesis ruled out malignancy or tuberculosis as the cause of ascites. Abdominal computed tomography was performed, and showed peritoneal carcinomatosis with multiple subcentimeter lesions in the liver, spleen, and adrenal glands. An omental biopsy obtained by interventional radiology showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, with rare acid-fast bacilli (AFB). A repeat biopsy was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, and the patient was immediately started on treatment with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

The patient's AFB sputum cultures have remained negative. He was informed that his mycobacterial isolate was sent to the local Department of Health laboratory to confirm antimicrobial susceptibility. His systemic symptoms improved days after starting treatment.

The patient's discharge plan is to continue treatment with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol as an outpatient. He will be followed up with outpatient infectious disease clinic, gastroenterology, hemodialysis, and pulmonary medicine specialists to monitor and manage his comorbidities. He was also advised to follow diet and lifestyle modifications to optimize his health. The patient was provided with all the necessary information and prescriptions for his follow-up appointments, medications, and referrals.

The patient was admitted to the hospital presenting with progressive muscle weakness, difficulty chewing, and an inability to lift his head. He achieved incomplete remission with treatment with pyridostigmine, which he increased to 60 mg five times a day. However, his symptoms worsened over a year ago. The patient received a pubis fracture operation which required general anesthesia wherein he had difficulty breathing and was accompanied by sinus tachycardia. After the anti-infection and symptomatic treatment, he was transferred to the respiratory intensive care unit, where trachea cannula was removed and the mechanical ventilator assistance was ended. He remained functionally independent with pyridostigmine treatment.

Medical History:

The patient had no known medical history of any muscle disorders and no parental consanguinity. The patient had normal hematological and biochemical investigations, normal immunological tests, no obvious abnormalities in heart, abdomen, and urinary tract ultrasound. However, a thoracolumbar scoliosis was observed on chest computed tomography (CT) scans.

Physical Examination:

The patient had a body mass index (BMI) of 20.3 kg/m2 and was unable to drum the cheeks. The patient had fatigable muscle weakness in his proximal upper extremity, distal upper extremity, proximal lower extremity, and distal lower extremity muscles. The patient had femoral hyperreflexia, atrophied facial muscles and slightly hypertrophied bilateral gastrocnemius muscles. The remainder of the physical examination was noted to be normal.

Diagnostic Test Results:

Repetitive nerve stimulation at low rates showed a marked decrement (>30%) in the accessory nerve (normal at a high rate). His electromyography showed a myogenic lesion in the right dorsal interosseous muscle. Exome sequencing showed 2 novel variant mutations [c.59G>A (exon2) and c.423G>C (exon5), Fig. A–C], which were compound heterozygous variants, on the CHRND gene according to a phenotype–genotype correlation. The anti-AChR and skeletal muscle receptor tyrosine kinase (MUSK) antibodies were negative in the serum. No occurrences of mtDNA mutations or copy number variations (CNVs) were observed in the mitochondrial DNA sequencing and CNS analyses.

Treatment:

The patient was functionally independent with pyridostigmine treatment. No further treatment was given.

Follow-up:

The patient's discharge was advised. Follow-up evaluations were recommended.

The patient presented with an incidentally detected prevesical mass. They underwent a complete excision with bladder sparing procedure that was successful. Discharge Summary:

Patient: 84-year-old man admitted with severe SARS-CoV-2 infected pneumonia.

Hospital course summary:

The patient presented to the fever clinic with symptoms of fever, cough, chest discomfort, and fatigue. He had a history of hypertension that was effectively controlled with medication, and surgery for disc herniation. The patient was a nonsmoker with no other chronic underlying diseases. After 4 days of antibiotic treatment, the fever resolved but the cough and chest discomfort worsened.

The patient was confirmed with the diagnosis of COVID-19 pneumonia and transferred to Wuhan Union Hospital. On admission, he was afebrile, with no tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension, or hypoxia. Initial laboratory investigations revealed elevated leukocytes and CRP, but normal hemoglobin, platelet count, and liver/renal function.

Despite treatment with antiviral therapy and other interventions, the patient's respiratory distress worsened on hospital day 5. He had intermittent fevers and rales in both lung areas. Laboratory results showed increased leukocyte, PCT, and CRP levels. Enhanced chest CT revealed multiple patchy ground-glass opacities and consolidations in both lungs.

The patient was treated with high flow nasal oxygen therapy, steroids, antibiotics, IVIG, and Chinese herbs. He also received medication to prevent stress-induced gastrointestinal bleeding. The patient's respiratory symptoms gradually improved and his oxygen saturation remained stable.

However, on hospital day 17, the patient experienced dark red stools. Laboratory results showed normocytic anemia. Repeat rRT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative in respiratory specimens but positive in stool specimens. The cause of GIB was not determined by imaging studies. Fasting and parenteral nutrition formulations were implemented. Intravenous resuscitation was started, and medication was administered to achieve hemostasis. Despite these measures, the patient's hematochezia was uncontrolled, and he developed altered mental status, tachycardia and hypotension. Massive transfusions were administered, but the patient's hemoglobin level continued to decline.

On hospital day 21, the patient suffered a cardiac arrest and expired before interventional radiology and endoscopy were available. The family refused to autopsy.

Final diagnosis: Severe SARS-CoV-2 infected pneumonia with complicated gastrointestinal bleeding and subsequent cardiac arrest.

Recommendations: No further recommendations given due to patient's death.
