DISCHARGE SUMMARY

PATIENT INFORMATION:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 68
Sex: Male
Admission date: [REDACTED]
Discharge date: [REDACTED]
Admission diagnosis: Bone pain
Discharge diagnosis: N/A

HOSPITAL COURSE:

[REDACTED] was admitted to our hospital with strong pain in his left hip. His medical history indicated that he had been experiencing left hip pain and numbness of the left lower extremity for several years, which had gradually become more intense over the past month. Anteroposterior hip radiograph revealed bone destruction in the greater trochanter area, and decreased bone density in the head and neck of the femur. Further investigations indicated Paget’s disease of bone. Bisphosphonate treatment was initiated, and the patient was receiving pamidronic acid at 90 mg every three months.

After two years of treatment, the patient was diagnosed with prostate adenocarcinoma, and treatment with bisphosphonates was stopped periodically. Radical surgical resection of the prostate gland was performed, and pamidronic acid at 90 mg every 3 months was again initiated. Eight months after the diagnosis of prostate cancer, a left hip arthroplasty was required due to a large area of bone destruction in the femur. Antiresorptive therapy was continued for the next 9 months until the outpatient clinic, where the patient was attending, closed.

The patient did not report to any other clinic for the next eight months. Eight months later, he was admitted to our department with strong pain in the left hip. Bone scintigraphy and CT scan of the left hip revealed findings which might be consistent with loosening of hip endoprosthesis. Preoperative treatment with bisphosphonates (once again pamidronic acid at 90 mg) was indicated, and the patient was referred to the orthopedics department, where replacement of hip arthroplasty was performed. Due to presence of bone pain the patient received another two doses of pamidronic acid at 90 mg every three months, which strongly relieved symptoms. At the moment the patient does not experience bone pain or any other symptoms of PDB and the serum level of alkaline phosphatase is normal. He is being followed in the outpatient clinic of our department, and possible re-initiation of antiresorptive therapy is dependent on presence of symptoms of the disease and the level of alkaline phosphatase.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

The patient has been advised to routinely exercise and maintain a healthy diet to promote proper bone health and overall well-being. He has been instructed to follow up with the outpatient clinic of our department for any further evaluation or treatment, as needed.

Discharge Summary

Admission Date: [Insert Date]               Discharge Date: [Insert Date]

Patient Name: [Insert Name]                  MR#: [Insert MR Number]

Reason for Hospitalization:

The patient was admitted to our hospital with a severe headache that lasted for 8 hours. Brain computed tomography (CT) scan showed that the patient had Fisher grade 2 and Hunt-Hess grade 2 subarachnoid hemorrhage. Cerebral angiography was performed immediately, which showed a bilobed 1.6 × 3.5 mm sized wide-neck aneurysm at left PcomA.

Hospital Course:

The patient was treated with stent-assisted coil embolization by request of the patient, as the patient was fearing surgical invasiveness. The procedure was performed under general anesthesia. A loading dose of clopidogrel (300 mg) was administered via Levin tube and a bolus of 1,000 IU of heparin was administered after femoral arterial puncture and was added by each hour. Procedural steps included the placement of two guiding systems at the level of the V2 segment of left vertebral artery (VA) and ascending cervical segment of left ICA by bilateral femoral puncture. Placement of a stent delivery microcatheter into left M1 of middle cerebral artery (MCA) via ipsilateral P1 by retrograde approach. Access of another microcatheter for coil delivery to aneurysmal sac via ipsilateral ICA and deployment of self-expandable stent from M1 to P1. Coil packing was performed with four detachable coils with stent-jail technique. There was no contrast filling in aneurysmal sac or decrease of blood flow from parent artery after coiling. 

Outcome:

The follow-up at 18 months revealed that the aneurysmal sac was completely occluded in the cerebral angiography. 

Summary:

The patient was admitted to our hospital with a severe headache that was diagnosed as subarachnoid hemorrhage. The patient had stent-assisted coil embolization and was discharged on [Insert Discharge Date]. Follow-up at 18 months revealed complete closure of the aneurysmal sac. Further outpatient treatment and follow-up visits with primary care physician and neurologist are recommended.

HOSPITAL COURSE:

A 32-year-old man presented with a bony, tender, six cm large mass of the manubrium that had shown progressive growth toward the suprasternal notch over the previous ten months. The patient's pain was increased by palpation and elevation of his arms. Plain radiographs showed an expansile osteolytic lesion of the sternum. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated focal cortical bone destruction, soft tissue extension and subchondral extension in relation to the sternoclavicular joints.

The patient underwent resection of the manubrium with wide margins and post-resection reconstruction with GORE® DUALMESH® PLUS Biomaterial mesh fixed with polyester separated stitches. Both the clavicles and the first ribs were fixed to the mesh. Thoracic inspection showed no mediastinal or lung nodules. Disarticulation of the body-manubrium joint was uneventful. A bilateral pectoralis major flap covered the mesh and allowed skin closure.

The patient was then discharged with instructions for follow-up appointments with the physician. 

TECHNICAL SUMMARY:

Histological analysis of the resected specimen revealed the presence of multinucleated giant cells, mononucleated small cells, and spindle cells. Occasionally, more than 100 nuclei could be perceived in the giant cells, a typical characteristic of giant cell tumor (GCT). The tumor growth had induced extensive bone erosion and focally infiltrated adjacent soft tissues. Blood-filled dilated spaces were seen, suggesting an association with an aneurysmal bone cyst. Less than one typical mitotic figure was seen per ten high power fields. Atypical mitosis, vascular invasion, and tumor necrosis were not detected.

Cytogenetic analysis was performed on 30 metaphases and showed a complex complement characterized by the presence of numerous marker chromosomes.

FOLLOW-UP INSTRUCTIONS:

The patient was instructed to follow-up regularly with his physician for monitoring and check-up.

A shave excision of the tumour was undertaken with particular care in avoiding embolization and ensuring that no remnants from fragmentation of the tumour were left behind both locally on the cusp and in the vicinity of ascending aorta and left ventricle. Aortic valve competence was confirmed intraoperatively with transesophageal echocardiographic approach before the aortotomy was closed.

Disposition and follow-up:
The patient made an uneventful recovery and remained free of symptoms throughout the hospital stay. No mass was detected by echocardiography in the patient during the 6-month follow-up period. The patient was discharged from the hospital with instructions for follow-up with his primary healthcare provider as needed.

HOSPITAL COURSE:

Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

HISTORY OF PRESENTING COMPLAINT:
The patient presented to the emergency department with a history of bright red blood per rectum followed by melena and hematemesis.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
The patient had a past medical history of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, and myocardial infarction.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
On initial laboratory evaluation, the patient had a white cell count of 14.1 K/CMM and a hemoglobin level of 9.7 g/dL. The patient underwent esophogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), which showed an ulcerated lesion with an overlying blood clot in the pre-pyloric antrum, and bleeding from the lesion was controlled with endoscopic clips. Computed tomography (CT) demonstrated findings consistent with severe acute cholecystitis with a large gallstone exerting mass effect on the gastric pylorus. The patient was placed on broad-spectrum antibiotics. Subsequent repeat EGD with biopsies showed severe chronic gastritis and ulcerative changes without signs of malignancy or Helicobacter pylori infection. An upper gastrointestinal series (barium swallow study) was completed, demonstrating a 6.1 cm×4.1 cm gallstone in the stomach with contrast extravasation into the gallbladder, suggestive of a cholecystogastric fistula resulting in gastric outlet obstruction.

SURGICAL HISTORY:
The patient underwent laparoscopy converted to open cholecystectomy with partial gastrectomy, Billroth II gastrojejunostomy, and intraoperative cholangiogram. Intraoperative findings confirmed a large gallstone in the stomach causing gastric outlet obstruction secondary to a cholecystogastric fistula.

POSTOPERATIVE COURSE:
Postoperatively, the patient had delayed return of gastric function, requiring prolonged nasogastric tube as well as endoscopy. The patient began tolerating oral feeds on postoperative day 16 and was discharged shortly thereafter.

- Severe chronic gastritis and ulcerative changes
- Cholecystogastric fistula resulting in gastric outlet obstruction

- Follow-up with primary care physician within two weeks of discharge

- Follow-up with surgeon as indicated for postoperative care
- Discharge medications: Please refer to medication list provided at the time of discharge.

Stable.

- Avoid strenuous activity for one week post-discharge.

- Follow-up with your healthcare provider as directed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient is a 64-year-old woman who underwent heart transplantation in 2012 and had a complicated post-transplantation course with recurrent antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) and new donor-specific antibodies (DSA) in 2014. She developed mild cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) in 2015. She developed severe fatigue and other related symptoms like loose stools, nausea, and emesis one month before the admission. She reported symptoms of fatigue again after a month of the first episode, for which she was admitted and was evaluated for unexplained anemia. Iron storage studies and renal function testing ruled out iron-deficiency anemia and other related disorders. She also tested negative for CMV and EBV and negative in stool for a multiplex gastrointestinal panel (FilmArray™ Gastrointestinal panel) and Clostridium difficile. She had a normal thyroid function test and a negative DSA. Blood cultures were negative for growth at 5-days of incubation. Her endomyocardial biopsy showed evidence of AMR (pAMR2) without hemodynamic compromise. Quantitative PCR detected Parvovirus B19 in the peripheral blood at >100 000 000 (>one-hundred million) copies/mL. Treatment with IVIG was started, in addition to plasmapheresis for AMR. After therapy, she experienced significant improvement of her fatigue and hemoglobin levels. At her last follow-up in May 2018, she reported a considerable improvement in her daily activities, such as tolerating short periods of exercise (walking) without chest pain or episodes of palpitation. Follow-up testing has revealed normal red blood cell counts and hemoglobin concentration with undetectable B19V by PCR. 

Recommendations:
1. Follow up with the Transplant Infectious Diseases consultant.
2. Close monitoring of the patient for any further signs and symptoms of AMR and DSA.
3. Review of medications and immunosuppression protocol.
4. Provide patient education regarding their current health status, medications, and the importance of regular follow-up appointments.

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with exertion-induced myalgia and progressive generalized muscle hypertrophy. Generalized body aches and cramps occurred at the peak of muscle aches. The patient did not present symptoms of myotonia. The patient had a history of muscle hypertrophy and hoarseness of voice from early childhood along with impaired hearing. Additionally, the patient had a history of mild dullness for mental activities and slowness since childhood. Three months prior to visiting our Institution, the patient was referred to a surgical oncologist by a physician with a possible diagnosis of rhabdomyosarcoma of the calves and he underwent a gastrocnemius muscle biopsy which showed non-specific changes.

Physical Exam:

Examination revealed sparse scalp, facial and body hair, yellow tinge on face, dry skin, and cold extremities. Voice was hoarse. He had normal mental functions. Facial and bulbar muscles were normal. Thyroid gland was diffusely enlarged. He had severe generalized muscle hypertrophy and huge calves. Tone was normal. He had minimal difficulty in rising from the floor and muscle power was otherwise normal. Deep tendon reflexes were sluggish. ECG showed low QRS voltage and bradycardia. 2D echocardiogram revealed left ventricular global hypokinesia, reduced left ventricle function, trivial mitral regurgitation (pulmonary artery systolic pressure 34 mm Hg), and moderate pericardial effusion (anterior-1.0 cm, posterior-1.7 cm, and lateral-1.4 cm). EMG revealed myopathic process with short duration small polyphasic motor unit potentials. No pseudomyotonic discharges were observed. Nerve conductions were normal. Audiometry revealed bilateral conductive hearing loss, moderately severe on the right and mild to moderate on the left side. Muscle biopsy was not performed.

Impression and Plan:

The diagnosis of HS was considered. The patient received levothyroxine replacement at a dose of 1.6 μg/kg/day and at 2 months follow-up showed remarkable improvement in symptoms and significant reduction in the muscle hypertrophy. Thyroxine dose was increased and maintained at 100 μg/day. Hearing had improved significantly on follow-up. Repeat serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dl and creatine kinase was 142 U/L. At 6 months, he had no muscle symptoms. Special tests such as antithyroid peroxidase antibody or antithyroglobulin levels were not tested in either case due to monetary constraints. The patient was discharged with a stable condition.

Patient Information: 
Name: [REDACTED]

Gender: Male

Discharge date: [REDACTED]

Presenting Complaint:
The patient presented with traumatic brain injury after a cement block fell through his tent, striking him on the right side of his head.
 
Hospital Course:
After initial examination, the patient was found to have left hemiplegia, prominent scalp veins, a bulging fontanelle, irritability, and a depressed level of consciousness. Due to the patient's history of neurological deterioration and observed signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP), urgent surgical intervention was required since CT scanning was unavailable at the field hospital. Under general anesthesia, the patient underwent a typical trauma flap craniotomy/craniectomy procedure. Multiple burr holes were placed with a Hudson Brace, and then a Gigli saw was used to perform a craniectomy in three large pieces, roughly corresponding to the frontal bone, parietal bone, and squamous temporal bone. The surgical team achieved epidural hemostasis using bipolar cautery and Surgicel (Ethicon, Cincinnati, OH, USA). Evacuation of a small intraparenchymal hematoma and brain elevation out of the large craniectomy defect resulted in significant brain relaxation. The surgical team ensured hemostasis and laid stellate dural flaps on the brain surface, covering the entire defect with a thin layer of Fibrillar hemostatic agent (Ethicon). The three bone flaps were then placed on the surface of the dura/fibrillar cushion in approximate anatomic position. The surgical team reapproximated the scalp under mild tension in a standard fashion. The patient remained intubated after surgery, but was extubated on postoperative day 1. He was transferred out of the pediatric ICU after several days.

None reported.

Due to the conditions in Haiti, long-term clinical or radiographic follow-up was not available at the time of discharge. During hospitalisation, electrocardiograms during chest pain showed repolarisation abnormalities indicative of myocardial ischaemia.
Diagnostic coronary angiography was performed within 24 h, revealing a markedly large left anterior descending artery (LAD), together with a non-dominant right coronary artery. Minor wall abnormalities in both the right and the left coronary artery were found, with no signs of significant coronary stenosis. After removing the arterial sheath, haemostasis was accomplished by manual compression of the brachial artery, followed by a pressure bandage for 4 h.
Thirty minutes after removal of the arterial sheath, the lower right arm turned white and became cold and painful, due to arterial occlusion. The pressure bandage was carefully removed. Shortly thereafter, she again experienced chest pain. Intravenous nitroglycerin was immediately administered resolving her symptoms, and she was treated with a calcium antagonist accordingly. She was free of symptoms during outpatient follow-up.

Reason for Admission: Extraoral swelling on left cheek

Hospital Course:
The patient was an 11-year-old boy who presented with a nonhealing extraoral swelling on his left cheek for 6 months, which periodically discharged pus and gradually grew larger. The patient underwent dermatological surgery before and had gone through multiple regimens of antibiotic therapy, but the swelling persisted. On examination, a reddish abscess was observed on the left cheek with an unobvious sinus tract 2 cm above the inferior border of the mandible. The vestibular mucous membrane corresponded to the apex of the root, and the periodontal tissue was normal without an intraoral sinus. A radiopaque mass inside the crown and pulp chamber of tooth 36 was detected, along with an irregular periapical radiolucent but non-noticeable area associated with the distal root apex. Based on the findings, the patient was diagnosed with an odontogenic subcutaneous abscess with a cutaneous fistula on the left cheek secondary to chronic periradicular periodontitis of tooth 36.

The patient underwent root canal treatment (RCT) after abscess incision drainage and returned with a reduced abscess after 5 days. During the second visit, RCT was performed, and the root canals of tooth 36 were cleaned and shaped under irrigation. The canals were dressed with medicaments, and the OCST was closed at the third visit after 2 weeks. The root canals were obturated after debridement of the lesion at a subsequent visit, following which the abscesses became flatter. Ultimately, the patient underwent chronic granuloma debridement of the lesion under Scandonest local anesthesia, which healed in two weeks.

Outcome:
After six months, the lesion healed completely. The defect on the cheek had eventually become no different from the surrounding tissue, leaving only a slightly hyperpigmented region of the skin. Postoperative radiography demonstrated satisfactory recovery, with the periapical lesion having disappeared.

Odontogenic subcutaneous abscess with a cutaneous fistula on the left cheek secondary to chronic periradicular periodontitis of tooth 36.

Course of Treatment:
The patient underwent RCT. In the first visit, abscess incision drainage was performed, and the root canals were cleaned and shaped under irrigation. In the second and third visits, the canals were dressed with medicaments and closed after obturation. In further visits, chronic granuloma debridement of the lesion under Scandonest local anesthesia was performed.

The patient's condition had improved significantly, with complete healing of the abscess and disappearance of the periapical lesion on radiography. The patient had no further complaints when discharged.

The patient is advised to attend regular dental check-ups and maintain proper oral hygiene. In case of any recurrence of abscess or discomfort, the patient is advised to seek immediate medical attention.

Discharge Summary:

Admitting Diagnosis: Suspected Pyometra.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 74-year-old obese woman with a history of diabetes and hypertension, was admitted to our gynecology clinic for outpatient hysteroscopy. The procedure revealed a thickened white endometrium and pyometra. Three days later, the patient presented to the accident and emergency department with symptoms of profuse foul-smelling vaginal discharge, and bleeding per rectum, suggestive of uterine sepsis. Intravenous antibiotics were started, and the patient was monitored. A pipelle endometrial sample was taken and sent for histology. 

Diagnostic Testing:
The pipelle biopsy revealed pus cells only, and vaginal swabs showed no pathogens. Her CEA level was within normal range, and CA-125 was slightly raised at 73. Given the clinical picture, an MRI scan was performed, revealing pyometra but no apparent tumor. 

Treatment:
A repeat hysteroscopy was done under general anaesthetic, and drainage of the pyometra was performed. About 50ml of pus was drained, and an endometrial biopsy was taken. Pus culture showed mixed anaerobic growth, and the repeat endometrial biopsy revealed acute on chronic endometritis. The patient improved clinically with intravenous antibiotics and was discharged home. 

Follow-up:
The patient presented to the accident and emergency department ten days later complaining of abdominal pain, diarrhea, and vomiting, with bleeding per rectum. A contrast CT scan of the abdomen revealed no significant findings. A sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy revealed diverticular disease with prominent thickened folds. Conservative treatment was initiated, and the patient improved. The patient presented to the surgical team three months later with acute abdominal pain. A CT scan revealed an inflamed thick-walled sigmoid colon that tracked down to the uterus, a colouterine fistula. The decision was made to perform a laparotomy, and a Hartmann's operation with total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. The patient made a slow but complete recovery.

Outcome:
At six months follow-up, the patient reported being asymptomatic. The patient deceased later due to an unrelated cause.

The patient, a 44-year-old non-smoking African American female with a history of stage 3 squamous cell lung cancer, was transferred to our hospital due to acute hypoxic respiratory failure. She had recurrent pleural effusions, new onset insulin-dependent diabetes, hypothyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency attributed to durvalumab therapy. Diagnosed with PAH associated with SLE/Sjogren's syndrome overlap induced by PD-L1 inhibitor therapy, she was treated with high-flow oxygen, dobutamine, norepinephrine, furosemide, intravenous treprostinil, and sildenafil. Unfortunately, her condition worsened and she developed refractory RV failure with cardiogenic shock. Ultimately, support was withdrawn. 

History and Examination:
Two years prior, the patient was diagnosed with squamous cell lung cancer and received multiple chemotherapies. She had also been started on durvalumab therapy but developed new onset insulin-dependent diabetes, hypothyroidism, and adrenal insufficiency, which were attributed to autoimmunity induced by durvalumab. Two months before being transferred to our hospital, she presented with dyspnea, anasarca, bilateral exudative pleural effusions, and a pericardial effusion. 

Upon presentation at our hospital, she was severely volume overloaded and hypoxemic. Venous lactate level was 3.9 mmol/L, and B-type natriuretic peptide level was 628 pg/ml. Chest computed tomography showed mild diffuse ground-glass opacities, pulmonary artery enlargement, and bilateral pleural effusions. Right ventricular (RV) enlargement with reflux of contrast into the liver and a pericardial effusion were noted. After ruling out alternative diagnoses, serologic workup revealed positive ANA, positive SS-A, and positive rheumatoid factor, resulting in a diagnosis of SLE/Sjogren's syndrome overlap constellation. Treatment with prednisone and hydroxychloroquine was initiated. The patient was treated for severe PAH with RV failure and hypoxemic respiratory failure with high-flow oxygen, dobutamine, norepinephrine, furosemide, intravenous treprostinil, and sildenafil. Discharge Summary:

Patient: 7-year-old female

Admission Date: July 2007
Discharge Date: August 2007

Reason for admission: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) following a Hemiscorpius lepturus scorpion sting

Hospital Course:

Upon admission, the patient presented with bloody urine, vomiting, agitation, and restlessness. Examination revealed a tender and erythematic area with local edema on the right leg (4 × 6 cm) and a temperature of 39.6°C, pulse of 125/min, and blood pressure within normal limits (100/60 mmHg). Hematology revealed hemoglobin = 10.2 g/dL, white blood cells = 24,000/mm3, and platelets = 175,000/mm3. Urinary analysis showed 3+ hemoglobinuria and microscopic hematuria without proteinuria.

Polyvalent antivenom, cefazoline, and 20 meq/L sodium bicarbonate in dextrose water were administered. However, during the first week of hospitalization, the patient's SCr and BUN levels gradually rose to 8.6 and 100 mg/dL, respectively, while hemoglobin and platelet count dropped to 8 g/dL and 47,000/mm3, respectively. A blood smear showed fragmented erythrocytes and burr cells, and total serum protein level was 5.9 g/dL. Urinary analysis showed 3+ proteinuria, 3+ hemoglobinuria, and erythrocyte casts.

Bone marrow aspiration revealed essential hypercellular marrow with erythroid hyperplasia and a shift to the left in myelopoiesis. The diagnosis of HUS was made based on microangiopatic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure.

The patient received packed cell, fresh, frozen plasma and platelets several times. Hydrocortisone (10 mg/kg/day) was administered, and hemodialysis was performed. In the second week, platelets rose to normal levels (248,000/mm3) but the lactate dehydrogenase level dropped to 1430 IU/L. No renal biopsy was performed.

After one month, the patient was discharged with a SCr level of 6.7 mg/dl on an every-other-day dialysis program.

Final Diagnoses:

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) following a Hemiscorpius lepturus scorpion sting

Follow-up Care:

The patient was discharged on an every-other-day dialysis program. Close follow-up is recommended to monitor kidney function.

Instructions given to patient/family:

- Follow the dialysis schedule as prescribed by the healthcare provider.
- Keep all follow-up appointments with the healthcare provider.
- Monitor blood pressure and report any changes to the healthcare provider.
- Avoid future contact with scorpions or other venomous animals.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Hospital: [REDACTED]

Admission Date: [REDACTED]

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Discharge Diagnosis:
- Hypercalcemia-induced acute severe pancreatitis
- Acute renal cortical necrosis (RCN)
- Severe renal failure requiring dialysis
- Tuberculosis

Hospital Course:
The 22-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital with symptoms of pain abdomen and vomiting for 5 days. She had leukocytosis, distended abdomen, and diffuse abdominal tenderness. On presentation, she was oliguric and had an elevated serum creatinine level (2.6 mg%). Her USG and CT scan showed an enlarged pancreas with peripancreatic collections and omental inflammatory stranding. She was diagnosed with acute pancreatitis and managed conservatively with bowel rest and parenteral antibiotics. Due to oliguric renal failure, she was initiated on hemodialysis. Her serum calcium level was found to be high (12.8 mg/dl), and it was considered to be the cause of acute pancreatitis. Ultrasound of her neck was normal, and her PTH level was within normal limits. However, 1, 25-dihydroxyvitamin D level was found to be high (318 pmol/L). In the course of investigation, a lesion with high fluoro-deoxyglucose uptake was found in the patient's terminal ileum on PET-CT, and colposcopy showed mucosal nodularity with an ulcer and mild luminal narrowing in the terminal ileum. Lymph node biopsy showed necrosis with noncaseating granuloma containing Langhans giant cells, and biopsy from the ileal mucosa showed multiple discrete and large nonconfluent granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells; some of the granulomas showed central suppuration. GeneXpert test from the tissue for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex was positive, and QuantiFERON TB gold assay was positive. The patient was diagnosed with tuberculosis and was started on four-drug antituberculous therapy (ATT) at a modified dose. Two months after starting ATT, serum calcium level reduced to 9.1 mg/dl, and 1, 25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels reduced to 18.16 pmol/L. The patient had a patchy cortical necrosis with fibrinoid necrosis of the medium-sized arteries in the renal biopsy. Antinuclear antibody and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were negative, and serum complement level was normal. The patient's urine output improved, but she developed uremic symptoms and was found to be dialysis dependent at the end of 6 months.

Hospital Course Summary:
The 22-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital with pain abdomen and vomiting for 5 days. She was oliguric on presentation, and her serum creatinine was elevated. She was diagnosed with acute pancreatitis, managed conservatively, and initiated on hemodialysis due to oliguric renal failure. The patient's serum calcium level was found to be high, and 1, 25-dihydroxyvitamin D level was elevated. Further investigation led to a diagnosis of tuberculosis, and the patient was started on four-drug antituberculous therapy (ATT) at a modified dose. Two months after starting ATT, serum calcium and 1, 25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels reduced. However, the patient developed uremic symptoms and was found to be dialysis dependent at the end of 6 months due to renal failure requiring dialysis.

The onset of muscle activity was determined for each muscle during each repetition of the prone leg lift.

The patient responds well to daily weight-bearing exercise and range-of-motion exercises. Postoperatively, the patient’s course was uneventful. The patient was discharged from the hospital, and follow-up outpatient visits were recommended.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

HOSPITAL COURSE

The 3-year-old boy with a penile deformity was admitted to the pediatric surgery polyclinic for an evaluation. The patient had sustained a penile injury from a piece of shrapnel that lodged in his penis during an explosion in Syria.

Urogenital examination revealed a circumferential, band-like stricture in the penis. A 10-Fr Foley catheter was placed in the bladder, but urethral catheterization was difficult. The patient was treated with intravenous antibiotics for 2 weeks, and elective surgery was performed to repair the urethra.

During surgery, the glans penis was suspended and the skin was degloved. A full-thickness urethral rupture was present below the glans penis, and there was a 1.5 cm gap between the glans penis and the corpus cavernosum. Scar tissue was excised from the distal aspect of the corpus cavernosum and repaired with sutures. Using a 10-Fr catheter, retrograde catheterization was applied to the proximal urethra.

The proximal and distal ends of the urethra were prepared for anastomosis. Single full-layer sutures were applied over the Foley catheter for primary anastomosis. The patient was monitored for 20 days postoperatively while the Foley catheter and suprapubic catheter remained in place. The Foley catheter was removed, and the patient displayed normal urination with no complications.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS

Penile stricture due to traumatic injury, managed with urethral reconstruction.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS

1. Keep the Foley catheter in place for 5 days after discharge.
2. Handle the Foley catheter as instructed before you leave the hospital. 
3. Continue the antibiotic therapy as prescribed by the doctor.
4. Please make a follow-up appointment with your physician in 1 month. 
5. Any emergency situation during or after the recovery period, come into the nearest emergency department.
6. Avoid physical activities that may create too much pressure or cause damage to the penile area.
7. Abstain from sexual activity until your doctor advises it is safe to resume.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS

None specified. 

FOLLOW-UP CARE

The patient will follow up with his physician in 1 month after discharge.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: N/A
Discharge Date: N/A

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted to Changde Hospital with complaints of edema in his lower legs and foamy urine, which were eventually diagnosed as nephrotic syndrome. 

Hospital Course: 
The patient was treated with prednisone therapy for three months and then transferred to Second Xiangya Hospital for further investigation and treatment. Upon admission, bilateral lower extremity edema was still present. Laboratory studies showed persistent albuminuria, with an initial total 24-hour urinary protein loss of 9.6 g and a serum albumin level of 13.4 g/l. The creatinine clearance rate was 58 ml/min, with normal blood urea nitrogen levels, but grossly elevated serum cholesterol levels. The patient tested negative for antibodies against HIV. Renal biopsy showed membranous nephropathy and the patient was administered prednisone and tacrolimus. After three months of treatment, the 24-hour urinary protein loss was reduced to 4.8 g/day and the level of serum albumin rose to 20.2 g/l.

However, the patient developed a fever and started coughing up purulent sputum, and was subsequently diagnosed with pneumonia in Hanshou Hospital. He was treated with various combinations of penicillin, ceftriaxone, and itraconazole, but continued to experience increased fever. He was transferred again to Second Xiangya Hospital. After admission, the patient was found to have a body temperature of 39.2°C, with inspiratory moist rales audible in the right inferior lung. A 2-cm hard subcutaneous nodule was palpable at the right lower abdomen. The white blood cell count was 19.7×109/l with 85% neutrophils. Tests for antibodies against tuberculosis were negative, and no Mycobacterium tuberculosis was found in the sputum and hydrothorax. A chest computed tomography scan revealed a nodule in the right lower lung field with pleural effusion. 

After one week, the patient developed left hip pain, and magnetic resonance imaging revealed a brain abscess in the right temporal occipital junction, as well as a larger abscess in the left gluteal region. Pathogens isolated from sputum and pus from the subcutaneous abdomen were identified as Nocardia asteroides. Other pathogens, including bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi were not isolated. The patient was therefore diagnosed with nocardiosis. Antibodies against HIV were tested again and found to be positive.

Treatment was initiated with surgical drainage of the hip abscess and the oral administration of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. The patient was discharged after 50 days of hospitalization. The trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy was continued, and the patient remained in a satisfactory condition. The results from the CT and MIR scans showed that the size of the lung and brain abscesses decreased gradually after three months and disappeared completely after six months.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to our clinic with binocular diplopia for six months along with refractive changes over his right eye for one year. The patient had no known systemic medical illness or ocular diseases, but he experienced a limitation of upgaze and protrusion of his right eye, as well as downward and outward deviation. The CT scan revealed a giant osteoma occupying the right fronto-ethmoid sinus, pushing the optic nerve away, and partially extending to two-thirds of the depth of the medial orbital wall.

Postoperative pathology confirmed the diagnosis of osteoma.

The patient experienced upgaze restriction and slight enophthalmos during the first month after the operation, which resolved spontaneously after three months. A 19-year-old male patient presented to our clinic with binocular diplopia and refractive changes over his right eye. The patient is being discharged with a diagnosis of VWD.

The patient is currently in good condition.

The patient will be discharged with refills for her oral contraceptive pills and follow-up appointments for future replacement of the LNG-IUS. Hospital: University Hospitals Leuven

Reason for Admission: Acute laparotomy for small bowel obstruction resulting in an ischemic bowel and a 30 cm enterectomy

Treatment Provided: Medial and lateral fasciotomy of both lower legs, continuous venovenous hemofiltration and intermittent hemodialysis therapy, thyroid hormone substitution, disinfection with PVP-I, wound care

Hospital Course:
The 13-year-old male patient was hospitalized at the PICU of the University Hospitals Leuven after acute laparotomy for small bowel obstruction resulting in an ischemic bowel and a 30 cm enterectomy. Postoperatively, the patient suffered from severe septic shock with acute septic cardiomyopathy and multiple organ failure including liver failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Within hours, he developed a compartment syndrome of the lower extremities and concurrent rhabdomyolysis with a level of creatine kinase (CK) reaching to 250,000 U/L, requiring urgent medial and lateral fasciotomy of both lower legs on ICU day 1. Acute kidney injury (AKI) initially required continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) and, after 10 days, intermittent hemodialysis (IHD) therapy.

Fasciotomy wounds were initially marginally perfused with important edema of the lower legs and feet, necessitating postponing the closure of the fasciotomy wounds until after a month. In order to prevent infection in these high-risk wounds, the subcutaneous tissue and the surrounding skin was disinfected daily with antiseptic PVP-I solution at a concentration of 10%. Wound cultures remained sterile during the entire open wound treatment interval, and from ICU day 12 onward, daily wound care was skipped on several occasions allowing the patient some rest, given the good clinical wound evolution.

Septic shock, liver failure, and DIC resolved within a week, and the patient was weaned from the ventilator by day 14. Acute kidney injury however did not recover, and triglycerides were rising without apparent reason, contributing potentially to acute pancreatitis. Diagnostic workup revealed plasma TSH levels at day 23 that were highly increased, and levels of T4 and T3 were diminished, whereas reverse T3 was slightly increased. There was a high suspicion of hypothyroidism secondary to absorption of povidone iodine after 3 weeks of extensive wound care with PVP-I. Significant systemic iodine absorption was documented by very high levels of urinary iodine excretion. Disinfection with PVP-I was formally stopped at ICU day 23, and thyroid hormone suppletion was initiated. 

The fasciotomy wounds on the left side were closed on ICU day 30. The fasciotomy on the right leg could not be approximated because of excessive of traction and healed spontaneously after one month. Finally, at day 54, the patient could be discharged from the intensive care unit. 

Follow-up Plan:
The patient was evaluated 4 months later in outpatient pediatric clinic and was doing very well; kidney function and renal ultrasound were reassuring.

The patient presented to our emergency room with complaints of fever and mental deterioration. Physical examination revealed left costovertebral angle tenderness and thrombocytopenia, while the laboratory results showed an elevation of C-reactive protein. Upon admission, we performed serology tests and chest/abdomen CT scans to exclude various disorders.

We performed skin biopsies from the pigmented areas of the forehead and nose and found diagnostic findings of generalized argyria. We reviewed outside pathology slides obtained from the left thigh muscles and found unspecified myopathy, rather than inflammatory myopathy. We performed electromyography and nerve conduction studies and found mild motor dominant polyneuropathy in both upper and lower extremities. A heavy metal analysis of hair samples showed all levels within acceptable ranges and copper levels below normal.

Discharge Diagnosis:
1. Generalized argyria
2. Myopathy
3. Polyneuropathy

The patient was discharged after slowly tapering off of steroids. She will transfer to a rehabilitation institution.

HOSPITAL COURSE:

This 73-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital for surgery for spondylosis. He had end-stage renal disease due to diabetic nephropathy. Four days after admission, he developed fever, and pneumonia was suspected by computed tomography (CT) examination. Intravenous tazobactam-piperacillin was administered. After 7 days of thrice-daily administration of 2.25 g tazobactam-piperacillin, the antibiotic was changed to ciprofloxacin for suspected atypical pneumonia. After intravenous administration of 400 mg ciprofloxacin once daily for 7 days, he was found to be in a state of unconsciousness on the morning of a dialysis day.

MEDICAL HISTORY:

The patient had a medical history of end-stage renal disease due to diabetic nephropathy and atrial fibrillation.

DIAGNOSIS:

The patient was diagnosed with hypoglycemic encephalopathy after a head nonenhanced CT examination revealed no intracranial lesion. An endocrine test revealed that counter-regulatory hormones were elevated, but C-peptide and insulin levels were high and normal, respectively (C-peptide 3.68 ng/mL, insulin 8.01 μIU/mL), suggesting hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. Chest-abdominal CT examination did not reveal insulinoma.

TREATMENT:

The patient received glucose infusions and his blood glucose level normalized, although his consciousness did not improve.

CONDITION AT DISCHARGE:

The patient's consciousness did not improve, and he died 73 days after admission due to aspiration pneumonia.

The patient was admitted to the hospital with a delayed-onset postoperative endophthalmitis in the left eye.

Final Diagnosis:
Delayed-onset postoperative endophthalmitis caused by scedosporium apiospermum that led to enucleation followed by prosthesis.

Patients who have undergone enucleation need to be monitored for phantom pain, conjunctivitis, socket infection, and hygiene.

A 70-year-old female was admitted to the hospital for treatment of a right-sided thyroid tumor. Follow-up and Prognosis:
Subsequently, normal tissue from the deceased mother was also tested positive for the L790F mutation. Basal serum calcitonin was immeasurable and no biochemical signs of pheochromocytoma or primary hyperparathyroidism have been present after 1 year of follow-up. The prognosis is good.

Discharge Summary

This is a discharge summary for a 34-year-old male patient who presented with blunt abdominal trauma following a fall.

Hospital Course:

On presentation, the patient was hypotensive and exhibited depressed fracture of left frontoparietal skull bone, contusion with abrasion of left side of face, mild chest wall hematoma, and abdominal guarding. The patient underwent intubation and rapid sequence induction. Results from the focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) were positive. The patient also exhibited left subcutaneous emphysema with fractures of the left 6th, 7th, and 10th ribs. Chest tube was inserted and massive transfusion protocol was activated.

An exploratory laparotomy was then performed, revealing shattered spleen requiring splenectomy. Otherwise, formal exploration showed no other findings.

Postoperatively, the patient exhibited low hemoglobin and high white blood cell count, as well as high myoglobin and high sensitive troponin T. A CT scanning of the head revealed further findings of comminuted depressed fracture of left frontoparietal bone with minimal subdural hematoma, subarachnoid hemorrhage, tiny hemorrhagic contusions of left temporal area, and fracture of left zygomatic arch. Neck and chest CT scanning revealed further findings of evidence of C6 facet fracture and fractures of left 5–8 ribs anteriorly and left 6-7, 9–12 ribs posteriorly with left hemo- and pneumothorax and bilateral lung contusions.

The patient experienced some gastrointestinal issues after being transferred out of the trauma intensive care unit, with episodes of abdominal distention, vomiting, and a waxing and waning course of partial distention. The patient was returned to the TICU where further CT scans of the abdomen indicated intussusception at the distal ileum. The patient initially declined operative intervention, however ultimately agreed at a later time, leading to the successful removal of impacted fecal matter, multiple adhesions, and a resection of a small bowel loop when perforation was observed. The side-to-side anastomosis was fashioned using gastrointestinal anastomosis (GIA) linear cutting staplers. Oversewing of the anastomotic staple line with 3-0 Vicryl sutures was done. Omental defect was closed with 3-0 Vicryl sutures. Postoperative testing revealed unremarkable results, leading to the stable discharge of the patient.

Follow-up care instructions included complying with a scheduled postoperative check-up, with ongoing care from a dedicated medical professional to ensure a smooth and safe recovery.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 23-year-old primigravida of Indian origin

Admission Date: April 2015

Discharge Date: June 2015

Hospital: Community hospital

Medical History: Hypertension, currently on medication

Chief Complaints: Jaundice, upper abdominal pain, and decreased urine output

Upon admission, the patient complained of sudden onset moderate upper abdominal pain associated with vomiting. She also had decreased urine output and exhibited symptoms of hypoglycemia. There was a gradual improvement in her general status, normalization of aminotransferase activity and renal function. She was discharged in June 2015 with complete clinical and biochemical recovery.

Follow-up:

Two weeks later, the patient underwent a follow-up abdominal USG, which showed stable intrahepatic calcifications. The USG-guided biopsy ruled out any rare malignant cause and showed punctuated calcifications with a foamy residual cell infiltrate.

Based on the medical records and imaging results, the patient was diagnosed with acute liver failure. The etiology of the disease was attributed to intrahepatic calcifications predominant in the right lobe of the liver, which were most likely due to a parasitic infection. During her stay at the hospital, she received treatment in the ICU with dialysis and blood transfusions. Her liver function improved gradually, and she was discharged from the hospital with a complete recovery.

The X-rays of both legs/knees revealed an anterolateral dislocation of the proximal tibiofibular joint. The dislocation was treated with closed reduction under spinal anesthesia, and the joint was stable when tested. The patient was advised to avoid weight bearing for 2 weeks.

Follow-up:
At 6 months of follow-up, the patient reported playing football at the same level as before the injury.

Summary:
The patient presented with pain in the right leg after a fall during a football match. The subsequent clinical examination and X-rays revealed an anterolateral dislocation of the proximal tibiofibular joint, which was treated effectively with closed reduction. The patient was advised to avoid weightbearing for 2 weeks. At 6 months of follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic and resumed playing football at the same level as before the injury.
